Batches that were already cancelled stay cancelled=true; the next run retries them, SendGrid returns 400 on a second cancel, and that throw aborts the rest of the batch until the poisoned row ages out and the leading deleteMany removes it. findMany has no orderBy, so one too-late reminder can be first and block reminders that are still cancellable. The unscheduled-send query below still does not exclude cancelled=true or CANCELLED/REJECTED bookings, so any reminder row that cancellation failed to delete is scheduled and sent anyway.

No tests for the new reminder-cancellation behavior

This change replaces the SendGrid cancel-then-DELETE sequence and the awaited reminder deletes with a cancelled flag, a deferred cron cancel, and an immediateDelete mode, but adds no tests. Nothing covers the cron selecting cancelled rows and POSTing scheduled_sends, skipping DELETE /v3/user/scheduled_sends/{id} (which clears the cancel and lets the email send), a cancel inside the 15-minute cron gap or SendGrid's 10-minute cutoff, the 100-slot immediateDelete path, or cancel, reschedule, workflow delete, and paid-booking cancel actually stopping both email and SMS. Those are the production paths this PR is supposed to fix.

Paid cancellation returns before reminders are cancelled

If the booking is paid, handleCancelBooking refunds it, sets status to REJECTED, and returns at line 464. Workflow reminder cancellation is only reached at line 485, after that return. Paid cancellations therefore never set cancelled=true and never call Twilio or SendGrid. Already scheduled workflow emails and SMS for refunded bookings are still sent. The new cron cannot recover them, because it only cancels rows with cancelled=true, and this path never writes that flag. The booking is also REJECTED rather than CANCELLED, so a later status check for CANCELLED would miss it too.

Request-reschedule dropped the awaited reminder delete

requestReschedule marks the booking CANCELLED and then calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder from forEach without awaiting them. The previous code awaited prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany after starting the provider cancels. The email helper only persists cancelled=true inside that unawaited call, which is what the cron needs in order to stop SendGrid; the SMS helper cancels Twilio and deletes the row in the same unawaited call, and SMS has no cron fallback. If the mutation returns before those promises settle, reminders for the booking the user just asked to reschedule are still delivered, and the API has already reported success.

Reschedule cancel is not awaited and immediately consumes SendGrid cancel slots

On reschedule, handleNewBooking walks the original booking's workflowReminders with forEach and calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(id, referenceId, true) without awaiting. forEach does not return those promises, so the try/catch around it never sees async failures, and the handler can finish the response while the SendGrid calls are still in flight. Passing true takes immediateDelete, which POSTs a cancel for every reminder that already has a referenceId, including sends up to 72 hours away, and puts those entries back into SendGrid's 100-slot scheduled_sends queue — the cap this PR is trying to stay under. If that POST fails, the helper swallows the error and does not set cancelled, so the cron will not retry and the old booking's workflow email is still sent after the reschedule. Direct attendee reschedules only cancel reminders on this path.

Workflow and step saves can lose the cancellation record

Workflow deletion calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true) and deleteScheduledSMSReminder inside forEach, then immediately awaits workflow.deleteMany. Step removal does the same at line 521 and then deletes the WorkflowStep. Both deletes cascade to WorkflowReminder. The provider calls are not awaited, so the rows can disappear before SendGrid or Twilio cancel finishes. immediateDelete also does not set cancelled=true, and a failed or frozen provider call then has no row left for the cron to retry, so those messages are still sent. Because every scheduled reminder for the workflow is cancelled immediately, one delete can also fill SendGrid's 100 pending-cancellation slots until the original send times. The same mutation dropped awaited reminder deletes when an event type is removed (line 376) and when a step is edited (line 574): those used to await workflowReminder.deleteMany and now only start unawaited manager calls. If those calls do not finish, the old reminders stay scheduled while the mutation also creates new ones, so both the old and the new messages go out.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Failed app import throws out of booking and availability flows

getCalendar awaits appStore[calendarType] with no try/catch. A rejected dynamic import now throws, whereas a missing implementation previously returned null. CalendarManager.createEvent and updateEvent only catch errors from calendar.createEvent/updateEvent, not from getCalendar, so one broken app chunk fails the whole EventManager create/update instead of returning success: false for that credential. deleteEvent has the same gap. getCachedResults does Promise.all on every getCalendar call, so one rejected import fails busy-time lookup for every connected calendar. That can 500 availability, or, if an upstream caller treats the failure as no busy data, hide conflicts and allow double booking. Catch import failures in getCalendar and return null, which callers already handle as "calendar not implemented".

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reschedule cleanup is not awaited after getCalendar became async

After the booking is already updated to CANCELLED, calendar and video cleanup runs in bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...). forEach discards the promise returned by an async callback, so the await getCalendar and the subsequent calendar.deleteEvent / deleteMeeting are not part of Reschedule's completion. The try/catch around the forEach only catches synchronous throws, not rejections from those awaits, which become unhandled rejections. The function then sends the reschedule email and returns true. On a serverless runtime the invocation can finish or freeze before the external calls finish, and because the row is already cancelled this path will not retry. The original calendar event and video meeting can remain, so the slot stays busy and a live meeting is left for a cancelled booking. Await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...)) or use a for...of loop so both deletes are joined to the handler and failures are caught.

false_positives.candidate:
Eager import() promises load every app and can reject unhandled

appStore calls import() for every integration while the module is evaluating, instead of exposing lazy thunks such as () => import("./applecalendar"). The first import of @calcom/app-store therefore starts loading every calendar, video, CRM, and payment package even when the caller only needs one (for example deletePayment or a single getCalendar). That keeps the cold-start and memory cost of the old static barrel and adds a burst of parallel module loads. Each import() promise is also stored with no .catch(). If any app module rejects and that key is not awaited, the rejection is unhandled; Node's default unhandledRejection behavior throws and can exit the process, including for an app the current request never uses. A failed optional app should not be able to crash the server. Lazy-load on first access and attach rejection handling so an unused or broken app degrades instead of rejecting in the background.

Recurring cancel never joins per-calendar deletes to apiDeletes

When cancelling all remaining occurrences, calendar deletion is bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... const deletedEvent = await calendar?.deleteEvent(...); apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); }). forEach does not return those promises. The push happens only after deleteEvent has already settled, and it pushes the resolved value rather than the in-flight promise. The later await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) therefore does not wait for this work and cannot observe its failures. The handler still returns "Booking successfully cancelled." The non-recurring branch in the same function was converted to a for...of that pushes calendar.deleteEvent's promise before awaiting; this recurring branch was only given an inner await and still races the request lifetime. Recurring events can remain on connected calendars. Build an array of delete promises (per credential and per updated booking) and await them with the rest of apiDeletes.

WipeMyCal reschedule uses forEach(async) and drops cleanup

WipeMyCal reschedule marks the booking CANCELLED, then starts cleanup with bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) / deleteMeeting(...) }). Array.forEach does not await async callbacks, and the surrounding try/catch cannot see their rejections. The handler continues to sendRequestRescheduleEmail and returns true while Google/Outlook deletion and video deletion are still in flight (or not started, if the runtime suspends first). Failures are unhandled rejections rather than logged errors. A cancelled booking can leave the external event and meeting in place, blocking the time slot. Replace forEach with an awaited Promise.all(map(async ...)) or a for...of loop.

getCalendar promises are started and sometimes discarded

getCalendar is now async, but getCalendarCredentials still calls it synchronously inside flatMap, before the app.variant === "calendar" check. When the variant is not calendar (types ending in _calendar still enter this filter, including *_other_calendar apps), the returned promise is dropped. If that promise rejects — getCalendar awaits a dynamic import that can reject — nothing handles it, which is an unhandledRejection introduced by this change. When the promise is kept, the exported calendar field silently changed from a Calendar instance to Promise<Calendar | null> while getCalendarCredentials stayed synchronous. getConnectedCalendars was updated to await item.calendar, but any other caller that still invokes calendar.listCalendars() without awaiting will throw at runtime. Only call getCalendar when the result is retained, and attach a catch (or await it) on every promise that is started.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check rejects split schedules and ignores duration

The new working-hours gate uses workingHours.find and treats a match as "outside hours" (lines 139-150). The callback returns true when the slot's UTC weekday is in an entry and the slot start is outside that one range. find therefore succeeds if any same-day window does not contain the slot. A normal lunch-break schedule (two rows such as 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00 on the same weekdays) rejects every slot, because each slot misses at least one window. This runs for all fixed hosts, including 1:1 events, so those users see no bookable times. The end minute is also copied from the slot start (line 142 uses slotStartTime for both start and end) instead of the slot end, so event length is never compared to the window end and a round-robin slot taken from a longer host can run past the fixed host's hours. A weekday with no matching entry is not rejected at all, so a fixed host with no hours that day is treated as free when the slot came from someone else.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Override containment is inverted for multiple ranges

Date overrides are scanned with find (lines 106-130), and a truthy callback is treated as "slot is not within the override", which makes checkIfIsAvailable return false. The callback returns true when the slot is outside a single range (ends at or before that range's start, or starts after that range's end). Two override windows on the same day, which is how a break is stored, therefore disqualify every slot: each slot is outside at least one range, so the fixed host has no availability that day. A slot is also treated as inside a range unless it is completely before or completely after it, so a slot that only partially overlaps (starts before the window and ends inside it, or starts inside and ends after it) is accepted and can extend past the override. The all-day block on line 114 compares two separately constructed dayjs objects with ===, which is reference equality and never succeeds, so a zero-length override is not reliably treated as an all-day block.

false_positives.candidate:
Converted override minutes are shifted again for DST

Override bounds are converted to invitee-local minutes using utcOffset() of the override's own date (lines 212-223). buildSlots then runs every slot, including those override minutes, through getTime, which adds organizerDSTDiff - inviteeDSTDiff (lines 102-110). That term corrects working hours that were converted with today's offset rather than the booking date's offset. Override minutes are already based on the booking date, so the extra term moves them whenever today's DST offset differs from the booking day's and the organizer and invitee are not on the same DST schedule. Example: organizer America/New_York, attendee in UTC, today in July (EDT, utcOffset -240) and the booking in January (EST, utcOffset -300). organizerDSTDiff is 60 and inviteeDSTDiff is 0, so every override slot is shown one hour late. Asia/Kolkata and Asia/Dhaka have no DST, so the new test does not catch this.

Date-override hit returns available and skips busy times

checkIfIsAvailable returns true as soon as any date override is considered to cover the slot (the dateOverrideExist branch around line 133), before the busy-interval loop. Busy times from calendars and existing bookings are the only conflict filter applied to slots generated from working hours, and this function is that filter. It runs for every fixed host, which includes ordinary 1:1 and collective events (non-round-robin users are marked isFixed), and again for round-robin non-fixed hosts. On any day a host has a date override, slots during meetings are shown as free and can be double-booked.

Override day comparison mixes server-local and UTC dates

Whether an override applies to a slot is decided by comparing formatted calendar dates (lines 110-111). slotStartTime is time.utc(), so its format() is the UTC date. The override side is dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") with no .utc(), so format() uses the Node process timezone. On any server whose TZ is not UTC, an adjusted override whose UTC date differs from the server-local date will not match the slot, and the fixed-host override is ignored or applied to the wrong day. Example: server in America/Los_Angeles, override adjusted to 02:00 UTC formats as the previous local evening while the slot formats as the UTC date. The check this PR adds then does not run.

Override timezone shift keeps only clock time and can wipe the day

The new conversion adds inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset to the override instants and then stores only .hour() and .minute() (lines 219-223). Those minutes are applied to whichever invitee day contains the unadjusted override.start (the filter at lines 206-208), not the day of the shifted time. When the offset crosses midnight, the clock wraps onto the wrong day. Example: organizer Asia/Kolkata, override stored as 02:00Z-04:00Z meaning 02:00-04:00 local, attendee in UTC. The offset is -330 minutes, hour() becomes 20:30, and that is added to the UTC day of 02:00Z, so slots show at 20:30Z the same date instead of 20:30Z the previous day. If only the start wraps, startTime exceeds endTime. Organizer IST 09:00-18:00 viewed from America/New_York (offset -630 minutes) becomes start 22:30 and end 07:30. buildSlots drops any range with start >= end (line 68), but the override block has already removed that user's normal working hours (lines 228-245), so the attendee sees no slots on the override day.

Tests miss fixed-host overrides and timezone day boundaries

The only new assertion re-fetches a personal-event date override with the attendee in Asia/Dhaka (+6) instead of Asia/Kolkata (+5:30) and expects the same UTC slot list. A 30-minute offset does not cross midnight or a DST change, so it does not catch override slots landing on the wrong day, ranges with start after end being dropped, or the extra DST shift in getTime. There is no round-robin case with a fixed host and a date override, which is the behavior the PR says it fixes, and no case where an override day also has a booking or calendar busy time. createBookingScenario never installs the hosts/isFixed rows, so the new checkIfIsAvailable branches are not exercised and the double-book and split-window regressions would not fail CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing sender crashes the re-link path

The match check indexes integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] directly. Integrations created before sender was stored, or created by build_integration when pipeline state has no sender, have no sender object. That raises KeyError, or TypeError if sender is null, and the install 500s instead of rendering the installation-failed page. This is exactly the re-link branch (Integration exists, no OrganizationIntegration), so those records cannot be reinstalled. The inequality also does not require both values to be non-empty strings, so a null sender login and a missing github_authenticated_user would compare equal and be allowed through. Read sender with a safe lookup and deny unless both logins are present and equal.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
Security tests never reach the checks they describe

test_installation_not_found used to assert "The GitHub installation could not be found." when the installation API returned 404. It now calls the callback with state ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which is not the pipeline signature 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3, so it fails the state check and never reaches build_integration. test_github_user_mismatch mutates the installation webhook body (installation id and sender login) but keeps HTTP_X_HUB_SIGNATURE sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486 from the original fixture, so signature verification rejects it when enabled, and then it reuses that same hardcoded state for a second user while asserting only the generic "Invalid installation request." string. That string is also returned for a state mismatch, a bad code, and a missing token, so the test can pass without comparing octocat to sender "attacker" or showing that no OrganizationIntegration was created. The token stub returns access_token regardless of redirect_uri. Recompute the webhook signature, drive a callback whose state actually matches that pipeline, and assert the specific denial for user mismatch, missing sender, and Integration.DoesNotExist.

Token request drops redirect_uri sent on authorize

The authorize redirect includes redirect_uri, but the access-token POST only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. GitHub's token endpoint, following RFC 6749 section 4.1.3, requires the same redirect_uri on the token request when it was included in authorization; otherwise it returns an error instead of access_token. This handler then always shows the invalid-installation page, so every install fails after the user authorizes, and that page is the same one used for real verification failures, so a manual check of the error UI does not prove the happy path. The comment says this mirrors OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params, which includes redirect_uri. Tests stub the token URL and ignore the POST body, so they stay green. Send the same redirect_uri used in the authorize request, build that URL with urlencode (the current f-string leaves redirect_uri unencoded), and accept both form and JSON token bodies the way the shared callback view does.

User-info fetch errors bypass the error page

After the token exchange, get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) is called with no try/except. HTTP errors, network failures, and a non-mapping response propagate as an uncaught exception and a 500, unlike a missing access_token or a bad state, which return the installation-failed page. A GitHub /user failure during install therefore aborts opaquely, and the exception can capture the request that carries the new user access token into error reporting. Catch API failures and treat a missing login the same as the other verification failures.

User-match check skipped when Integration does not exist

The new control is supposed to reject a mismatch between the OAuth GitHub login and the user who installed the app, but that comparison runs only after an Integration row is already loaded. On Integration.DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation returns pipeline.next_step() with no check. build_integration never reads github_authenticated_user; it fetches /app/installations/{id} with the GitHub App JWT, which can see every installation of this app, not only ones the OAuth user owns. Webhook creation of the Integration races the browser redirect, and any installation whose Sentry row is missing or was deleted takes this path. Combined with installation_id coming from the query string, an attacker can link a chosen GitHub App installation to the current Sentry organization and inherit the app's access to that account's repositories. Fail closed unless the OAuth user is verified against the installing user, or against installations visible to that user's token, before the org link is created.

installation_id is saved before OAuth state is validated

OAuthLoginView writes installation_id into the pipeline with bind_state before it checks that state matches pipeline.signature and before the authorization code is exchanged. bind_state persists the session immediately, and PipelineAdvancerView leaves csrf_protect = False, so a cross-site GET to /extensions/github/setup/?installation_id=<attacker> overwrites an in-progress install even when state is missing or wrong and the view then returns the error page. The later legitimate OAuth callback usually has no installation_id, and GitHubInstallation falls back to that poisoned value (request.GET.get("installation_id", pipeline.fetch_state("installation_id"))). The victim's org is then attached to the attacker's GitHub App installation whenever the sender check is skipped, or their own install is broken if the check runs. Persist installation_id only after state validation succeeds, and do not update pipeline state on the failure path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued is frozen at import time

queued is declared as queued: datetime = timezone.now() on the dataclass. That expression is evaluated once when the class body runs, not when an instance is created. Every AssignmentSource.from_integration() call on the inbound webhook path therefore stores the same timestamp: the moment this module was first imported in the process. Long-lived web and worker processes make that value hours or days old, so the field cannot distinguish or order the rapid successive assignee changes this PR is about. Dataclass equality includes queued, so distinct events for the same integration also compare equal for the life of the process, and to_dict() writes that stale timestamp into every sync_assignee_outbound payload. This needs field(default_factory=timezone.now). The new test only checks that queued is not None, so it does not catch the shared value.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
to_dict() embeds a datetime in Celery task kwargs

to_dict() returns asdict(self), so queued is a raw datetime. sync_group_assignee_outbound passes that dict straight to sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async as assignment_source_dict. A JSON task transport (Celery JSON serializer, or Sentry taskworker) cannot encode datetime and raises TypeError while enqueueing. That apply_async call is synchronous inside GroupAssignee.assign and deassign, so an inbound webhook can persist the assignee and then fail, and the change is never pushed to any other integration. from_dict only does cls(**input_dict) inside a ValueError/TypeError handler and does not parse ISO-8601 strings. If a serializer stringifies the timestamp, queued is left as a string; if construction raises, from_dict returns None. The outbound task treats a None source as "not an echo" and performs the sync anyway, which brings the assignee loop back. self.tasks() runs eagerly and does not round-trip the serializer, and no test calls from_dict(source.to_dict()), so CI will not catch this.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
Echo guard drops every linked issue on the source integration

should_sync returns False for the entire integration whenever sync_source.integration_id matches org_integration.integration_id. AssignmentSource does not record the external issue key, and sync_group_assignee_outbound attaches that same source to every GroupLink on the Sentry issue. A group may be linked to multiple external issues on one integration; GroupLink uniqueness is on the external-issue id, not the integration. An assignee webhook from Jira ticket A therefore skips outbound sync for ticket A and also for ticket B on the same Jira integration, so ticket B's assignee stays stale even with outbound assignee sync enabled. sync_group_assignee_inbound already has external_issue_key, and the outbound task already loads the target ExternalIssue, so the guard should skip only the originating issue. Skipping that one key still stops the echo; GroupAssignee.assign does not enqueue outbound sync when the assignee is unchanged, so a follow-up webhook that maps to the same Sentry user will not bounce.

Inbound wiring and cross-integration sync are untested

The new test calls GroupAssignee.objects.assign directly with an AssignmentSource and only covers the matching-integration assign case. test_assignee_sync_inbound_assign and test_assignee_sync_inbound_deassign call sync_group_assignee_inbound, which is the production webhook entry point that must pass assignment_source into assign and deassign, but they never assert that outbound sync to the source integration is skipped. Removing those assignment_source= arguments in sync.py would leave both inbound tests green and restore the loop. There is also no test that a second integration still receives the outbound update, and no test that deassign with a matching source skips outbound (test_assignee_sync_outbound_unassign still expects assignment_source=None). A guard that dropped every sourced sync, or a deassign path that forgot the source, would pass CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Metric alert handler is abstract and crashes when constructed

MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler and has an empty body. StatefulDetectorHandler still has abstract methods (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the new build_occurrence_and_event_data), so instantiating MetricAlertDetectorHandler raises TypeError. The class remains MetricAlertFire.detector_handler, and Detector.detector_handler constructs it for any detector whose slug is metric_alert_fire. Previously this was a concrete DetectorHandler whose evaluate() returned an empty list. process_detectors does not catch that TypeError, so one such detector aborts the whole batch instead of no-opping. Implement the abstract methods, or keep a concrete DetectorHandler until a real stateful implementation exists.

true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
evaluate docstring still says it returns a list

StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate's docstring says it returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult. This PR changes the return type to a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Callers that follow the docstring will iterate keys or treat the result as a sequence of evaluation objects. Update the docstring to describe the dict.

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Occurrence tests never assert the measured value

build_mock_occurrence_and_event accepts value and never uses it, and MockDetectorStateHandler.build_occurrence_and_event_data only forwards to that helper. Assertions therefore stay green if evaluate passes the wrong measurement. Concrete mismatches already in the tests: test_state_results_multi_group has group_2=10 but builds the expected occurrence with 6; test_results_on_change evaluates 100 but expects an occurrence built with 6; TestEvaluate.test_dedupe evaluates 8 but expects 6. Put value on the occurrence (for example evidence_data) and pass the actual packet value, or the new hook argument is untested.

false_positives.candidate:
Fired occurrence fingerprint is not tied to the resolve fingerprint

On a non-OK transition, evaluate_group_key_value publishes whatever IssueOccurrence build_occurrence_and_event_data returns, and it never sets or checks occurrence.fingerprint. On the later OK transition it publishes a StatusChangeMessage whose fingerprint is always build_fingerprint(group_key) (`{detector_id}` or `{detector_id}:{group_key}`). Issue resolution matches on that fingerprint. The new hook is not given the fingerprint, and the abstract method does not require the subclass to use build_fingerprint, so an occurrence opened under any other fingerprint will not be resolved when the detector returns to OK. Pass build_fingerprint(group_key) into the hook or overwrite the returned occurrence's fingerprint before publishing.

Occurrences are published before dedupe and detector state are committed

process_detectors sends each result to Kafka via create_issue_occurrence_from_result and only then calls handler.commit_state_updates(), which is what persists the dedupe value and active/priority transition queued during evaluate. This PR is what starts attaching an IssueOccurrence to threshold breaches on that path. If publish raises on a later group key, or the process stops before the commit, the dedupe key and stored status are unchanged. The same packet is evaluated again as a new transition and another occurrence is emitted. Occurrence ids are chosen by the subclass and are not derived from detector id, group key, and dedupe value, so the retry is not idempotent and users can get duplicate issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Occurrence context drops the adjusted schedule_type

get_monitor_environment_context copies monitor.config and, when schedule_type is present, replaces it with monitor.get_schedule_type_display() so the issue event can show a human-readable schedule type. The returned dict ignores that copy and sends monitor_environment.monitor.config instead. The display conversion never reaches Kafka, so contexts.monitor.config.schedule_type stays the raw stored value (typically an integer) on every monitor incident occurrence. The payload also aliases the live config dict, so any later in-place mutation of the event context mutates the in-memory monitor. Return the adjusted copy.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

false_positives.candidate:
Incident opens before failure_issue_threshold consecutive failures

In try_incident_threshold, when failure_issue_threshold is greater than 1, the code loads at most that many recent check-ins (ordered by date_added, then reversed) and returns early only if one of them is CheckInStatus.OK. It never requires the window to contain failure_issue_threshold rows. A shorter history has no OK row, so execution still sets MonitorEnvironment.status to ERROR, get_or_creates a MonitorIncident, emits issue occurrences, and sends monitor_environment_failed. A new or ACTIVE monitor with failure_issue_threshold of 3 therefore opens an incident on its first failed check-in, and stays in ERROR so later failures keep attaching occurrences, until a success resolves it. The configured consecutive-failure tolerance is ignored whenever fewer than N check-ins exist. An empty slice also falls through this check and then raises IndexError on previous_checkins[0], aborting failure processing instead of returning False. Require len(previous_checkins) >= failure_issue_threshold before transitioning.

Mixed failure-reason text does not match the documented message

get_failure_reason is shown as the Failure reason evidence on monitor issues. Its docstring specifies strings such as "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected" and "A failed check-in was detected". For more than one failure it formats each status as "%(count)d %(status)s" using the bare words missed/timeout/error, joins them, and appends a single "check-ins detected". Mixed failures therefore render as "2 missed, 1 timeout and 1 error check-ins detected" (no per-status "check-in(s)", and a plural noun for the whole list). The singular path returns "An error check-in was detected" (or missed/timeout), not the documented sentence. The docstring also misspells the summary as "humam readible". The evidence copy users see for multi-status incidents is wrong relative to the function's own contract.

Non-failure check-ins count toward the failure threshold

The threshold gate only tests whether any row equals CheckInStatus.OK. Every other status, including in-progress check-ins that are stored as MonitorCheckIn rows, is treated as part of the failure streak and also occupies a slot in the limited window. With failure_issue_threshold 2, a recent window of one in-progress check-in plus one error contains no OK row, so the environment is marked ERROR and an incident is opened after a single real failure. An in-progress row can also push an older OK check-in out of the N-row window so that success is ignored. Only error, missed, and timeout rows should count toward the consecutive-failure threshold.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Comma-separated shard list is emitted as one metric tag

shard_tag is the comma-joined list of every shard that process handles, and it is sent as the shard tag on spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes, and as shards on spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce. DogStatsD encodes tags as a comma-separated key:value list and does not escape commas inside values, so a tag like shard:0,1,2 is parsed as shard:0 plus stray tags 1 and 2. Those timers and gauges will be dropped or attributed to the wrong series. With the CLI default --flusher-processes 1, every assigned partition is concatenated into that single value, so this breaks as soon as the consumer has more than one partition, not only when multiple flusher processes are enabled. The value also changes on every rebalance (high cardinality) and can exceed backend tag-length limits. wait_produce uses the key shards while the other metrics use shard, so they would not group together even after the value is fixed. The unhealthy counter already tags one shard id; the produce metrics should do the same, or use a bounded process index, and must not embed commas. The same comma-joined string is also set as the Sentry tag sentry_spans_buffer_shards.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_basic wait after advancing drift is a no-op

test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op so the flusher does not block, then calls time.sleep(0.1) after setting current_drift to 9000, with a comment that this gives the flusher time to process. That call uses the same patched time.sleep, so it returns immediately and does not wait. step.join() sets SpanFlusher.stopped before it waits for the worker; if the worker has not yet observed the advanced drift and produced, it leaves its loop and the (msg,) = messages assertion fails. The synchronization added to fix that race does not run. Save the original time.sleep before monkeypatching and wait on that saved function (the flusher looks up time.sleep at call time, so it will still see the no-op), and only then join.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_basic wait after advancing drift is a no-op

test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op so the flusher does not block, then calls time.sleep(0.1) after setting current_drift to 9000, with a comment that this gives the flusher time to process. That call uses the same patched time.sleep, so it returns immediately and does not wait. step.join() sets SpanFlusher.stopped before it waits for the worker; if the worker has not yet observed the advanced drift and produced, it leaves its loop and the (msg,) = messages assertion fails. The synchronization added to fix that race does not run. Save the original time.sleep before monkeypatching and wait on that saved function (the flusher looks up time.sleep at call time, so it will still see the no-op), and only then join.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can return without stopping every flusher process

SpanFlusher.join sets stopped, then calls next_step.join(timeout) before waiting on flusher workers. The deadline is that same timeout, and the new loop breaks as soon as it has passed, skipping process.terminate() for every worker not yet visited. If next_step.join consumes the timeout, or the first stuck worker uses up the rest, the remaining shard flushers are never signaled. close() intentionally does not stop them, so join() is the only shutdown path. Those workers are daemons, but the consumer process stays up across rebalances, so a leaked flusher keeps calling flush_segments and producing to the buffered-segments topic for shards that may already have been revoked and assigned to another consumer. That races Redis flush state and emits duplicate segments. This is a regression from the previous single-process join, which always called terminate() after the wait even if the deadline had already passed. Workers that do get terminate() are never join()ed, so join() can return while they are still alive, and there is no try/finally, so an exception from next_step.join skips cleanup entirely. Always stop every worker (kill if needed) and join() it, including on the timeout and exception paths.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

false_positives.candidate:
Flusher restart does not wait for the old worker to exit

When a flusher is unhealthy, _ensure_processes_alive calls kill() only for multiprocessing.Process, then _create_process_for_shards starts a replacement and overwrites self.processes without joining the previous worker. kill() returns before the process has actually died, and the old Process object is dropped, so the supervisor no longer tracks it and never reaps it. The thread backend used whenever produce_to_pipe is set is not interrupted at all (kill/terminate are skipped for non-Process workers). A hung thread therefore keeps flushing the same shards after a new thread is started; each hang restart adds another live flusher until MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS trips, and those threads all call flush_segments and produce, duplicating segments and racing done_flush_segments. On the process backend the replacement is spawned while the killed worker may still be inside Redis flush or Kafka produce. Join (or join-after-kill) the old worker, and do not start a second thread while the first is alive, before creating the replacement.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and races the commit loop

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says a processing error must not block commits for other messages, but the assertion requires that the partition was not committed (len(committed_offsets) == 0 or the partition is absent). The worker completes the offset in a finally block even when result_processor raises, so after both messages (offsets 100 and 101) the factory's commit callback should record 102 once the commit loop runs. That loop waits 1 second before its first commit, and the test breaks out as soon as both calls have run (usually a few hundred milliseconds), so it passes without ever observing a commit and will fail on a slower run once the commit arrives. Wait long enough for the commit thread and assert the offset required by the chosen retry policy.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
--mode help misstates parallelism and omits the new mode

uptime_options still says "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." Mode parallel builds a MultiprocessingPool; batched-parallel is the thread-pool mode; thread-queue-parallel, added in this change, is not described at all, nor is the fact that --max-workers becomes the queue count in that mode. Operators selecting the new mode from --help will misunderstand the concurrency model.

Any submit exception is acked and the message is never retried

submit()'s bare except marks the BrokerValue offset complete after logging. That path runs for build_payload_grouping_key failures, Queue.put failures (including queue.ShutDown after the pool is shut down), and the decoder's AssertionError on FilteredPayload. The commit loop will then commit that offset, so the result is never retried and never sent to a DLQ. Returning None from the decoder is an intentional skip and matches serial mode; unexpected exceptions are not. Serial processing lets those exceptions fail the strategy so Arroyo can retry. A transient grouping error or a put failure therefore permanently drops an uptime result. Only complete offsets that were actually handled or deliberately filtered, and let unexpected submit failures propagate so the partition is not acked past them.

Graceful shutdown depends on Python 3.13-only queue APIs

Queue.shutdown and queue.ShutDown were added in Python 3.13. FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown() and the worker catches queue.ShutDown, with no fallback. On 3.11/3.12, shutdown raises AttributeError, which the bare except logs and swallows, so workers blocked in Queue.get() never wake. Each worker.join then waits out its 5 second timeout (default 20 queues is up to about 100 seconds) and in-flight DB work is abandoned when the daemon threads die at process exit. If this runtime is not guaranteed to be 3.13+, shutdown needs a compatible unblock path, such as a sentinel or get(timeout) that observes the shutdown flag.

Offset commits run on a background thread against the Kafka consumer

_commit_loop is a daemon thread started from SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls commit_function, which invokes Arroyo's commit callback (result_consumer commit_offsets). That callback stages or commits offsets on the Kafka consumer. The confluent_kafka Consumer is not thread-safe, and Arroyo runs submit/poll and its own ONCE_PER_SECOND commit on the processor thread that owns the consumer. Committing from this side thread races with poll() and can raise inside librdkafka, commit a torn offset map, or deadlock when close() joins the commit thread while it is inside the callback and the callback needs the processor thread. Perform commits from poll() and from join/close on the processor thread, and force a final commit there after in-flight work has finished.

Queue-depth assertion races the worker threads

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts get_stats()["total_items"] > 0. The pool's workers are already running and the test handler only appends to a list, so they can dequeue every item before get_stats() runs. The assertion fails intermittently on a fast machine. Block the handler until after the depth check, or pause the workers before submitting.

Rebalance kills the shared pool and later results are committed unprocessed

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategies, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/join and ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown both call queue_pool.shutdown(). Arroyo calls close() then join(), then create_with_partitions() again on every assignment, including ordinary rebalances during deploys. shutdown() stops the workers and Queue.shutdown()s the queues, so later Queue.put raises queue.ShutDown. The new strategy still submits into that dead pool; submit()'s except block marks the offset complete without calling the result processor, and the new strategy's commit thread commits those offsets through the new commit callback. In the steady state the queues are empty, so nothing is outstanding and the commit cursor advances: those uptime results are skipped permanently. If a backlog left outstanding offsets, commits freeze and processing never resumes until the process is restarted. The OffsetTracker is also shared and never reset, so revoked partitions and the new assignment share one cursor. Recreate the pool per create_with_partitions (and tear it down only with that strategy), or do not shut the pool down on strategy close.

Shutdown abandons queued work and never commits the in-flight tail

close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown(). The commit loop then exits after at most one more pass, so offsets completed while workers finish are never committed and will be redelivered. FixedQueuePool.shutdown also sets worker.shutdown = True before Queue.shutdown(immediate=False). The worker loop checks that flag before Queue.get(), so it will not drain: it finishes at most the item already dequeued and leaves the rest outstanding. Combined with unbounded queues, a restart replays the whole buffered backlog, which can duplicate uptime incidents or notifications if handling is not idempotent. join() ignores the timeout Arroyo passes and calls close() again; Arroyo already calls close() before join(), so Queue.shutdown() runs twice and the second call raises queue.ShutDown, logged as an error for every queue on every shutdown. Drain first (do not set the worker flag until the queue is empty; let shutdown(immediate=False) unblock get), then force one final commit on the processor thread, make close() idempotent, and honor join's timeout.

Unbounded queues never apply backpressure and can OOM the consumer

Each work queue is queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and submit() always put()s without blocking or raising MessageRejected. The class docstring says queues provide natural backpressure, but they never fill. If handling is slower than the topic, or one item is slow, the consumer keeps polling and retains every later message in the queues, in WorkItem (full payload), and in OffsetTracker.all_offsets, because a commit cannot move past the oldest outstanding offset on that partition. get_committable_offsets then walks range(start, max_offset+1) while holding the partition lock every second, so a large backlog also stalls workers completing offsets. poll() only emits a gauge, so the healthcheck keeps succeeding until the process OOMs. This is worse than batched-parallel, which caps memory at max_batch_size, under the exact slow-item failure this mode is meant to solve. Bound the queues and signal backpressure from submit so read-ahead stays finite and the processor can still poll. A worker that exits is also never restarted, so one dead thread permanently stalls its queue and that partition's commit cursor.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key joins name and parent with underscore, so distinct resources collide

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name and parent with "_", but both values are resource UIDs and Grafana UIDs may contain underscores. A deny for dashboard "report" in folder "q1_2024" and a check for dashboard "report_q1" in folder "2024" produce the same key (namespace.perm_<user>_<action>_report_q1_2024). Check treats any hit as definitive deny and does not consult permissions, so one resource's deny is applied to the other for 30 seconds. That is a wrong authorization decision, not just a missed cache optimization.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key drops identity type and collides anonymous with renderer

Check builds the denial-cache key from only the subject id (checkReq.UserUID), not the identity type. This package's own Check tests use subjects "anonymous:0" and "render:0", so both parse to UserUID "0" and share one key for the same namespace, action, name, and folder. The denial lookup at the start of Check returns Allowed:false on any hit, before getRendererPermissions or anonymous permission logic runs. Renderer is supposed to be allowed dashboards:read, folders:read, and datasources:read unconditionally, but an anonymous deny for that dashboard (or the reverse, a renderer deny for an action anonymous is allowed) sticks for shortCacheTTL (30s) and 403s the other identity. Image rendering, alert screenshots, and anonymous access can deny each other.

Sticky denial cache skips the DB refresh and outlives a stale folder tree

A denial-cache hit in Check returns Allowed:false immediately and never reaches the new path that reloads permissions when the cached scope set does not allow the resource. Denials are also stored whenever the post-refresh checkPermission call is false, including when the negative answer came from the cached folder tree rather than from fresh permission rows. checkInheritedPermissions returns false if ParentFolder is missing from that tree, which is exactly the case for a dashboard just created in a new child folder whose access is inherited from an ancestor. Folder cache and denial cache are both 30s, but they are written at different times, and nothing deletes a denial when permissions are later reloaded or the folder tree is rebuilt. So a check that races permission insert, or that runs while the folder tree is stale, keeps 403ing for up to 30s even after a later reload has already cached the grant. That reintroduces the creator lockout this PR is fixing, and a refreshed perm cache cannot override the denial because the denial entry is consulted first.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Filtered Grafana rows are rendered without React keys

FilterViewResults builds a KeyedRuleWithOrigin key specifically to avoid duplicate list keys, and the previous GrafanaRuleLoader was rendered with key={key}. The replacement GrafanaRuleListItem omits that prop, while the datasource and unknown branches in the same map still set key. Grafana rows are therefore unkeyed siblings of keyed rows. As infinite scroll appends pages, React can reuse the wrong row instance (open More menu or silence-drawer state) and will warn about missing keys. getGrafanaRuleKey on line 209 also has a stray closing brace (`rule.uid}}`), so putting key={key} back without fixing that helper still yields malformed keys.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item does nothing without a ruler rule

The list menu shows Silence notifications because useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities allows it for Grafana alerting rules, and handleSilence only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer is mounted only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true, where rule is the optional ruler-rule prop. GrafanaRuleListItem passes only promRule, so that condition is false and the click is a no-op. SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer still requires a RulerGrafanaRuleDTO; the list needs a fetch-on-demand or a drawer that can create the silence from the prom rule uid and labels. The new GrafanaGroupLoader test only asserts the menu item is present and never clicks it.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete stays hidden in the list view without a ruler rule

The new list passes only a Prometheus rule into RuleActionsButtons, and AlertRuleMenu now treats the Grafana prom-rule delete ability as enough for canDelete. The Delete item is still rendered only when rulerRule is truthy (canDelete && rulerRule) and the click passes that ruler rule into handleDelete. The list no longer loads ruler rules, so rulerRule is undefined and Delete never appears, even for users with folder delete permission. RuleActionsButtons already ignores the ruler argument and calls showDeleteModal with the uid identifier built from the prom rule, so the gate is leftover and removes an action that would otherwise work.

Federated rule groups are no longer immutable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities used to set isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) (true when the group has source_tenants) and treat those rules as immutable. It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false and drops the isFederatedRuleGroup import. useAlertRuleAbility still goes through this for every CombinedRule, not only the new list. Update, delete, pause, restore, and permanent delete therefore become supported for federated Mimir/GEM groups whenever the user otherwise has permission. Editing those rules through the normal form rewrites the ruler group and can strip source_tenants, breaking cross-tenant evaluation.

Menu test asserts the incomplete action set

The new More-menu test grants AlertingRuleUpdate and AlertingRuleDelete, defines a Delete menuitem selector, and then asserts the menu contains exactly four items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export). That locks in the missing Delete and Pause actions introduced by dropping ruler rules. It also never clicks Silence, so it does not notice that the drawer does not open. A green run of this file does not cover the list-view action regressions, and RulesTable RBAC tests mock useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities entirely, so they do not execute the skipToken permission logic either.

Pause is unreachable once ruler rules are dropped from the list

canPause is now true for an editable Grafana alerting rule based on useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, but the Pause item is still rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) is true, and it passes that ruler rule into MenuItemPauseRule. GrafanaRuleListItem never supplies a ruler rule, so Pause cannot appear in the list the PR is migrating. Dropping the rulerRule check is not sufficient: MenuItemPauseRule still requires a RulerGrafanaRuleDTO. The prom rule already has uid and isPaused, but nothing maps those into the pause action, and onPauseChange is not wired from RuleActionsButtons either.

Recording rules lose export and pause in prom-rule abilities

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities uses isAlertingRule (Prometheus alerting type only) as the support flag for ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently. The ruler ability path uses isGrafanaManagedAlertRule, which is true for both Grafana alerting and recording rules, and the comment here says every GrafanaPromRuleDTO is Grafana-managed by definition. Recording rules in the new list therefore lose Export, and Pause stays unsupported even after the rulerRule menu gate is fixed. Silence correctly depends on alerting type; these other actions should not. Detail views that still use ruler abilities will keep showing Export and Pause for the same recording rule, so the two UIs disagree.

Rule view links drop the returnTo back-navigation target

The removed list item built the view href with createReturnTo() so the rule detail back link returned to the current list URL, including search filters. The new GrafanaRuleListItem always links to `/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view` with no returnTo query param. Opening a rule from the group list or the filtered list therefore loses that context, and back navigation no longer returns to the same filtered results. Group-loader tests only assert that the href contains the view path, so they do not catch the missing parameter.

skipToken still grants Grafana Duplicate on non-Grafana rules

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities is called with skipToken (converted to undefined) whenever the menu has no Grafana Prometheus rule, including every datasource-managed rule. useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable(undefined) returns loading:false, so MaybeSupported becomes AlwaysSupported, and Duplicate is then [true, user has Grafana AlertingRuleCreate] via toAbility(getRulesPermissions('grafana').create). AlertRuleMenu ORs that tuple with the ruler ability (canDuplicate), so an editor who may create Grafana-managed rules but may not write external rules still sees Duplicate and the clone flow is started with the cloud rule identifier. skipToken is meant to skip the check, but it does not return [false, false]. View and Explore are the same shape (supported plus a global permission even when the rule is missing) and will leak if callers OR them the same way. Existing RBAC tests mock these hooks, so they never execute this path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range queries are split after early interpolation

runSplitQuery now passes every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before querySupportsSplitting. applyTemplateVariables interpolates with TemplateSrv.replace, and during dashboard or Explore queries that replaces $__range, $__range_s, and $__range_ms from the active time range. querySupportsSplitting then calls isQueryWithRangeVariable on that already-substituted expr, so the macro is gone and the query is treated as splittable. The comment on querySupportsSplitting says these queries must not be split: the backend fills $__range from the time range of the request it actually receives, and a split chunk is not the range the user selected. After this change, rate({job="app"}[$__range]) over several days is rewritten to a fixed full-window duration (for example [7d]) and then executed as one-day chunks, each looking back the whole window. Merged results do not match an unsplit query. The new tests cannot catch this: they stub replace to rewrite only $__auto and $step, so $__range stays in the expression under test and the guard still looks like it works. Check isQueryWithRangeVariable on the raw expr and keep those targets in the non-splitting partition before interpolating.

Expressions that interpolate to empty hang shard splitting

runShardSplitQuery used to interpolate with interpolateVariablesInQueries and then drop targets with an empty expr. It now filters on the raw expr and only then calls applyTemplateVariables. A target whose whole expression is a variable, such as $query, passes the filter because the raw string is non-empty, then becomes expr: '' after substitution, and is still passed to splitQueriesByStreamShard. If that target is alone in a group (non-shardable groups are queued first, so one empty query next to shardable queries is enough), runNextRequest calls runSplitQuery, which filters the empty expr out and calls runSplitGroupedQueries with an empty request list. That function immediately evaluates requests.filter(...)[0].partition and throws TypeError. The throw is inside a .then() with no rejection handler, so the subscriber never errors or completes and the whole request hangs, including valid sibling queries. Previously the empty target was removed before grouping and the other queries ran. The same filter-before-map in runSplitQuery (line 298) also keeps an empty interpolated expr in a split group and sends it to runQuery, which fails the batch with a Loki parse error.

Shard path applies template variables twice

runShardSplitQuery already maps each target through applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters) before sharding. For every shard group it then calls runSplitQuery with a sub-request that still carries request.filters and the already interpolated targets, and runSplitQuery maps those targets through applyTemplateVariables again. Substitution is not idempotent: the first pass turns an escaped $$ into a literal $, and the second pass treats that $ as a variable, so a label value or query text containing $name can be expanded to a different variable. Ad hoc filters are applied on both passes (the old interpolateVariablesInQueries call did not receive request.filters; both new call sites do), so matchers are inserted once before the shard selector is injected and again after. The executed LogQL ends up with duplicate label matchers, for example {job="x", env="prod", __stream_shard__=~"1|2", env="prod"}. The shard test now expects applyTemplateVariables five times (once up front plus once per shard group), which locks in the double pass instead of interpolating once.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin request completion logs drop traceID

Plugin Request Completed (eventName grafana-data-egress) used to append traceID from tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false), which includes the ID even when the span is not sampled. That call and the tracing import were removed when the line switched to m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info. instrumentContext only stores endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname; it does not store traceID, and grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext does not add one either. Info does not take a context.Context, so the span cannot be read at log time unless it was already copied onto the logger. Nothing in this change attaches traceID, so these egress logs can no longer be joined to distributed traces, including unsampled ones.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards receiver and context

TestLogger.FromContext ignores both the receiver and the context and returns NewTestLogger(), a blank logger. LoggerMiddleware now emits its only line via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info, so those calls are recorded on the discarded instance. InfoLogs, WarnLogs, and ErrorLogs on the injected TestLogger stay empty, and contextual fields are never applied. That breaks the Logger contract, which says FromContext keeps this logger's context and adds attributes from the given context. Tests using this fake cannot observe plugin request completion logs and will fail if they assert that a line was written.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Contextual logging move is untested

ContextualLoggerMiddleware is new and has no tests, and the logger middleware change that stopped passing pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID, and traceID as explicit log fields is also untested. metrics_middleware_test.go only renames the constructor and still only checks Prometheus series. Nothing asserts that QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, and CollectMetrics attach those attributes (or that stream RPCs do not), or that Plugin Request Completed still contains them and traceID after FromContext. A wrong attribute list, middleware order, or FromContext implementation would still pass CI.

FromContext fallback silently drops request context

grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext type-asserts infra log's FromContext result to *log.ConcreteLogger. On failure it returns d.New() and ignores ctx. New with no arguments does not read contextual attributes, so pluginId, endpoint, datasource name/UID, and user are omitted while the caller still logs. LoggerMiddleware now depends entirely on FromContext for those fields, so this branch emits Plugin Request Completed with no plugin identity and no error. It also throws away the logger infra log returned, even if that value already had the right fields. Fall back to the original wrapper (return d) or otherwise keep ctx, and do not hide the type mismatch.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check and insert are not atomic

When device_limit is positive, CreateOrUpdateDevice counts rows in one WithDbSession and, if the count is under the limit, inserts in a second WithDbSession. Nothing wraps the two statements in a transaction or takes a lock, and the unique key is only on device_id, so it does not cap the number of rows. Concurrent anonymous requests that all observe count < limit will all insert. With 50 simultaneous new device ids and a limit of 10, all 50 can commit and the table stays at 50; nothing rolls the extras back. That is the multi-instance, multi-user load this cap is meant to control, so AnonymousDeviceLimit is not a hard limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit denial is cached as success

tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault before CreateOrUpdateDevice, and a cache hit returns nil without touching the database. The cache TTL is 29 minutes and the entry is not removed when tagging fails. Authenticate now treats a nil TagDevice result as success and only denies access for ErrDeviceLimitReached. So the first request from a new device over the limit is rejected, but that rejection is stored as a successful cache entry. Every later request for that device id skips the limit check and is issued an anonymous identity, and the device is never inserted, so it never consumes a slot. A concurrent request can also observe the cache entry and be authenticated before the first request's limit check finishes. After one denial, the cap does not apply to that client for the rest of the TTL, on every instance that has seen it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous auth now waits on the database even when the limit is off

Device tagging used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout and did not block login. Authenticate now calls TagDevice on the request path for every anonymous authentication, including when device_limit is 0, which disables enforcement. A local-cache miss waits for a database write before an identity is returned; a non-zero limit adds a COUNT(*) first, and that count is not cached. The cache is per process, so each instance repeats the work. A slow database delays every new anonymous session, and because the call is synchronous an unauthenticated client can force a count-and-write per request by rotating X-Grafana-Device-Id. Previously that work could not stall the request.

Device limit does not actually gate anonymous access

The new access check only denies authentication when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate then still returns an anonymous identity, when X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent or when web.RemoteAddr cannot be parsed as an IP. Existing tests show client IP is taken from X-Forwarded-For, so a non-IP forwarded-for value forces the parse-failure path even if a device id is sent. Any other tagging error is only logged in client.go and authentication continues, so a request that makes the insert fail is granted access and is not counted. The device id is also chosen by the client, so many users can send one already-accepted id and all pass the update path while occupying a single slot. Omitting the header is enough to use anonymous access with no limit check at all. As written, device_limit does not bound anonymous access.

Limit tests never cover the allow-existing or auth paths

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only inserts one device and asserts that a second new device id returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. It never checks the behavior the new branch claims: an already-registered device must still be updated and accepted once the count is at the limit. A broken updateDevice WHERE clause that rejects every device, including known ones, would still pass. Nothing at the AnonDeviceService or Anonymous.Authenticate level covers the limit either, so the 29-minute cache treating a failed tag as success, and a missing device-id header still receiving an anonymous identity, are both untested. The new test runs on SQLite only, so MySQL/Postgres placeholder or rows-affected differences in the new UPDATE are not exercised.

Provider signature change breaks Wire startup

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService no longer takes an anonstore.AnonStore and now requires db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a bare int64 device-limit argument. Grafana builds the server with Google Wire and commits pkg/server/wire_gen.go; this PR does not update wire.go or wire_gen.go, and the only updated call sites are tests. The generated injector still calls the old signatures, so the server package will not compile. Regenerating Wire also cannot satisfy a raw int64, so ProvideAnonDBStore has to be dropped from the provider set (it is now called internally) or the limit must be injected via *setting.Cfg. Until that is done the binary does not build.

device_limit is undocumented and 0 means unlimited

auth.anonymous.device_limit is read with MustInt64(0) but conf/defaults.ini and the configure-grafana docs are not updated. Operators discover settings from defaults.ini, and generated config docs come from that file, so the new cap is invisible. The code treats 0 as 'do not enforce' rather than 'allow zero devices', and that is not stated anywhere a user will see it. Setting device_limit = 0 to try to disallow anonymous devices silently leaves the limit disabled.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Success-path debug logs at Error level dump every cleaned ID

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log at Error after every ID fetch and every delete (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including batches that find nothing. These are leftover debug statements: the fetch log's err is always nil because a real error already returned, and the messages fire on the normal success path. Error-level lines are what most Grafana deployments alert on, so every cleanup cycle will raise false errors for alert, dashboard, and API annotations plus orphaned tags. Each line also includes the full ID slice and the SQL condition. Batch size is configurable and the new test uses 32767, so a single line can be megabytes, flooding log pipelines and risking dropped real errors. Remove these calls, or at most log a count at Debug without the ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup interval accidentally reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

Run() now ticks the background cleanup loop every 1 minute instead of every 10 minutes. Nothing in the PR description or the annotation deadlock fix calls for this, and it changes every job in this service (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history, and annotations), not just annotation cleanup. clean() uses a 9-minute timeout that was paired with the 10-minute interval so one pass finished before the next tick. With a 1-minute ticker, any pass longer than a minute (likely now that each annotation batch is a separate SELECT plus DELETE, and on large tables) leaves a tick buffered, so the next pass starts immediately and cleanup runs back-to-back. That multiplies database load and can increase the write contention this change is meant to reduce. Restore the 10-minute interval unless a documented, intentional schedule change is actually wanted.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite IN-list is built with quadratic string concatenation

When the database is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, deleteByIDs inlines IDs by repeatedly assigning values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v).
