Each iteration copies the whole string, so n IDs cost O(n²) allocations before the DELETE is sent. The new test sets the batch size to 32767, and orphaned-tag cleanup can emit several lists of that size; that is on the order of gigabytes of temporary strings and multi-second stalls on the cleanup goroutine, which runs the other cleanup jobs only after annotations finish. Build the list with strings.Builder (and consider chunking) so large SQLite batches stay linear.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Latencies are recorded on the wrong store's metric

On Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) and never records a storage sample, so unified-storage create failures show up as legacy failures and storage error latency is missing. Update does the same on line 129 (recordLegacyDuration for a storage error). DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine calls recordStorageDuration (line 166) with the legacy start time, so legacy delete-collection latency and errors are added to the storage histogram and the legacy series stays empty. Dashboards and any mode-promotion checks that compare legacy vs storage success will attribute outages to the wrong store and can page or block migration incorrectly.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful delete metrics use the object name as the kind label

The delete success path calls recordStorageDuration with name (the object name) as the third argument, while the error path two lines above and every other method pass options.Kind. That label is the resource kind. Every successful delete therefore emits a unique series per object name, which is unbounded cardinality on a hot write path and can exhaust Prometheus memory. Success and failure also cannot be aggregated together because they do not share the same label value, so delete success rate is not measurable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request context

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine and derive its context with context.WithTimeoutCause on the incoming request context (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163). A child context is cancelled as soon as its parent is cancelled, and the apiserver cancels the request context when the handler returns — which is immediately after these methods return success. The 10s timeout therefore never keeps the legacy call alive; Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection run with an already-cancelled context and fail. Mode 3 reads only from unified storage, so the missed legacy write is invisible to API clients, but rollback to a legacy-read mode drops every write made in mode 3. The new playlist mode 3 integration tests that expect the legacy HTTP API to show k8s writes will fail or flake for the same reason.

Background legacy writes use the caller's objects without a copy

The legacy goroutines call Legacy.Create with the same obj pointer passed to Storage.Create (line 55), Legacy.Update with the same objInfo (line 139), and Legacy.DeleteCollection with the same listOptions (line 165). k8s create/update/delete-collection mutate those values in place (generated name, UID, resourceVersion, continue/resourceVersion on list options), and the caller may keep using them after the method returns. The goroutine therefore races with the storage layer and the client. Legacy create can also reject the object because resourceVersion/UID were already set by unified storage, or it can persist a different name than the one returned to the client. Deep-copy the inputs before the unified call (and clear server-assigned resourceVersion on the legacy copy) before handing them to the goroutine.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes

Destroy closes Storage and then Legacy immediately and does not track the goroutines started by Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Those goroutines can still be inside Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection after Legacy.Destroy returns, which races with teardown and can panic or hit a closed database. Shutdown also drops the backup writes the goroutines were supposed to finish. A WaitGroup (or similar) should be added around the legacy goroutines and waited on in Destroy before calling Legacy.Destroy.

Expected NotFound responses are logged as errors

Get logs every Storage.Get error at Error level, including NotFound (line 71). List (line 87) and Delete (line 102) do the same, and the apierrors.IsNotFound guard that the old Delete used was removed. NotFound on get/delete is a normal client result (the playlist tests even delete twice and expect it). Those calls will flood error logs and hide real storage failures. Log NotFound at a higher verbosity, or not at all, and keep Error for unexpected failures.

Legacy update no longer writes the object stored in unified storage

The previous Update loaded the unified object, ran objInfo.UpdatedObject once, and passed an updateWrapper so Legacy.Update received the exact object just written to unified storage. That wrapper is gone. Legacy.Update is now invoked with the original objInfo, so it loads the legacy row and re-runs UpdatedObject plus the client's preconditions against that row. Mode 3 serves reads from unified storage, so the resourceVersion on the update is the unified one and will not match legacy; a normal precondition check fails the legacy update with a conflict and the backup copy is never updated. Even if legacy ignores resourceVersion, a patch is applied to drifted legacy state instead of replacing it with the unified result, so the stores diverge. Delete has the same precondition problem: line 112 forwards the caller's DeleteOptions, including a unified-storage resourceVersion precondition, into Legacy.Delete.

Legacy write failures are not logged

The goroutines in Create (line 56), Delete (line 113), Update (line 140), and DeleteCollection (line 166) only feed the legacy error into a duration metric and otherwise discard it. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy create/update/delete/delete-collection failures. With writes now best-effort and easy to cancel, a broken legacy path produces no log line, so operators cannot tell which object diverged or why (conflict, timeout, cancelled context, validation). Log errObjectSt/err with the object name before recording the metric.

Mode 3 playlist tests assume legacy is updated before the handler returns

The new mode 3 cases (file at line 132, unified storage at line 191, etcd at line 287) reuse doPlaylistTests. That helper creates, updates, and deletes through the k8s client and then immediately requires the legacy /api/playlists API to match (search at line 529 and getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 returns after the unified write and only then writes legacy on another goroutine whose context is tied to the request. The legacy HTTP read therefore races the backup write and, because that context is cancelled when the request ends, will often never see the object. These new integration cases will fail or flake until the test waits for the legacy write or the dual writer detaches that work from request cancellation.

Unified NotFound skips the legacy delete

Delete returns immediately on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound, and never starts the legacy delete. The previous implementation still deleted from legacy when unified storage returned NotFound, and only treated other errors as fatal. After a failed or cancelled legacy delete, a retry sees NotFound in unified storage (the source of truth for reads) and now leaves the legacy object in place permanently. Orphans also remain for objects that exist only in legacy. NotFound should still be returned to the client, but the async legacy delete should run so the backup store is cleaned up.

Unit tests never check that the legacy write happens

Mode 3 success tests register legacy mock expectations but return as soon as the unified call finishes (Create at line 65, and the same pattern in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection) and never call AssertExpectations or wait for the goroutine. The defining behavior — an asynchronous legacy write — is therefore untested, and a cancelled or skipped legacy call still passes. Legacy and unified also share one testify mock, so method names like Create cannot be attributed to a store; the "unified store fails" create case only stubs the legacy Create expectation, which the synchronous storage call consumes by accident. testify mocks are not thread-safe, so the background call can also race or panic after the test function returns.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock does not re-check cache, so waiters reload and can clear it

GetWebAssets copies entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, drops that lock, and only then takes the write lock. It never looks at the cache again after Lock. Every caller that observed a nil cache—the concurrent first requests this change is meant to protect—runs the manifest load while holding the exclusive lock and then unconditionally assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result. A later waiter whose load fails stores nil and wipes an entry an earlier waiter already published, so following non-dev calls miss the cache and reload. Even when every load succeeds, the missing re-check serializes a full disk read per waiter instead of returning the value the first loader stored. After acquiring the write lock, return the existing cache when Env is not Dev and it is already set, and do not replace a populated cache with a failed nil result.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock does not re-check cache, so waiters reload and can clear it

GetWebAssets copies entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, drops that lock, and only then takes the write lock. It never looks at the cache again after Lock. Every caller that observed a nil cache—the concurrent first requests this change is meant to protect—runs the manifest load while holding the exclusive lock and then unconditionally assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result. A later waiter whose load fails stores nil and wipes an entry an earlier waiter already published, so following non-dev calls miss the cache and reload. Even when every load succeeds, the missing re-check serializes a full disk read per waiter instead of returning the value the first loader stored. After acquiring the write lock, return the existing cache when Env is not Dev and it is already set, and do not replace a populated cache with a failed nil result.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL gate is an inverted no-op that can panic and misreports the feature

enableSqlExpressions is the only explicit SQL-expression gate, but it is not a real flag check. It sets enabled to the negation of FlagSqlExpressions and then returns false from both branches, so the flag cannot turn the feature back on. That matches the security intent, but it hides the kill switch, and the error returned to callers (line 131) is "sqlExpressions is not implemented", which is false — the feature existed and is being disabled because of the RCE/LFI vulnerability. The flag read also panics if ExpressionQueryReader.features is nil. This case did not touch features before, so a reader built without toggles now crashes on SQL queries instead of returning a controlled error. Return false without reading the flag, and use an error that says SQL expressions are disabled.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy SQL path fails as invalid SQL and error-logs every query

The explicit reject added in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery does not cover the frontend entry point. UnmarshalSQLCommand always calls NewSQLCommand, and NewSQLCommand still calls sql.TablesList for every non-empty expression. reader.go itself notes that ExpressionQueryReader has not replaced the existing parser, so this is the path dashboard and alert evaluation use. TablesList now always fails because the stub RunCommands returns an error, and that failure is mapped to a BadRequest whose public message is "error reading SQL command" (lines 33-35). That text is wrong: the statement was not parsed or rejected as invalid SQL; the DuckDB engine was removed to close the RCE/LFI issue. Before returning, TablesList logs the raw expression and the assembled SELECT json_serialize_sql(...) command at Error (pkg/expr/sql/parser.go:28), and NewSQLCommand logs the raw SQL again at Warn (line 32). Instances that had enabled SQL expressions will therefore show a misleading invalid-query error and emit error-level logs containing the expression text on every panel refresh and every alert evaluation. Reject the feature in NewSQLCommand/UnmarshalSQLCommand before calling TablesList, with a stable disabled-feature error, and do not log the statement at Error.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test that SQL expressions stay disabled

This change set is the in-tree fix for the SQL-expression RCE/LFI issue, but it adds or updates no tests. Nothing asserts that ReadQuery rejects SQL queries even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, that UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand fail closed without executing a statement, or that DB.RunCommands and DB.QueryFramesInto do not run SQL or touch the filesystem. The disable is an always-false helper with inverted flag logic plus stub methods that return "not implemented". Restoring a DuckDB call inside RunCommands, or changing the helper so the feature flag reaches NewSQLCommand while a later DB implementation executes queries, would not fail CI. Add a regression test for both entry points that expects a disabled-feature error with the flag on and asserts the supplied statement is not executed.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Same-key index builds are no longer single-flighted

BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the whole build, so a second GetIndex blocked until the finished index was published. The mutex is now taken only around the cache insert. getOrCreateIndex still does check-then-act (GetIndex, and on a miss build) and even has a TODO that same-key builds must not run together. After startup, two Search calls, or a Search and a watch event, for a namespace that was not built during init (count at or below InitMinCount) both see a cache miss and both call BuildIndex. Memory indexes both succeed and the later cache write overwrites the earlier one without closing it, so documents already written to the discarded index disappear from search and the Bleve index is leaked. File indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory; the loser fails with a path-exists error, so the caller gets a search error even if the other build published a usable index. Parallel builds of different keys are fine, but same-key builds need a per-key lock or singleflight held from the existence check through cache publish.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs ranges the index cache without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no RLock, while BuildIndex writes that map under cacheMu. Narrowing the lock means builds now publish into the map concurrently, during startup and for later cold namespaces. In Go, a concurrent map read and write is a fatal runtime error, not a missed update. init also calls TotalDocs immediately after starting the watch goroutine that can BuildIndex on a cache miss, and TotalDocs is part of the SearchBackend interface so any other caller can hit the same crash. Hold cacheMu.RLock for the whole iteration.

false_positives.candidate:
File-backed indexes cannot be reopened, so restart fails startup

When size is above FileThreshold (the zero value is 0, so any positive count takes this branch unless the option is overridden), BuildIndex calls bleve.New on a directory under Root and never bleve.Open. bleve.New fails if that path already exists, and a failed builder returns without closing the index or removing a partial directory. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer and any error aborts construction, so a restart after a successful file index, or a retry after a build that left the directory behind, cannot start the storage server. The comment that was removed even said the last RV should be checked so an unchanged index can be skipped. Open an existing index when the directory is present, and delete or uniquely name the directory if a build fails, or every file-backed namespace wedges process startup.

Init failure in the constructor leaks the backend and watchers

NewResourceServer calls Init and, on error, logs and returns nil without calling cancel or Stop. lifecycle.Init may already have opened the database. If search.init succeeded and initWatcher then failed, search.init has already started a WatchWriteEvents poller and an event goroutine on context.Background. The caller never receives the server, so it cannot Stop those resources, and the connection pool and pollers live until the process exits. On the error path, stop the lifecycle/backend and cancel the server context, while still returning the original init error.

Parallel index builders share err and can hide failures

Each errgroup worker assigns s.build's result to the outer err variable and then returns err. When WorkerThreads is greater than 1 those goroutines race on that variable. A failed build can return nil if another worker stores nil into err before the return, so group.Wait succeeds and NewResourceServer starts with some namespaces never indexed. A successful worker can also return another worker's error and fail startup. This is a real data race, not just a logic race. totalBatchesIndexed is incremented from the same goroutines with no synchronization, so the trace attribute is racy as well. Use a local error inside the closure and an atomic counter.

Search index misses writes committed during startup indexing

init lists every namespace and only afterward calls WatchWriteEvents. That snapshot records the latest resource version and the SQL poller only returns history newer than that snapshot. The RV returned by build is discarded. Any create, update, or delete committed after a namespace was listed and before the watch snapshot, including writes from other HA replicas, is neither in the bulk index nor replayed. The watch starts only after the slowest namespace finishes, so namespaces that finished early have a gap as long as the rest of the index build, which is the long operation this change is about. Search will keep serving missing, stale, or already-deleted objects until that document is written again. Record the RV before listing, or buffer watch events first, and replay history from that RV after the bulk load.

Search watch loop panics when the event channel closes

After indexing, init starts a goroutine that loops on v := <-events and calls handleEvent, using context.Background rather than the server context. The SQL backend poller closes that channel when the backend stops (it selects on backend done and defers close). A receive on a closed channel yields a nil event, and handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type, which panics. An unrecovered goroutine panic crashes the process during graceful shutdown, skipping the rest of cleanup. server.Stop cannot stop the loop because it only cancels s.ctx. The loop must exit when the channel is closed or the context is cancelled, and the watch must be tied to the server lifetime.

Startup index build cannot be cancelled or given a deadline

The context now used for the full index build is created from context.Background inside NewResourceServer, which does not accept a caller context. The only cancel is Stop, and Stop cannot run until NewResourceServer returns, which is blocked on GetResourceStats and every ListIterator in the index build. A stuck database call therefore hangs process startup with no deadline, and a shutdown signal cannot abort the build. The old request context cancelled too early; this replacement needs a long but bounded startup context that process shutdown can cancel.

Storage-server integration test is skipped on Postgres

TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration coverage for the storage-server target, and this PR makes that target initialize unified storage and build the search index during construction. The change skips the test whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB is postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone but works locally. Postgres is a primary deployment database, so CI no longer runs storage-server startup there, and a startup regression from eager init will not be caught. Fix the Postgres failure instead of skipping it.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Login-cache test never removes the IdPs it creates

testCacheIDPForLogin registers cleanup as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove (line 381 inside the create loop, and again at line 425) instead of the alias just created (idp-alias-N). The method reference is bound to a proxy for the literal alias "alias", so the 20 providers this test creates are never removed, and cleanup may DELETE a non-existent alias. This class does not otherwise delete those brokers: onAfter only removes a user named member. The new test links ten of them to whichever organization getAll().get(0) returns and asserts exact login-cache sizes (5, 10, 11). Leftover public enabled IdPs change those counts on another run and will also change testCacheIDPByOrg, which asserts an exact getByOrganization size of 6 for the same organization. The new test is therefore order-dependent on the pre-existing leak in testCacheIDPByOrg (same wrong "alias" cleanup). Clean up each created alias (and unlink org brokers) so the realm is isolated.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Cached getForLogin results have unstable order

getForLogin stores delegate ids with Collectors.toSet() and, on a hit, copies them into another HashSet before returning identityProviders.stream(). Set iteration order is undefined and can change between requests even when membership is unchanged. The previous implementation was the interface default, which returned the delegate getAllStream order. OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean sorts that stream with IDP_COMPARATOR_INSTANCE; List.sort is stable, so providers that compare equal (the usual case when guiOrder is unset or tied, if the comparator has no unique tiebreaker) keep this random order and can swap on the login page on every load. Callers that do not sort lose the previous query order entirely. Cache and return the ids in encounter order (List or LinkedHashSet), not a HashSet.

Login-list invalidation uses wrapped isEnabled as membership

update() takes the pre-image from getById() (line 91) and passes it to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate. With the organization feature on, getById() returns the organization-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() is false unless the IdP is enabled and its organization exists, the organization provider is enabled, and the organization itself is enabled. LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() applies ENABLED via IdentityProviderModel::isEnabled, so that override runs. The login list is filled from the JPA delegate's getForLogin, which filters only stored enabled / link-only / hide-on-login plus organization id and kc.org.broker.public, not organization enabled state. If an org-linked IdP is updated while its organization is disabled or missing, the wrapped original already fails the predicate. If the update also makes the raw model ineligible (hide-on-login, link-only, disabled, or broker-public turned off), both sides fail and the method returns without invalidating the .idp.login.* keys. The id stays in the cached set. A later getForLogin expands those ids with getById and does not re-apply hide-on-login, link-only, broker-public, or organization-id checks. OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled(). After the organization is enabled again, that broker is shown on the login page even though it was configured as hidden, link-only, or not public, and getForLogin breaks its contract. The same skip happens when the organization feature is off if the caller mutates the instance returned by getByAlias/getById and passes it to update(): createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel then returns the cached model without copying, so the before/after comparison sees only the new state. Load the pre-image from the JPA delegate (raw flags, not the wrapper) or always invalidate the login keys, and drop resolved models that no longer match the requested mode. testCacheIDPForLogin never updates an org-linked login IdP while the org is disabled, so this is untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider

CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() is specified to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS Provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the platform keystore provider (SUN for the Java 8 default JKS keystore, and typically SUN for the Java 9+ default PKCS12 keystore). That provider is not BC and does not implement ECDSA (SHA256withECDSA and the other SHA*withECDSA algorithms are on SunEC). Callers that pass this object to Signature.getInstance or Cipher.getInstance, or that treat a non-null result as "BC is available" / compare the name to BC or BCFIPS, will throw NoSuchAlgorithmException or take a non-BC path. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null for the same method to mean there is no BC; a non-null wrong provider bypasses those null checks. Return null or throw; do not hand back the keystore provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() is a new abstract method and breaks existing implementations

order() was added to the public CryptoProvider interface with no default body. In-tree Default, Elytron, and FIPS implementations were updated, but any already-compiled implementor (a downstream or older crypto provider jar, or a test double) has no order() method. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider loads every provider via ServiceLoader and then calls CryptoProvider::order. That invocation throws AbstractMethodError and aborts detection entirely, so init fails even if a valid newer provider is also on the classpath. Source compatibility for external implementors is broken as well. Give the method a default that is higher than AuthzClientCryptoProvider's 100 (for example default int order() { return 200; }) so existing providers still outrank the authz-client stub and do not crash provider detection.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
AuthzClient.create permanently latches the process-wide crypto provider

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) before building the client. init only runs detection while the static cryptoProvider field is null; later calls, including the server's own init, are ignored. Detection uses ServiceLoader on that classloader only, which does not see providers visible solely on a child or thread-context classloader. If this runs first in a JVM whose view of the classpath is the authz-client jar (AuthzClientCryptoProvider, order 100) without Default, Elytron, or FIPS (order 200), the stub is installed for the whole process and cannot be replaced. The stub throws UnsupportedOperationException for getSignature, getPemUtils, ciphers, certificate utilities, and truststore wrapping, so a later embedded server or in-process testsuite that expected its own CryptoProvider fails on ordinary crypto calls. Do not latch a lower-priority provider forever: also search the context classloader, and allow a later init to replace the current provider when a higher-order one is found.

ECDSAAlgorithmTest cannot compile with this module's dependencies

ECDSAAlgorithmTest imports org.keycloak.crypto.ECDSAAlgorithm and org.keycloak.crypto.JavaAlgorithm and calls ECDSAAlgorithm.getSignatureLength() and JavaAlgorithm.getJavaAlgorithm(). Those types live in keycloak-server-spi, not in keycloak-core. authz/client/pom.xml only depends on keycloak-core (plus logging, httpclient, and jackson); this PR adds junit and hamcrest but not keycloak-server-spi. Maven test-compile of keycloak-authz-client-tests will fail with cannot find symbol, so the only test of the new ECDSA ASN.1 conversion never runs. Add a test-scoped dependency on the module that contains org.keycloak.crypto, or stop referencing those types and hardcode the JCA algorithm names and signature lengths.

ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key and never check DER with JCA

The suite builds one KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and no ECGenParameterSpec, so the JDK default curve (secp256r1) is used for testES256, testES384, and testES512. ES384 and ES512 therefore never produce 48-byte or 66-byte R and S values; those components stay about 32 bytes and are only zero-padded to 96 or 132. Every real ES512 DER signature uses a long-form SEQUENCE length (content longer than 127 bytes), so ASN1Encoder.writeLength and ASN1Decoder.readLength's long-form path is never executed. The only assertion is that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip to each other. The DER from concatenatedRSToASN1DER is not passed to Signature.verify and is not compared to the original JCA signature, so an encoder that this decoder accepts but JCA or another JOSE stack rejects still passes, including for ES256. Initialize P-256, P-384, and P-521 for the matching algorithms and verify the converted DER with Signature.verify.

Tied crypto providers are chosen silently instead of failing startup

detectProvider used to abort startup with IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It now sorts by order() descending and keeps the first, logging the rest only at debug. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so they tie, and ServiceLoader/classpath enumeration order picks the winner. A deployment that contains both the FIPS provider and a non-FIPS provider, which previously refused to boot, now starts and can run non-FIPS algorithms with no warn or error. Constructors of every discovered provider still run before the choice, so the non-selected provider has already mutated JVM security state (provider insertion, securerandom.strongAlgorithms, KeyManagerFactory/TrustManagerFactory properties) while the process continues. Nothing in this PR tests two providers that share the top order. Fail when more than one provider shares the highest order (AuthzClientCryptoProvider at 100 can still coexist with a single order-200 provider), and if a priority is intended give FIPS a strictly higher order than Default and Elytron.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Null Clients type resource NPEs permission checks

When no per-client authorization resource exists, hasPermission sets resource from AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource and immediately calls PolicyStore.findByResource(server, resource) with no null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null if the Clients type resource was never created (init skips existing admin-permissions clients) or was deleted. findByResource then dereferences null and the admin call fails with 500 instead of denying the permission. Treat a null type resource as no all-clients permission.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

false_positives.candidate:
A per-client resource suppresses all-clients permissions

hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) loads the authorization resource named with the client id and, if that row exists, evaluates only that resource. The Clients type resource (all clients) is consulted only when no per-client resource exists. A per-client resource is created for any permission that targets that client, including a permission for a different user or a different scope. An administrator granted manage, configure, view, or map-roles on all clients then loses that grant on the client, because their all-clients policy is attached to the type resource and is never evaluated; a per-client grant of scope A also hides an all-clients grant of scope B. Evaluate both resources, and let a per-client policy override all-clients only for the scopes that policy actually covers. PermissionClientTest only covers a lone per-client grant or a lone all-clients grant, never both.

All-clients view bypasses an explicit per-client view deny

ClientPermissionsV2.canView(ClientModel) returns true as soon as canView() is true. canView() is true not only for the view-clients/manage-clients admin roles, but also when a fine-grained permission grants the view scope on the Clients resource type (all clients). The per-client check is then skipped, so a Logic.NEGATIVE view permission for that same caller on one client is never evaluated. requireView(client) and every admin operation gated on canView(client) (client representation, protocol mappers, client scopes) still succeed for the client that was explicitly denied. Negative permissions are already part of this model (user FGAP tests use Logic.NEGATIVE on the same permission API). Short-circuit only on the admin-role helper (canViewClientDefault), then evaluate the per-client decision so an explicit deny overrides all-clients view. The new client tests never create a negative permission, so this bypass is untested.

Client deletion throws when v1 and v2 admin-permission features are both enabled

The removal listener runs when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (v1) is enabled and then calls management().clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException. The two flags are independent, so enabling v2 does not turn v1 off. Deleting a client then throws from the provider event listener and can roll back the removal. Guard the v1 cleanup with the same condition management() uses (v1 evaluator actually selected), or make the v2 removal path a no-op instead of throwing. Role and group removal in this listener call management() as well; clients() is the override that now throws.

Client permission resources are returned with a null display name

getResourceName resolves Users policies to "All users" or the username, but has no Clients branch and falls through to resource.getDisplayName(). Per-client resources are stored with the client UUID as the name and no display name, and the all-clients resource is stored as name "Clients" without a display name, so the admin permissions API returns null. The console cannot show which client a permission applies to, unlike users in the same API. Resolve the stored id to the clientId, return a label such as "All clients" for the type resource, and fail clearly if the client no longer exists, matching the user path.

Client tests rotate myclient's secret and leave realm mutations behind

testConfigureOnlyOneClient calls generateNewSecret and invalidateRotatedSecret on myclient and never restores the original secret. realmAdminClient is injected as client myclient using the secret from the realm config, and AbstractPermissionTest's @InjectRealm does not request a per-method lifecycle, so the realm is shared by every method in the class. The next test that must obtain a token authenticates with a secret that no longer exists and fails. The same class also leaves other shared state: testManageOnlyOneClient renames myclient and moves a default client scope to optional, and testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient creates myclient-role and myclient-subRole with no cleanup. AfterEach only deletes scope permissions. Restore the secret, name, and scopes, and delete the roles, or results depend on test order.

Existing admin-permissions clients never receive the Clients schema

AdminPermissionsSchema.init returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and that is the only place schema scopes and the per-type all-resource records are created. This change adds the Clients resource type and the configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes, but realms that already enabled admin permissions V2 already have that client (created earlier with only Users). After upgrade those scopes and the Clients resource are never inserted, so creating a Clients permission fails with a missing-scope validation error and all-clients evaluation cannot find the type resource. init must add any schema scopes and resource types that are not already present instead of treating a non-null admin-permissions client as fully initialized.

canExchangeTo throws instead of returning an authorization decision

ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException. AdminPermissions.evaluator installs this class whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and token exchange calls clients().canExchangeTo to decide whether the caller may exchange into another client's audience. That call now fails the token request with an unhandled server error instead of allow or deny. The same class throws from isPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, and setPermissionsEnabled; this PR only guards the removal listener, and only behind the v1 feature flag. A boolean permission check must not throw — return false until exchange is actually implemented (getEvaluationContext in this class is unused). Otherwise enabling v2 breaks token exchange and any client management-permissions endpoint that still reaches these methods.

requireView javadoc claims a boolean result for void methods

requireView and requireViewClientScopes are void and throw ForbiddenException when the matching can* check is false, but the new javadoc says each "Returns true if canView()/canViewClientScopes() returns true". That describes the boolean methods, not these require* methods. Neighboring require* docs correctly say they throw ForbiddenException. Callers reading the interface will think these methods return a decision instead of aborting the request.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Caution falsely says the Operator fails without rolling-updates

The new caution says that during preview the `rolling-updates` feature must be enabled or the Keycloak Operator will fail. That contradicts both the note later in this same section and the operator test added in this PR. UpgradeTest.createInitialDeployment returns immediately when the update strategy is null and does not set spec.features.enabled to rolling-updates. Those cases still call deployKeycloak with wait-for-ready, and a cache max-count change is expected to roll rather than fail. So a normal Keycloak CR reconciles, becomes ready, and applies the documented 26.1-compatible default (recreate only on image change, roll on other config) with the preview feature off. The feature is only enabled in that test when spec.update.strategy is set explicitly. As written, the caution tells every Operator user that an upgrade breaks unless they turn on a preview feature, which will cause unnecessary preview opt-in or blocked upgrades. Narrow the warning to explicit spec.update usage, or change the test if fail-closed is actually required.

Changed exit codes 3 and 4 are never asserted

This PR changes CompatibilityResult.RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 and adds FEATURE_DISABLED = 4, and the guide tells users to branch automation on those codes. testFeatureNotEnabled only checks that stderr contains the disabled-feature sentence and never asserts the process exit code is 4; it also covers only the metadata subcommand, not check. testWrongVersions only checks the incompatibility log line and never asserts exit code 3. CLIResult.assertError succeeds for any non-zero status, so leaving recreate at 4, or picocli.exit collapsing the custom code to 1, would still pass. That docs-vs-code mismatch (docs already said 3, the constant was 4) is exactly what this PR is fixing, and nothing locks the new contract.

Exit code 4 is documented as an upgrade decision

The new exit-code row says code 4 means "Rolling Upgrade is not possible" because `rolling-updates` is disabled. That is the same decision wording as exit code 3, and the paragraph above the table says these codes are how automation determines the upgrade type. The implementation does not decide compatibility: both update-compatibility check and update-compatibility metadata print "Unable to use this command. The preview feature 'rolling-updates' is not enabled." and exit 4 before reading metadata or comparing versions. The only other upgrade type this guide defines is recreate (shut the deployment down before applying config). A pipeline that treats "rolling is not possible" as that outcome will take an unnecessary outage when the flag was merely omitted. Describe code 4 as a precondition failure, state that the upgrade type was not determined, and note that the metadata subcommand returns 4 as well; the table currently sits only under the check command.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-groups VIEW is treated as permission to manage groups

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns true if hasPermission finds either the VIEW or MANAGE scope on the all-groups resource. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup authorizes group creation with requireManage(), which calls this method, and any other caller of canManage()/requireManage() treats it as a write check. A fine-grained admin granted only view access to groups can therefore create top-level groups. That contradicts canManage(GroupModel) in the same class, which correctly requires only MANAGE, and contradicts V1, which only checks the manage-users role. The new javadoc on GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage repeats the same mistake by documenting VIEW as sufficient. canManage() must require the MANAGE scope only.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Group-scoped user search and counts use authorization resource ids, not group ids

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission is what UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource pass to the user store (session attribute UserModel.GROUPS, and getUsersCount) so that an admin who cannot view all users only sees members of groups they may view. The callback passes groupResource.getId() into hasPermission and stores that same value. hasPermission treats the argument as a group id and looks it up with resourceStore.findByName, but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource stores the group id as the resource name and the authorization store assigns a different resource id. The lookup therefore misses. findByType(GROUPS) also cannot see per-group resources, because getOrCreateResource never calls setType, so only the type resource named "Groups" (if present) is visited. The set ends up empty or filled with authorization UUIDs. User search pagination then either is not restricted to the permitted groups or is restricted to ids that match no membership, and the count API returns 0 or a count for a non-existent group. Return the group id (resource name), skip the type resource, and persist instance resources with type Groups.

false_positives.candidate:
A per-group permission resource hides all-groups grants

hasPermission looks up the per-group resource by name and, if it exists, evaluates only that resource. The all-groups resource is used only when no per-group resource exists. Creating any permission on a group (including one for a different administrator) creates that resource, after which an admin who holds VIEW or MANAGE on all groups is denied for that group because their all-groups policy is never evaluated. canView, canManage, canViewMembers, canManageMembers, and canManageMembership all go through this helper. GroupsResource.getGroups and GroupResource.getSubGroups no longer short-circuit on global canView() and now depend entirely on canView(group), so listing is affected as well. The new tests never combine an all-groups grant with a specific grant for another user. Evaluation has to combine the instance resource and the resource-type resource under the schema decision strategy; preferring the instance resource drops legitimate grants and also drops all-groups denies when only the instance is evaluated.

Existing admin-permissions clients never gain the Groups schema

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and no other path creates the Groups resource type, the "Groups" all-resource, or the new scopes manage-membership, manage-members, and view-members. Realms that already enabled fine-grained admin permissions (the client was created when only Users and Clients existed) do not pick up this change, and turning admin permissions off and on does not help if the client row remains. Creating a group permission then fails in getScope with "Scope [view-members] does not exist". GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission also calls getResourceTypeResource, gets null, and invokes policyStore.findByResource and resource.getScopes() with no null check, so group admin calls from users without manage-users/view-users become 500s instead of a deny. Upgrade must add the missing scopes and the Groups type resource to existing admin-permissions clients, or init/getResourceTypeResource must create them lazily.

Group deletion throws when FGAP V2 is enabled

GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException (as do the other GroupPermissionManagement methods). AdminPermissions.registerListener still handles GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent by calling management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled. management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, and therefore GroupPermissionsV2, whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. With both features on, which is the normal combination if V1 is a default feature and V2 is enabled for this work, realm.removeGroup and the admin delete-group API fail with that exception and the group is not removed. If only V2 is enabled, the listener is not registered at all, so the V2 authorization resource named by the group id is never deleted and remains orphaned on the admin-permissions client. Group removal needs a V2 cleanup path; the V1 listener must not call the throwing methods while V2 is active.

Group permission resources have no human-readable name

getResourceName resolves only the Users resource type ("All users" or the username) and otherwise returns resource.getDisplayName(). Group resources created by getOrCreateResource use the group id as the name and never set a display name, and the new Groups type is not handled here. Permission listings for group policies therefore show a null name or a raw id instead of the group name or path, and there is no "All groups" label for the type resource. A missing user already throws ModelIllegalStateException; a missing group is silently unlabeled. Resolve group resources the same way users are resolved.

Public group permission methods were removed and renamed

GroupPermissionEvaluator is public. This change deletes getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel) and renames getGroupsWithViewPermission() to getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() with no bridge method. In-repo callers were updated, but any extension that implements the interface or calls the old methods will fail to compile or throw NoSuchMethodError at runtime. If this interface is part of the supported admin-permissions contract, keep the old methods as deprecated delegates; otherwise call the break out in the release notes.

requireManageMembers javadoc cites the wrong check

The javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws ForbiddenException when canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. The implementation enforces canManageMembers, which is the manage-members scope, not manage-membership. Those are different permissions (managing the users in a group versus changing a user's group membership). An implementor or caller following the javadoc will check or document the wrong scope.

false_positives.candidate:
Account UI error message no longer interpolates

error-invalid-multivalued-size was changed from i18next placeholders ({{0}}, {{1}}, {{2}}) to a Java MessageFormat choice string ({0} / {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}). This bundle is for the React account console. Sibling validation messages in the same file (error-invalid-length-too-short, error-number-out-of-range, and so on) still use {{0}} and {{1}}. i18next will not substitute {0} and does not understand ChoiceFormat, so a multivalued profile-attribute failure is shown to the user as the raw pattern, including the choice syntax, instead of the attribute name and the min/max limits. The '<' only needed special handling in the Java theme checker; this frontend string must keep {{ }} placeholders.

Admin UI error message switched to MessageFormat

error-invalid-multivalued-size in the keycloak.v2 admin UI bundle was changed from {{0}}/{{1}}/{{2}} to Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}. That bundle is loaded by the React admin console, whose other parameterized messages use i18next {{ }} interpolation. ChoiceFormat is not evaluated there, so admins see the literal {0} and {2,choice,...} text when a multivalued attribute fails size validation. The Java MessageFormat version belongs only in the server theme bundles (themes/.../admin and login), not in this UI file.

Choice-format exemption skips HTML sanitizing normalizeValue deletes every {n,choice,...} subformat (replaced with "...") before the OWASP sanitizer runs, for linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit* and error-invalid-multivalued-size. The comment says the intent is only to ignore the '<' ChoiceFormat operator, but the regex drops the entire subformat, so markup inside it is never compared to English and never sanitized. verifySafeHtml loads both the translation and the English bundle with new PropertyResourceBundle(FileInputStream) (lines 68 and 77). That constructor decodes properties as ISO-8859-1. The checker therefore does not see the string that will be rendered. When sanitized text differs from the message, the code trims the shared prefix and suffix and then calls value.substring(start, value.length() - end) and sanitized.substring(start, sanitized.length() - end). The suffix walk is allowed to overlap the prefix, so start can be greater than length - end. true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor null-checks grantType instead of rawTokenId

The fourth Objects.requireNonNull still passes grantType, with the message Null rawTokenId not allowed. A null rawTokenId is accepted. encodeTokenId concatenates the raw id with string +, so null becomes the literal suffix :null. Every such token shares that jti suffix, so ids are no longer unique, and the constructor does not enforce the invariant it claims.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Access-token id matcher is inverted and reads the wrong slice

isAccessTokenId is what expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, and expectAuthReqIdToToken now use to assert the new jti. The grant shortcut is characters at indexes 4 and 5 of the six-character prefix (onrtac is ac), but the matcher uses substring(3, 5), which is ta for that id. The condition is also backwards: it returns false when that slice equals the expected shortcut. For every built-in shortcut these helpers pass, the wrong slice is not equal to the expected value, so the inverted check does not fire and any id with a colon and a UUID suffix passes, including the na fallback used when GRANT_TYPE was never set. The new assertions therefore do not fail if grant encoding is missing or wrong, and they never check session type or token type. A prefix shorter than 5 characters throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException from the matcher instead of a mismatch.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grant shortcuts are not constrained to the two-character encoding

Decoding assumes every grant shortcut is exactly two characters and contains no colon, so the prefix is always six characters and the first colon separates the raw id. getShortcut() is documented as usually like a 3-letter shortcut, and postInit only checks that the two maps end up the same size. A unique shortcut of any other length is stored, encodeTokenId writes it into the jti, and getTokenContextFromTokenId then throws IllegalArgumentException because the prefix length is not 6. That exception text says the token id is expected to have length 6, but the check is only on the prefix; a valid id is six characters, a colon, and a UUID, so the message is wrong. The lazy reload in getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut, meant for grants deployed after startup, inserts the new shortcut with no length check and no collision check, so a duplicate shortcut overwrites another grant and later tokens decode as the wrong grant type.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
First offline access token is encoded as an online session

createTokenResponse calls createClientAccessToken, which stamps the jti session-type from userSession.isOffline(), before generateRefreshToken() and before the online session may be deleted. On the first offline_access response the login session is still online at that point, so the prefix is online (on…). Lines 116-120 then issue an offline refresh token and, when the FIRST_OFFLINE_ACCESS note is set, remove that online user session. Offline sessions live in a separate store but keep the same session id, so today's validation only finds the session by falling back from online to offline. The prefix names the store that no longer holds the session. Callers that use it to pick a single store, which is the stated reason for encoding session type, will miss the session and reject the access token returned with that first offline refresh token. ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType has the same order and is stricter: generateAccessToken() at line 139 runs first, then any offline refresh token causes removeUserSession at lines 142-146, not only the first-offline-access case. Later refreshes are fine because the loaded session is already offline. No test issues an offline_access token and checks the session-type characters.

getShortcut() has no default and breaks existing grant factories at startup

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an existing extension SPI, and getShortcut() was added as a new abstract method with no default implementation. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit loads every OAuth2GrantTypeFactory and calls getShortcut(). A custom grant factory built against the previous interface throws AbstractMethodError there, and Keycloak fails to start. A default method that returns a stable two-character fallback would keep existing providers loading.

setFormParams leaves the cached grant type stale

Context snapshots grant_type from the constructor form parameters, and getGrantType() returns that field. setFormParams replaces formParams but does not update grantType. A caller that uses this public setter to change the request parameters after construction will encode the original grant type, or na if the original map had no grant_type, rather than the grant type actually being processed. The getter should read the current form parameters, or the setter should refresh the cached value.

true_positives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recovery-code login form crashes unless storage returns Keycloak's internal model

The bean loads a credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential and immediately calls Optional.get() and RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel. That parser requires credentialData and secretData in the hashed recovery-code schema and throws NoSuchElementException or RuntimeException otherwise. When user storage's updateCredential returns true, createRecoveryCodesCredential does not persist that model; it only sends a JSON array of raw codes on a UserCredentialModel. isConfiguredFor can still be true, so the authenticator renders this bean. A provider that stores the updateCredential payload and returns it, or that implements supportsCredentialType, updateCredential, isConfiguredFor, and isValid but not getCredentials, makes recovery-code login fail with a server error before a code can be submitted. There is no fallback to a local credential or a default index. Only the test storage papers over this by rebuilding a model in getCredentials.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getCredentials drops the stored id and renumbers codes

updateCredential sets an id with KeycloakModelUtils.generateId, but getCredentials ignores that CredentialModel and returns a new one from RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues. That factory does not copy the stored id and assigns fresh indexes starting at 0 to whatever list it is given. The same method now sets an id on OTP credentials because listing and deletion need it; recovery codes are returned with a null id, so account-console delete and removeStoredCredentialById cannot target them. If used codes are removed from the stored list, the remainder is renumbered and the login page asks for code 0 instead of the next original number. The rebuilt view also cannot be written back: its credentialData is metadata JSON, not the raw list isValid reads.

false_positives.candidate:
New test never checks replay, next-code index, revocation, or local fallback

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only checks that setup writes no Keycloak DB credential, that the storage flag is set, and that the first displayed code logs in once. It never submits that code again, never asserts a later login asks for the next index, never disables or deletes the credential, and never covers a user storage that returns false from updateCredential so the helper must keep the local hashed credential. Those are the paths this change adds and the ones the new storage implementation gets wrong, so the suite stays green while replay and revocation are broken.

Plaintext recovery codes are sent to user storage

createRecoveryCodesCredential JSON-encodes the raw generatedCodes list and puts that string in the UserCredentialModel passed to updateCredential. The RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel argument already contains only hashes. Local storage persists those hashes; this path gives the federation provider every unused code in cleartext and drops userLabel and generatedAt, so they cannot be stored either. BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage writes that string unchanged into credentialData and keeps it for later equality checks. A storage dump or credential-update log discloses all backup codes, which authenticate as the user. Verification only needs the existing hashRawCode/verifyRecoveryCodeInput helpers, so the hashed secret data should be what is handed off, and the reference provider should not keep reversible codes.

Recovery codes cannot be disabled in the new storage support

disableCredentialType clears OTP and otherwise only logs that the type is unsupported. getDisableableCredentialTypesStream only reports OTP, so recovery-authn-codes is not advertised as disableable. Admin REST disableCredentialType and account-console removal therefore leave myUser.recoveryCodes set. isConfiguredFor stays true and isValid still accepts the codes, so an administrator cannot revoke recovery codes after this provider has stored them.

User-storage recovery codes are reusable and not ordered

isValid deserializes the stored raw code list and returns true if any entry equals the submitted value, then leaves the list unchanged. Recovery codes are one-time and must be used in order: the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider hashes the input, matches only the next remaining code, and deletes it. credentialManager().isValid stops at the user-storage validator when that provider supports and is configured for the type, so the local provider never runs for credentials accepted by CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator does not consume the code after a successful check; it only re-reads the credential. The same backup code can be replayed forever, and a code other than the one the login form requested is accepted. The new test logs in only once, so it does not catch this.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing delegate makes getSubGroupsCount return null

When the cached group has already been deleted, getSubGroupsCount returns null instead of a count. GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount copies that value straight into GroupRepresentation.subGroupCount, so a list request that races with a delete can return 200 with a group whose subGroupCount is null. Other GroupModel implementations do not do this: a subgroup count query returns 0 when the parent row is gone, and null is also how the admin API signals that the count was not requested. Callers that unbox the Long (comparisons, arithmetic, longValue()) still NPE, so the crash is moved out of this method rather than removed. Return 0L when modelSupplier.get() is null.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrency test never joins the reader and can miss the race

createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti starts a non-daemon reader that calls groups() in a loop, but never waits for that thread to enter the loop or to finish. deletedAll is set true immediately after the deletes and caughtExceptions is asserted on the next line, so the assertion can run before any list call has started or before an in-flight list has recorded its exception. A regression of the original NPE can therefore pass CI. There is also no finally that stops and joins the thread: if group.remove() throws before deletedAll.set(true), the reader stays in while (!deletedAll.get()) forever, keeps issuing admin requests against the shared realm for the rest of the suite, and can hang JVM shutdown because the thread is not a daemon. The same managedRealm.admin() client is used from both threads, so a client-side concurrency failure is also treated as a product failure. Start the reader behind a latch, delete only after it has begun, and in a finally set the stop flag and join with a timeout before asserting.

false_positives.candidate:
Paged subgroup streams still NPE if the group was deleted

The null-delegate race is only handled in getSubGroupsCount. The paged overloads still dereference the lazy delegate unconditionally: getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer) at line 256, getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer) at line 262, and getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer) at line 268 all do modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...). If the group was removed after the CachedGroup was loaded, modelSupplier.get() returns null and these methods throw NullPointerException. Those overloads back the admin children API (search and pagination), so delete-while-list still returns 500 on that endpoint. Guard the null delegate the same way and return Stream.empty() instead of chaining the call.

The checker therefore does not see the string that will be rendered. OWASP's sanitizer strips specific code points such as bidi overrides (U+202E and similar) only when they are real Unicode characters; read as Latin-1 those UTF-8 bytes are different characters and are not removed, so a translation can carry them and still compare equal after sanitize. Reported "Illegal HTML" snippets for non-English files will also be mojibake. Use PropertyResourceBundle(new InputStreamReader(fis, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) for both files.

Illegal-HTML diff can throw and abort the plugin

When sanitized text differs from the message, the code trims the shared prefix and suffix and then calls value.substring(start, value.length() - end) and sanitized.substring(start, sanitized.length() - end). The suffix walk is allowed to overlap the prefix, so start can be greater than length - end. Example: value "aaa<x>aaa" becomes "aaaaaa" after a disallowed tag is removed; start is 3 and end is 4, and sanitized.substring(3, 2) throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. That exception is not caught in verify() (only IOException is wrapped in MojoExecutionException), so one offending message crashes the Maven plugin with a stack trace instead of recording the violation and continuing with the other keys and files. The new tests use short non-overlapping diffs, so they do not catch this.

loginTotpStep1 was changed to "Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:". That sentence is Italian. The login page for the lt locale will show Italian setup instructions instead of Lithuanian. Replace it with a Lithuanian translation of the English loginTotpStep1 ("Install one of the following applications on your mobile:").

Decoding assumes every grant shortcut is exactly two characters and contains no colon, so the prefix is always six characters and the first colon separates the raw id. getShortcut() is documented as usually like a 3-letter shortcut, and postInit only checks that the two maps end up the same size. A unique shortcut of any other length is stored, encodeTokenId writes it into the jti, and getTokenContextFromTokenId then throws IllegalArgumentException because the prefix length is not 6. That exception text says the token id is expected to have length 6, but the check is only on the prefix; a valid id is six characters, a colon, and a UUID, so the message is wrong. The lazy reload in getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut, meant for grants deployed after startup, inserts the new shortcut with no length check and no collision check, so a duplicate shortcut overwrites another grant and later tokens decode as the wrong grant type.

The candidate goes into deeper detail about the runtime consequences of this mismatch, but clearly covers the core documentation discrepancy pointed out in the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
First offline access token is encoded as an online session

createTokenResponse calls createClientAccessToken, which stamps the jti session-type from userSession.isOffline(), before generateRefreshToken() and before the online session may be deleted. On the first offline_access response the login session is still online at that point, so the prefix is online (on…). Lines 116-120 then issue an offline refresh token and, when the FIRST_OFFLINE_ACCESS note is set, remove that online user session. Offline sessions live in a separate store but keep the same session id, so today's validation only finds the session by falling back from online to offline. The prefix names the store that no longer holds the session. Callers that use it to pick a single store, which is the stated reason for encoding session type, will miss the session and reject the access token returned with that first offline refresh token. ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType has the same order and is stricter: generateAccessToken() at line 139 runs first, then any offline refresh token causes removeUserSession at lines 142-146, not only the first-offline-access case. Later refreshes are fine because the loaded session is already offline. No test issues an offline_access token and checks the session-type characters.

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an existing extension SPI, and getShortcut() was added as a new abstract method with no default implementation. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit loads every OAuth2GrantTypeFactory and calls getShortcut(). A custom grant factory built against the previous interface throws AbstractMethodError there, and Keycloak fails to start. A default method that returns a stable two-character fallback would keep existing providers loading.

setFormParams leaves the cached grant type stale

Context snapshots grant_type from the constructor form parameters, and getGrantType() returns that field. setFormParams replaces formParams but does not update grantType. A caller that uses this public setter to change the request parameters after construction will encode the original grant type, or na if the original map had no grant_type, rather than the grant type actually being processed. The getter should read the current form parameters, or the setter should refresh the cached value.

When user storage's updateCredential returns true, createRecoveryCodesCredential does not persist that model; it only sends a JSON array of raw codes on a UserCredentialModel. isConfiguredFor can still be true, so the authenticator renders this bean. A provider that stores the updateCredential payload and returns it, or that implements supportsCredentialType, updateCredential, isConfiguredFor, and isValid but not getCredentials, makes recovery-code login fail with a server error before a code can be submitted. There is no fallback to a local credential or a default index. Only the test storage papers over this by rebuilding a model in getCredentials.

While the candidate elaborates heavily on the architectural reasons why the Optional might be empty or invalid, and the golden comment also mentions raw List deserialization, they both clearly point to the exact same unchecked Optional.get() bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getCredentials drops the stored id and renumbers codes

updateCredential sets an id with KeycloakModelUtils.generateId, but getCredentials ignores that CredentialModel and returns a new one from RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues. That factory does not copy the stored id and assigns fresh indexes starting at 0 to whatever list it is given. The same method now sets an id on OTP credentials because listing and deletion need it; recovery codes are returned with a null id, so account-console delete and removeStoredCredentialById cannot target them. If used codes are removed from the stored list, the remainder is renumbered and the login page asks for code 0 instead of the next original number. The rebuilt view also cannot be written back: its credentialData is metadata JSON, not the raw list isValid reads.
