false_positives.candidate:
User-storage recovery codes are reusable and not ordered

isValid deserializes the stored raw code list and returns true if any entry equals the submitted value, then leaves the list unchanged. Recovery codes are one-time and must be used in order: the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider hashes the input, matches only the next remaining code, and deletes it. credentialManager().isValid stops at the user-storage validator when that provider supports and is configured for the type, so the local provider never runs for credentials accepted by CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator does not consume the code after a successful check; it only re-reads the credential. The same backup code can be replayed forever, and a code other than the one the login form requested is accepted. The new test logs in only once, so it does not catch this.

Plaintext recovery codes are sent to user storage

createRecoveryCodesCredential JSON-encodes the raw generatedCodes list and puts that string in the UserCredentialModel passed to updateCredential. The RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel argument already contains only hashes. Local storage persists those hashes; this path gives the federation provider every unused code in cleartext and drops userLabel and generatedAt, so they cannot be stored either. BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage writes that string unchanged into credentialData and keeps it for later equality checks. A storage dump or credential-update log discloses all backup codes, which authenticate as the user. Verification only needs the existing hashRawCode/verifyRecoveryCodeInput helpers, so the hashed secret data should be what is handed off, and the reference provider should not keep reversible codes.

Recovery codes cannot be disabled in the new storage support

disableCredentialType clears OTP and otherwise only logs that the type is unsupported. getDisableableCredentialTypesStream only reports OTP, so recovery-authn-codes is not advertised as disableable. Admin REST disableCredentialType and account-console removal therefore leave myUser.recoveryCodes set. isConfiguredFor stays true and isValid still accepts the codes, so an administrator cannot revoke recovery codes after this provider has stored them.

New test never checks replay, next-code index, revocation, or local fallback

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only checks that setup writes no Keycloak DB credential, that the storage flag is set, and that the first displayed code logs in once. It never submits that code again, never asserts a later login asks for the next index, never disables or deletes the credential, and never covers a user storage that returns false from updateCredential so the helper must keep the local hashed credential. Those are the paths this change adds and the ones the new storage implementation gets wrong, so the suite stays green while replay and revocation are broken.

Caution falsely says the Operator fails without rolling-updates

The new caution says that during preview the `rolling-updates` feature must be enabled or the Keycloak Operator will fail. That contradicts both the note later in this same section and the operator test added in this PR. UpgradeTest.createInitialDeployment returns immediately when the update strategy is null and does not set spec.features.enabled to rolling-updates. Those cases still call deployKeycloak with wait-for-ready, and a cache max-count change is expected to roll rather than fail. So a normal Keycloak CR reconciles, becomes ready, and applies the documented 26.1-compatible default (recreate only on image change, roll on other config) with the preview feature off. The feature is only enabled in that test when spec.update.strategy is set explicitly. As written, the caution tells every Operator user that an upgrade breaks unless they turn on a preview feature, which will cause unnecessary preview opt-in or blocked upgrades. Narrow the warning to explicit spec.update usage, or change the test if fail-closed is actually required.

Exit code 4 is documented as an upgrade decision

The new exit-code row says code 4 means "Rolling Upgrade is not possible" because `rolling-updates` is disabled. That is the same decision wording as exit code 3, and the paragraph above the table says these codes are how automation determines the upgrade type. The implementation does not decide compatibility: both update-compatibility check and update-compatibility metadata print "Unable to use this command. The preview feature 'rolling-updates' is not enabled." and exit 4 before reading metadata or comparing versions. The only other upgrade type this guide defines is recreate (shut the deployment down before applying config). A pipeline that treats "rolling is not possible" as that outcome will take an unnecessary outage when the flag was merely omitted. Describe code 4 as a precondition failure, state that the upgrade type was not determined, and note that the metadata subcommand returns 4 as well; the table currently sits only under the check command.

Changed exit codes 3 and 4 are never asserted

This PR changes CompatibilityResult.RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 and adds FEATURE_DISABLED = 4, and the guide tells users to branch automation on those codes. testFeatureNotEnabled only checks that stderr contains the disabled-feature sentence and never asserts the process exit code is 4; it also covers only the metadata subcommand, not check. testWrongVersions only checks the incompatibility log line and never asserts exit code 3. CLIResult.assertError succeeds for any non-zero status, so leaving recreate at 4, or picocli.exit collapsing the custom code to 1, would still pass. That docs-vs-code mismatch (docs already said 3, the constant was 4) is exactly what this PR is fixing, and nothing locks the new contract.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client deletion throws when v1 and v2 admin-permission features are both enabled

The removal listener runs when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (v1) is enabled and then calls management().clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException. The two flags are independent, so enabling v2 does not turn v1 off. Deleting a client then throws from the provider event listener and can roll back the removal. Guard the v1 cleanup with the same condition management() uses (v1 evaluator actually selected), or make the v2 removal path a no-op instead of throwing. Role and group removal in this listener call management() as well; clients() is the override that now throws.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same inconsistency in the AdminPermissions removal event listener, where the listener is guarded by the V1 feature flag (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) while the underlying methods in the class check the V2 feature flag (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2). Although they highlight slightly different failure modes resulting from this mismatch (orphaned permissions vs. throwing an exception when both are enabled), they point to the exact same bug in the same location.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.

Treat a null type resource as no all-clients permission.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

canExchangeTo throws instead of returning an authorization decision

ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException. AdminPermissions.evaluator installs this class whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and token exchange calls clients().canExchangeTo to decide whether the caller may exchange into another client's audience. That call now fails the token request with an unhandled server error instead of allow or deny. A boolean permission check must not throw — return false until exchange is actually implemented (getEvaluationContext in this class is unused). However, the candidate explicitly identifies the exact issue mentioned in the golden comment in parentheses: '(getEvaluationContext in this class is unused)'. Since it catches the unused method, it is a partial/incidental match, though the primary recommendation is not to remove the unused method.

false_positives.candidate:
All-clients view bypasses an explicit per-client view deny

ClientPermissionsV2.canView(ClientModel) returns true as soon as canView() is true. canView() is true not only for the view-clients/manage-clients admin roles, but also when a fine-grained permission grants the view scope on the Clients resource type (all clients). The per-client check is then skipped, so a Logic.NEGATIVE view permission for that same caller on one client is never evaluated. requireView(client) and every admin operation gated on canView(client) (client representation, protocol mappers, client scopes) still succeed for the client that was explicitly denied. Negative permissions are already part of this model (user FGAP tests use Logic.NEGATIVE on the same permission API). Short-circuit only on the admin-role helper (canViewClientDefault), then evaluate the per-client decision so an explicit deny overrides all-clients view. The new client tests never create a negative permission, so this bypass is untested.

A per-client resource suppresses all-clients permissions

hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) loads the authorization resource named with the client id and, if that row exists, evaluates only that resource. The Clients type resource (all clients) is consulted only when no per-client resource exists. A per-client resource is created for any permission that targets that client, including a permission for a different user or a different scope. An administrator granted manage, configure, view, or map-roles on all clients then loses that grant on the client, because their all-clients policy is attached to the type resource and is never evaluated; a per-client grant of scope A also hides an all-clients grant of scope B. Evaluate both resources, and let a per-client policy override all-clients only for the scopes that policy actually covers. PermissionClientTest only covers a lone per-client grant or a lone all-clients grant, never both.

Existing admin-permissions clients never receive the Clients schema

AdminPermissionsSchema.init returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and that is the only place schema scopes and the per-type all-resource records are created. This change adds the Clients resource type and the configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes, but realms that already enabled admin permissions V2 already have that client (created earlier with only Users). After upgrade those scopes and the Clients resource are never inserted, so creating a Clients permission fails with a missing-scope validation error and all-clients evaluation cannot find the type resource. init must add any schema scopes and resource types that are not already present instead of treating a non-null admin-permissions client as fully initialized.

Client permission resources are returned with a null display name

getResourceName resolves Users policies to "All users" or the username, but has no Clients branch and falls through to resource.getDisplayName(). Per-client resources are stored with the client UUID as the name and no display name, and the all-clients resource is stored as name "Clients" without a display name, so the admin permissions API returns null. The console cannot show which client a permission applies to, unlike users in the same API. Resolve the stored id to the clientId, return a label such as "All clients" for the type resource, and fail clearly if the client no longer exists, matching the user path.

testConfigureOnlyOneClient calls generateNewSecret and invalidateRotatedSecret on myclient and never restores the original secret. realmAdminClient is injected as client myclient using the secret from the realm config, and AbstractPermissionTest's @InjectRealm does not request a per-method lifecycle, so the realm is shared by every method in the class. The next test that must obtain a token authenticates with a secret that no longer exists and fails. The same class also leaves other shared state: testManageOnlyOneClient renames myclient and moves a default client scope to optional, and testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient creates myclient-role and myclient-subRole with no cleanup. requireView and requireViewClientScopes are void and throw ForbiddenException when the matching can* check is false, but the new javadoc says each "Returns true if canView()/canViewClientScopes() returns true". That describes the boolean methods, not these require* methods. Neighboring require* docs correctly say they throw ForbiddenException. getGroupIdsWithViewPermission is what UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource pass to the user store (session attribute UserModel.GROUPS, and getUsersCount) so that an admin who cannot view all users only sees members of groups they may view. GroupsResource.getGroups and GroupResource.getSubGroups no longer short-circuit on global canView() and now depend entirely on canView(group), so listing is affected as well. The new tests never combine an all-groups grant with a specific grant for another user. Evaluation has to combine the instance resource and the resource-type resource under the schema decision strategy; preferring the instance resource drops legitimate grants and also drops all-groups denies when only the instance is evaluated.

Existing admin-permissions clients never gain the Groups schema

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and no other path creates the Groups resource type, the "Groups" all-resource, or the new scopes manage-membership, manage-members, and view-members. Realms that already enabled fine-grained admin permissions (the client was created when only Users and Clients existed) do not pick up this change, and turning admin permissions off and on does not help if the client row remains. Creating a group permission then fails in getScope with "Scope [view-members] does not exist". GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission also calls getResourceTypeResource, gets null, and invokes policyStore.findByResource and resource.getScopes() with no null check, so group admin calls from users without manage-users/view-users become 500s instead of a deny. Upgrade must add the missing scopes and the Groups type resource to existing admin-permissions clients, or init/getResourceTypeResource must create them lazily.

Group permission resources have no human-readable name

getResourceName resolves only the Users resource type ("All users" or the username) and otherwise returns resource.getDisplayName(). Group resources created by getOrCreateResource use the group id as the name and never set a display name, and the new Groups type is not handled here. Permission listings for group policies therefore show a null name or a raw id instead of the group name or path, and there is no "All groups" label for the type resource. A missing user already throws ModelIllegalStateException; a missing group is silently unlabeled. Resolve group resources the same way users are resolved.

requireManageMembers javadoc cites the wrong check

The javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws ForbiddenException when canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. The implementation enforces canManageMembers, which is the manage-members scope, not manage-membership. Those are different permissions (managing the users in a group versus changing a user's group membership). An implementor or caller following the javadoc will check or document the wrong scope.

Public group permission methods were removed and renamed

GroupPermissionEvaluator is public. This change deletes getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel) and renames getGroupsWithViewPermission() to getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() with no bridge method. In-repo callers were updated, but any extension that implements the interface or calls the old methods will fail to compile or throw NoSuchMethodError at runtime. If this interface is part of the supported admin-permissions contract, keep the old methods as deprecated delegates; otherwise call the break out in the release notes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider

CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() is specified to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS Provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the platform keystore provider (SUN for the Java 8 default JKS keystore, and typically SUN for the Java 9+ default PKCS12 keystore). That provider is not BC and does not implement ECDSA (SHA256withECDSA and the other SHA*withECDSA algorithms are on SunEC). Callers that pass this object to Signature.getInstance or Cipher.getInstance, or that treat a non-null result as "BC is available" / compare the name to BC or BCFIPS, will throw NoSuchAlgorithmException or take a non-BC path. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null for the same method to mean there is no BC; a non-null wrong provider bypasses those null checks. Return null or throw; do not hand back the keystore provider.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies that `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns the default keystore provider (`KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`) instead of BouncyCastle, which is the exact same issue described in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() is a new abstract method and breaks existing implementations

order() was added to the public CryptoProvider interface with no default body. In-tree Default, Elytron, and FIPS implementations were updated, but any already-compiled implementor (a downstream or older crypto provider jar, or a test double) has no order() method. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider loads every provider via ServiceLoader and then calls CryptoProvider::order. That invocation throws AbstractMethodError and aborts detection entirely, so init fails even if a valid newer provider is also on the classpath. Source compatibility for external implementors is broken as well. Give the method a default that is higher than AuthzClientCryptoProvider's 100 (for example default int order() { return 200; }) so existing providers still outrank the authz-client stub and do not crash provider detection.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue point out that adding an abstract `order()` method to the `CryptoProvider` interface without a default implementation breaks backward compatibility for existing implementations.

false_positives.candidate:
Tied crypto providers are chosen silently instead of failing startup

detectProvider used to abort startup with IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It now sorts by order() descending and keeps the first, logging the rest only at debug. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so they tie, and ServiceLoader/classpath enumeration order picks the winner. A deployment that contains both the FIPS provider and a non-FIPS provider, which previously refused to boot, now starts and can run non-FIPS algorithms with no warn or error. Constructors of every discovered provider still run before the choice, so the non-selected provider has already mutated JVM security state (provider insertion, securerandom.strongAlgorithms, KeyManagerFactory/TrustManagerFactory properties) while the process continues. Nothing in this PR tests two providers that share the top order. Fail when more than one provider shares the highest order (AuthzClientCryptoProvider at 100 can still coexist with a single order-200 provider), and if a priority is intended give FIPS a strictly higher order than Default and Elytron.

ECDSAAlgorithmTest cannot compile with this module's dependencies

ECDSAAlgorithmTest imports org.keycloak.crypto.ECDSAAlgorithm and org.keycloak.crypto.JavaAlgorithm and calls ECDSAAlgorithm.getSignatureLength() and JavaAlgorithm.getJavaAlgorithm(). Those types live in keycloak-server-spi, not in keycloak-core. authz/client/pom.xml only depends on keycloak-core (plus logging, httpclient, and jackson); this PR adds junit and hamcrest but not keycloak-server-spi. Maven test-compile of keycloak-authz-client-tests will fail with cannot find symbol, so the only test of the new ECDSA ASN.1 conversion never runs. Add a test-scoped dependency on the module that contains org.keycloak.crypto, or stop referencing those types and hardcode the JCA algorithm names and signature lengths.

ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key and never check DER with JCA

The suite builds one KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and no ECGenParameterSpec, so the JDK default curve (secp256r1) is used for testES256, testES384, and testES512. ES384 and ES512 therefore never produce 48-byte or 66-byte R and S values; those components stay about 32 bytes and are only zero-padded to 96 or 132. Every real ES512 DER signature uses a long-form SEQUENCE length (content longer than 127 bytes), so ASN1Encoder.writeLength and ASN1Decoder.readLength's long-form path is never executed. The only assertion is that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip to each other. The DER from concatenatedRSToASN1DER is not passed to Signature.verify and is not compared to the original JCA signature, so an encoder that this decoder accepts but JCA or another JOSE stack rejects still passes, including for ES256. Initialize P-256, P-384, and P-521 for the matching algorithms and verify the converted DER with Signature.verify.

AuthzClient.create permanently latches the process-wide crypto provider

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) before building the client. init only runs detection while the static cryptoProvider field is null; later calls, including the server's own init, are ignored. Detection uses ServiceLoader on that classloader only, which does not see providers visible solely on a child or thread-context classloader. If this runs first in a JVM whose view of the classpath is the authz-client jar (AuthzClientCryptoProvider, order 100) without Default, Elytron, or FIPS (order 200), the stub is installed for the whole process and cannot be replaced. The stub throws UnsupportedOperationException for getSignature, getPemUtils, ciphers, certificate utilities, and truststore wrapping, so a later embedded server or in-process testsuite that expected its own CryptoProvider fails on ordinary crypto calls. Do not latch a lower-priority provider forever: also search the context classloader, and allow a later init to replace the current provider when a higher-order one is found.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing delegate makes getSubGroupsCount return null

When the cached group has already been deleted, getSubGroupsCount returns null instead of a count. GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount copies that value straight into GroupRepresentation.subGroupCount, so a list request that races with a delete can return 200 with a group whose subGroupCount is null. Other GroupModel implementations do not do this: a subgroup count query returns 0 when the parent row is gone, and null is also how the admin API signals that the count was not requested. Callers that unbox the Long (comparisons, arithmetic, longValue()) still NPE, so the crash is moved out of this method rather than removed. Return 0L when modelSupplier.get() is null.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrency test never joins the reader and can miss the race

createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti starts a non-daemon reader that calls groups() in a loop, but never waits for that thread to enter the loop or to finish. deletedAll is set true immediately after the deletes and caughtExceptions is asserted on the next line, so the assertion can run before any list call has started or before an in-flight list has recorded its exception. A regression of the original NPE can therefore pass CI. There is also no finally that stops and joins the thread: if group.remove() throws before deletedAll.set(true), the reader stays in while (!deletedAll.get()) forever, keeps issuing admin requests against the shared realm for the rest of the suite, and can hang JVM shutdown because the thread is not a daemon. The same managedRealm.admin() client is used from both threads, so a client-side concurrency failure is also treated as a product failure. Start the reader behind a latch, delete only after it has begun, and in a finally set the stop flag and join with a timeout before asserting.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same concurrency bug in the test: not waiting for/joining the reader thread after setting `deletedAll` to true, causing a race condition where the assertion can run before an in-flight operation records its exception.

The null-delegate race is only handled in getSubGroupsCount. true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Comma-separated shard list is emitted as one metric tag

shard_tag is the comma-joined list of every shard that process handles, and it is sent as the shard tag on spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes, and as shards on spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce. DogStatsD encodes tags as a comma-separated key:value list and does not escape commas inside values, so a tag like shard:0,1,2 is parsed as shard:0 plus stray tags 1 and 2. Those timers and gauges will be dropped or attributed to the wrong series. With the CLI default --flusher-processes 1, every assigned partition is concatenated into that single value, so this breaks as soon as the consumer has more than one partition, not only when multiple flusher processes are enabled. The value also changes on every rebalance (high cardinality) and can exceed backend tag-length limits. wait_produce uses the key shards while the other metrics use shard, so they would not group together even after the value is fixed. The unhealthy counter already tags one shard id; the produce metrics should do the same, or use a bounded process index, and must not embed commas. The same comma-joined string is also set as the Sentry tag sentry_spans_buffer_shards.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same inconsistency described in the golden comment: 'wait_produce uses the key shards while the other metrics use shard, so they would not group together even after the value is fixed.' Although the candidate also discusses the formatting of the tag value (comma-separated list), it directly captures the golden comment's core issue regarding inconsistent tag keys ('shard' vs 'shards') across those specific metrics.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_basic wait after advancing drift is a no-op

test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op so the flusher does not block, then calls time.sleep(0.1) after setting current_drift to 9000, with a comment that this gives the flusher time to process. That call uses the same patched time.sleep, so it returns immediately and does not wait. step.join() sets SpanFlusher.stopped before it waits for the worker; if the worker has not yet observed the advanced drift and produced, it leaves its loop and the (msg,) = messages assertion fails. The synchronization added to fix that race does not run. Save the original time.sleep before monkeypatching and wait on that saved function (the flusher looks up time.sleep at call time, so it will still see the no-op), and only then join.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_basic wait after advancing drift is a no-op

test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op so the flusher does not block, then calls time.sleep(0.1) after setting current_drift to 9000, with a comment that this gives the flusher time to process. That call uses the same patched time.sleep, so it returns immediately and does not wait. step.join() sets SpanFlusher.stopped before it waits for the worker; if the worker has not yet observed the advanced drift and produced, it leaves its loop and the (msg,) = messages assertion fails. true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can return without stopping every flusher process

SpanFlusher.join sets stopped, then calls next_step.join(timeout) before waiting on flusher workers. The deadline is that same timeout, and the new loop breaks as soon as it has passed, skipping process.terminate() for every worker not yet visited. If next_step.join consumes the timeout, or the first stuck worker uses up the rest, the remaining shard flushers are never signaled. close() intentionally does not stop them, so join() is the only shutdown path. Those workers are daemons, but the consumer process stays up across rebalances, so a leaked flusher keeps calling flush_segments and producing to the buffered-segments topic for shards that may already have been revoked and assigned to another consumer. That races Redis flush state and emits duplicate segments. This is a regression from the previous single-process join, which always called terminate() after the wait even if the deadline had already passed. Workers that do get terminate() are never join()ed, so join() can return while they are still alive, and there is no try/finally, so an exception from next_step.join skips cleanup entirely. Always stop every worker (kill if needed) and join() it, including on the timeout and exception paths.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: breaking out of the loop early when the timeout/deadline has elapsed skips calling `terminate()` on the remaining flusher processes, leaving them running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
Flusher restart does not wait for the old worker to exit

When a flusher is unhealthy, _ensure_processes_alive calls kill() only for multiprocessing.Process, then _create_process_for_shards starts a replacement and overwrites self.processes without joining the previous worker. kill() returns before the process has actually died, and the old Process object is dropped, so the supervisor no longer tracks it and never reaps it. The thread backend used whenever produce_to_pipe is set is not interrupted at all (kill/terminate are skipped for non-Process workers). A hung thread therefore keeps flushing the same shards after a new thread is started; each hang restart adds another live flusher until MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS trips, and those threads all call flush_segments and produce, duplicating segments and racing done_flush_segments. On the process backend the replacement is spawned while the killed worker may still be inside Redis flush or Kafka produce. Join (or join-after-kill) the old worker, and do not start a second thread while the first is alive, before creating the replacement.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Flagged table widgets render an empty hardcoded table

When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, `tableResultComponent` ignores `result.data`, `result.meta`, column fields, aliases, and the loading state and instead renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with `columns={[]}` and `tableData.data: []`. An empty `columns` array is truthy, so the visualization will not infer columns from meta either. Any org with that flag on sees blank dashboard table widgets instead of the query results.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: passing hardcoded empty data and columns to `TableWidgetVisualization` when the feature flag is enabled causes it to render an empty table instead of actual query results.

false_positives.candidate:
Suspect-issue PR comments call helpers that are not on the workflow class

`get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` and `get_environment_info` are defined on `CommitContextIntegration` (the class that ends just before `OpenPRCommentWorkflow`), but `GitHubPRCommentWorkflow` and `GitlabPRCommentWorkflow` call them as `self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template(...)` / `self.get_environment_info(issue)`. Those workflow classes subclass `PRCommentWorkflow`, which holds an integration rather than inheriting these methods. The static helper also does `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title)`, and `_truncate_title` is not defined on `PRCommentWorkflow`. Generating a merged-PR suspect-issue comment therefore raises AttributeError, so the GitHub/GitLab comment task fails and no comment is posted.

Replay error context reads title/message that stored events do not have

`fetch_error_details` builds the Seer log from `data.get("title")` and `data.get("message")` on the raw nodestore payload. Stored error events usually keep the exception under `exception.values` / `metadata` (`type` and `value`); `title` is computed on the Event model and is often absent, and `message` is frequently empty. The log becomes `User experienced an error: ': ' at ...`, so exception type and value never reach the summary. The new test expects `ZeroDivisionError` and `division by zero` in that log after storing an exception-only event, which this field choice does not produce.

Error events are not ordered against replay segment timestamps

Chronological merge compares nodestore `timestamp` (unix seconds, and sometimes an ISO-8601 string) with the raw segment event `timestamp`. Recording segments are rrweb payloads whose timestamps are milliseconds. A seconds value is always less than a millisecond timestamp, so every error is emitted before every breadcrumb; if the stored timestamp is a string, `str < float` raises TypeError and the summarize request 500s. That is a regression for replays that have linked errors, because this endpoint previously summarized breadcrumbs without this comparison. The unit test avoids it by fabricating segment timestamps in seconds.

Error IDs are queried with page-filter dates the AI tab never sends

Error IDs now come from `query_replay_instance` using `start`/`end` from `get_filter_params(request, project)`. Segment loading (`fetch_segments_metadata`) does not use that window. The replay AI tab calls `/replays/{id}/summarize/breadcrumbs/` with no `statsPeriod`, `start`, or `end`. Depending on the default stats period, either the request 400s (breaking an endpoint that previously did not need dates) or error lookup is limited to a window shorter than replay retention, so older replays are summarized with no error context while their breadcrumbs still load.

Hidden span attributes are only removed while searching

`HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` (`is_segment`, `project_id`, `received`) is applied only inside the `searchQuery` branch. When the search box is empty the function returns `sortAttributes(attributes)` unfiltered, so those fields still render. When the user searches, the same names are excluded even if the query matches them. The hide list needs to apply before the search filter, not instead of the unfiltered list.

60s deadline is too short for a 100-identity refresh batch

`check_auth_identities` now has `processing_deadline_duration=60`, but `check_auth` still enqueues up to `chunk_size` (default 100) identities and this task refreshes them sequentially via external IdP calls. That routinely exceeds 60s. `check_auth` already sets `last_synced=now` before the task runs, so if the worker kills the task and does not retry the same id list, the unfinished identities are skipped until the next ~24h cycle and SSO validity is not refreshed. If it does retry, the same chunk keeps timing out and hammering the IdP.

Report URL validation rejects real browser documents and aborts the batch

`url` is a DRF `URLField`, whose default validator only allows http(s)/ftp. Reporting API document URLs include `about:blank`, `blob:`, `chrome-extension:`, and `file:` URLs, so those reports fail validation. The handler then returns 422 on the first invalid item and does not record metrics for any later valid reports in the same array. Browsers post mixed batches, and the previous dataclass path accepted unknown types and non-http URLs and still counted them.

Feedback summary ignores the environment page filter

The summary request sends the normalized datetime and `selection.projects`, but not `selection.environments`. The feedback list page is wrapped in page filters, so the list and search respect the environment selector while the summary does not. A user filtered to one environment still gets a summary of feedback from every environment in the project/date range, which can contradict the list beside it.

Trace waterfall wrapper dropped height: 100%

The waterfall root was a flex column with `flex-grow: 1` and `height: 100%`. It is now `<Flex direction="column" flex={1}>`, which does not set `height: 100%`. The trace view sizes this pane with a height chain rather than only flex-grow, so the waterfall can collapse and the virtualized span tree no longer fills the viewport.

Custom cell renderers cannot return falsy nodes

Both head and body renderers treat any falsy return as "use the fallback" (`if (cell)`), but the documented contract is that only `undefined` means fallback. A custom renderer that returns `0`, `''`, or `null` (valid React output, and a reasonable way to blank a cell) is discarded and the default field renderer runs instead.

Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-controlled negative offsets are sliced into the audit-log query

The mutex is now taken only around the cache insert. getOrCreateIndex still does check-then-act (GetIndex, and on a miss build) and even has a TODO that same-key builds must not run together. Memory indexes both succeed and the later cache write overwrites the earlier one without closing it, so documents already written to the discarded index disappear from search and the Bleve index is leaked. File indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory; the loser fails with a path-exists error, so the caller gets a search error even if the other build published a usable index. Narrowing the lock means builds now publish into the map concurrently, during startup and for later cold namespaces. In Go, a concurrent map read and write is a fatal runtime error, not a missed update. init also calls TotalDocs immediately after starting the watch goroutine that can BuildIndex on a cache miss, and TotalDocs is part of the SearchBackend interface so any other caller can hit the same crash. false_positives.candidate:
Search index misses writes committed during startup indexing

init lists every namespace and only afterward calls WatchWriteEvents. That snapshot records the latest resource version and the SQL poller only returns history newer than that snapshot. The RV returned by build is discarded. Any create, update, or delete committed after a namespace was listed and before the watch snapshot, including writes from other HA replicas, is neither in the bulk index nor replayed. The watch starts only after the slowest namespace finishes, so namespaces that finished early have a gap as long as the rest of the index build, which is the long operation this change is about. Search will keep serving missing, stale, or already-deleted objects until that document is written again. Record the RV before listing, or buffer watch events first, and replay history from that RV after the bulk load.

Parallel index builders share err and can hide failures

Each errgroup worker assigns s.build's result to the outer err variable and then returns err. When WorkerThreads is greater than 1 those goroutines race on that variable. A failed build can return nil if another worker stores nil into err before the return, so group.Wait succeeds and NewResourceServer starts with some namespaces never indexed. A successful worker can also return another worker's error and fail startup. This is a real data race, not just a logic race. totalBatchesIndexed is incremented from the same goroutines with no synchronization, so the trace attribute is racy as well. Use a local error inside the closure and an atomic counter.

Search watch loop panics when the event channel closes

After indexing, init starts a goroutine that loops on v := <-events and calls handleEvent, using context.Background rather than the server context. The SQL backend poller closes that channel when the backend stops (it selects on backend done and defers close). A receive on a closed channel yields a nil event, and handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type, which panics. An unrecovered goroutine panic crashes the process during graceful shutdown, skipping the rest of cleanup. server.Stop cannot stop the loop because it only cancels s.ctx. The loop must exit when the channel is closed or the context is cancelled, and the watch must be tied to the server lifetime.

File-backed indexes cannot be reopened, so restart fails startup

When size is above FileThreshold (the zero value is 0, so any positive count takes this branch unless the option is overridden), BuildIndex calls bleve.New on a directory under Root and never bleve.Open. bleve.New fails if that path already exists, and a failed builder returns without closing the index or removing a partial directory. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer and any error aborts construction, so a restart after a successful file index, or a retry after a build that left the directory behind, cannot start the storage server. The comment that was removed even said the last RV should be checked so an unchanged index can be skipped. Open an existing index when the directory is present, and delete or uniquely name the directory if a build fails, or every file-backed namespace wedges process startup.

Init failure in the constructor leaks the backend and watchers

NewResourceServer calls Init and, on error, logs and returns nil without calling cancel or Stop. lifecycle.Init may already have opened the database. If search.init succeeded and initWatcher then failed, search.init has already started a WatchWriteEvents poller and an event goroutine on context.Background. The caller never receives the server, so it cannot Stop those resources, and the connection pool and pollers live until the process exits. On the error path, stop the lifecycle/backend and cancel the server context, while still returning the original init error.

Startup index build cannot be cancelled or given a deadline

The context now used for the full index build is created from context.Background inside NewResourceServer, which does not accept a caller context. The only cancel is Stop, and Stop cannot run until NewResourceServer returns, which is blocked on GetResourceStats and every ListIterator in the index build. A stuck database call therefore hangs process startup with no deadline, and a shutdown signal cannot abort the build. The old request context cancelled too early; this replacement needs a long but bounded startup context that process shutdown can cancel.

TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration coverage for the storage-server target, and this PR makes that target initialize unified storage and build the search index during construction. The change skips the test whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB is postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone but works locally. Postgres is a primary deployment database, so CI no longer runs storage-server startup there, and a startup regression from eager init will not be caught. Fix the Postgres failure instead of skipping it.

false_positives.candidate:
Rebalance kills the shared pool and later results are committed unprocessed

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategies, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/join and ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown both call queue_pool.shutdown(). Arroyo calls close() then join(), then create_with_partitions() again on every assignment, including ordinary rebalances during deploys. shutdown() stops the workers and Queue.shutdown()s the queues, so later Queue.put raises queue.ShutDown. The new strategy still submits into that dead pool; submit()'s except block marks the offset complete without calling the result processor, and the new strategy's commit thread commits those offsets through the new commit callback. In the steady state the queues are empty, so nothing is outstanding and the commit cursor advances: those uptime results are skipped permanently. If a backlog left outstanding offsets, commits freeze and processing never resumes until the process is restarted. The OffsetTracker is also shared and never reset, so revoked partitions and the new assignment share one cursor. Recreate the pool per create_with_partitions (and tear it down only with that strategy), or do not shut the pool down on strategy close.

Offset commits run on a background thread against the Kafka consumer

_commit_loop is a daemon thread started from SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls commit_function, which invokes Arroyo's commit callback (result_consumer commit_offsets). That callback stages or commits offsets on the Kafka consumer. The confluent_kafka Consumer is not thread-safe, and Arroyo runs submit/poll and its own ONCE_PER_SECOND commit on the processor thread that owns the consumer. Committing from this side thread races with poll() and can raise inside librdkafka, commit a torn offset map, or deadlock when close() joins the commit thread while it is inside the callback and the callback needs the processor thread. Perform commits from poll() and from join/close on the processor thread, and force a final commit there after in-flight work has finished.

Unbounded queues never apply backpressure and can OOM the consumer

Each work queue is queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and submit() always put()s without blocking or raising MessageRejected. The class docstring says queues provide natural backpressure, but they never fill. If handling is slower than the topic, or one item is slow, the consumer keeps polling and retains every later message in the queues, in WorkItem (full payload), and in OffsetTracker.all_offsets, because a commit cannot move past the oldest outstanding offset on that partition. get_committable_offsets then walks range(start, max_offset+1) while holding the partition lock every second, so a large backlog also stalls workers completing offsets. poll() only emits a gauge, so the healthcheck keeps succeeding until the process OOMs. This is worse than batched-parallel, which caps memory at max_batch_size, under the exact slow-item failure this mode is meant to solve. Bound the queues and signal backpressure from submit so read-ahead stays finite and the processor can still poll. A worker that exits is also never restarted, so one dead thread permanently stalls its queue and that partition's commit cursor.

Shutdown abandons queued work and never commits the in-flight tail

close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown(). The commit loop then exits after at most one more pass, so offsets completed while workers finish are never committed and will be redelivered. FixedQueuePool.shutdown also sets worker.shutdown = True before Queue.shutdown(immediate=False). The worker loop checks that flag before Queue.get(), so it will not drain: it finishes at most the item already dequeued and leaves the rest outstanding. Combined with unbounded queues, a restart replays the whole buffered backlog, which can duplicate uptime incidents or notifications if handling is not idempotent. join() ignores the timeout Arroyo passes and calls close() again; Arroyo already calls close() before join(), so Queue.shutdown() runs twice and the second call raises queue.ShutDown, logged as an error for every queue on every shutdown. Drain first (do not set the worker flag until the queue is empty; let shutdown(immediate=False) unblock get), then force one final commit on the processor thread, make close() idempotent, and honor join's timeout.

Any submit exception is acked and the message is never retried

submit()'s bare except marks the BrokerValue offset complete after logging. That path runs for build_payload_grouping_key failures, Queue.put failures (including queue.ShutDown after the pool is shut down), and the decoder's AssertionError on FilteredPayload. The commit loop will then commit that offset, so the result is never retried and never sent to a DLQ. Returning None from the decoder is an intentional skip and matches serial mode; unexpected exceptions are not. Serial processing lets those exceptions fail the strategy so Arroyo can retry. A transient grouping error or a put failure therefore permanently drops an uptime result. Only complete offsets that were actually handled or deliberately filtered, and let unexpected submit failures propagate so the partition is not acked past them.

Graceful shutdown depends on Python 3.13-only queue APIs

Queue.shutdown and queue.ShutDown were added in Python 3.13. FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown() and the worker catches queue.ShutDown, with no fallback. On 3.11/3.12, shutdown raises AttributeError, which the bare except logs and swallows, so workers blocked in Queue.get() never wake. Each worker.join then waits out its 5 second timeout (default 20 queues is up to about 100 seconds) and in-flight DB work is abandoned when the daemon threads die at process exit. If this runtime is not guaranteed to be 3.13+, shutdown needs a compatible unblock path, such as a sentinel or get(timeout) that observes the shutdown flag.

Queue-depth assertion races the worker threads

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts get_stats()["total_items"] > 0. The pool's workers are already running and the test handler only appends to a list, so they can dequeue every item before get_stats() runs. The assertion fails intermittently on a fast machine. Block the handler until after the depth check, or pause the workers before submitting.

--mode help misstates parallelism and omits the new mode

uptime_options still says "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." Mode parallel builds a MultiprocessingPool; batched-parallel is the thread-pool mode; thread-queue-parallel, added in this change, is not described at all, nor is the fact that --max-workers becomes the queue count in that mode. Operators selecting the new mode from --help will misunderstand the concurrency model.

false_positives.candidate:
SET-to-ZSET change breaks in-flight segment keys on deploy

Segment buffers are now written with ZADD and read with ZCARD, ZUNIONSTORE, and ZSCAN (add-buffer.lua and _load_segment_data). The previous release stored the same span-buf:s:* keys as Redis SETs (SADD/SUNIONSTORE/SSCAN). There is no new key prefix, dual-read, or WRONGTYPE handling. On a rolling deploy, keys still held as SETs (redis_ttl defaults to 3600s) make ZADD and ZSCAN raise WRONGTYPE; one such error fails the whole non-transactional pipeline, so both insert and flush abort for any batch that touches an old key. Old processes still running set commands fail the same way on keys the new code has already converted to sorted sets. Segments that cannot be flushed remain until TTL and are then dropped, so in-flight spans are lost and the consumer retries until those keys expire.

Insert-time eviction ignores max_segment_spans and drops spans silently

When a segment has more than 1000 members the Lua script ZPOPMINs it down to 1000. That limit is hardcoded and is not SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001, and a constructor argument callers can change). The flush-time backstop that skipped segments with more than max_segment_spans, logged an error, and incremented spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded was removed from _load_segment_data. A segment of 1001 spans, which the default config previously flushed intact, now loses a span with no metric, log, or truncation flag on the flushed payload. Changing max_segment_spans has no effect. The cap also only runs inside the script, which is a separate pipeline from the earlier ZADD; if the script errors after that ZADD, nothing else enforces a span count before the flusher loads and produces the segment. ZPOPMIN keeps the highest end_timestamp_precise scores, so a root span that does not have the latest end time can be deleted while the has-root-span flag stays set and the segment is still flushed on the shorter root timeout, missing its root payload.

ZUNIONSTORE sums timestamp scores and evicts the wrong spans

Both ZUNIONSTORE calls (the span-key merge and the parent-key merge) omit AGGREGATE, so Redis uses SUM. Member scores are end_timestamp_precise values, and ZPOPMIN later drops the lowest scores to enforce the cap. If the same payload is in both inputs — a retry after a partial write, or the same span stored under its own id and under the parent id — the scores are added, roughly doubling the timestamp. Those members then sort as newer than spans with a real later end time, so once the segment is over the cap the script keeps the corrupted members and drops newly ingested spans. The union needs AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN) so each member keeps an actual timestamp.

Redirect walk cap cut from 10000 to 1000 without a failure signal

The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects to find the segment key was reduced from 10000 iterations to 1000, and the comment that this cap can fail to join a deep chain was removed. If the chain is longer than 1000, the script stops on an intermediate span id, records the new span's redirect to that intermediate node, and merges into the wrong buffer. Flush then emits a split or mis-joined trace and nothing increments a metric when the cap is hit. Typical traces are shallower than this, but the old limit was intentional and the new one fails closed only by silently attaching spans to the wrong segment.

No test covers eviction, score order, or the ZSET migration

The buffer tests only add end_timestamp_precise to existing fixtures of four or five spans that all use the timestamp 1700000000.0. Nothing builds a segment larger than 1000 spans, asserts that the lowest scores are the ones removed, checks that max_segment_spans is the cap that is actually applied, or merges two sorted sets that share a member and checks the resulting score. Insert-time eviction, wrong-span drops from summed scores, and ZSCAN of sorted-set segment keys can all regress without a failing test. The new audit-log paginator path is also untested.

Glossary still calls segment keys sets that hold every span

The SpansBuffer glossary still describes span-buf:s:* as set keys that contain all span payloads for a segment, and the insert steps above still say the payload is added to a set. Those keys are now sorted sets scored by end_timestamp_precise, and members over the cap are deleted during insert, so a flushed segment may already be missing spans. Operators following this text will run SCARD or SSCAN, which fail with WRONGTYPE on the new keys, and will not know truncation is expected.

Upsampled count sums sample_weight but nothing stores that weight

This change never writes sample_weight and never computes an inverse sample rate. The only data-path edit, _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling in the test factory, copies contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate (for example 0.1) onto the existing event field sample_rate, which is the server-side sampling rate, not a weight. ClickHouse sum skips nulls, and the aggregate does not use ifNull(sample_weight, 1), so events with a missing weight contribute nothing; toInt64 then truncates a fractional sum toward zero, so a stored rate of 0.1 becomes 0 rather than 10. OrganizationEventsStatsEndpoint only catches ValidationError, so if sample_weight is absent on the queried entity the chart request 500s instead of falling back to count(). The new stats test expects each 0.1-sampled event to contribute 10, which this code cannot produce. Once the allowlist is non-empty, error count charts for those projects will be zeroed, truncated, or failed.

Error detection is a substring match and treats negations as errors

_is_error_focused_query treats a discover query as error-only if the raw query string contains the substring event.type:error after lowercasing. That is true for negations and mixed filters: !event.type:error contains event.type:error, and so does event.type:error OR event.type:transaction. The helper says sample_weight must not be applied to transactions and that the check should err on the side of caution, but this match does the opposite of a parsed filter. For allowlisted projects, count() is then rewritten to sum(sample_weight) on a query that still includes transactions. That either fails in Snuba because the column is not on the transactions entity, or returns a meaningless sum. The stats endpoint does not catch SnubaError, so the chart 500s. The unit test only covers the exact strings event.type:error, event.type:transaction, and an empty query, so the false positive is untested.

transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling replaces a column only when its text is exactly count() (case-insensitive, stripped). In the top-events branch that rewritten list is passed as timeseries_columns / y_axes, but orderby=self.get_orderby(request) is left unchanged, so a normal sort=-count() still ranks groups by the raw count() aggregate while the plotted series is upsampled_count() as count. Top-N groups are chosen by sampled volume, so a low sample rate and high true volume group can be omitted; if the builder treats ORDER BY count() as a different aggregate from the alias, the top-events query errors instead. Equations (equation|count() * 2 and get_equation_list) and aggregate conditions in the query string (count():>N) are not rewritten either, so filters and equation series do not match the upsampled count series. Other count-derived y-axes such as epm() and eps() stay sampled, so one response can show an upsampled count beside a sampled rate. Columns that are already aliased, such as count() as errors, also fail the exact match and silently skip upsampling.

Shared cache around an in-memory option read slows and can fail stats

is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects calls cache.get and cache.set on Sentry's shared cache (Redis in production) on every events-stats query, including each dashboard split subquery, to avoid options.get of issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist. That option read is already a process-local dict lookup, so the cache adds a network round trip on a hot endpoint instead of removing work. Cache errors are not caught here, and OrganizationEventsStatsEndpoint does not catch them either, so a Redis timeout fails the chart. Keys are one per organization plus hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))), which is high-cardinality, and Python hash() is not a collision-resistant digest, so a collision would reuse another project set's allowlist boolean and could enable sum(sample_weight) for a set that is not fully allowlisted. invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called and can delete only one exact key, so it does not flush eligibility after an allowlist change. The docstring on _are_all_projects_error_upsampled, which says each call reads the latest configuration, is false once this 60-second cache is in front of it.

upsampled_count is a public discover aggregate and bypasses the allowlist

upsampled_count is registered on Discover's function converter without private=True, unlike the neighboring function in the same list (private defaults to false). It therefore becomes a user-facing function on every discover endpoint that shares this converter, not only the allowlisted stats path. Clients can request yAxis=upsampled_count(), or use it in other discover and alert queries, for projects that are not allowlisted and for queries that include transactions. The aggregate itself has no allowlist or dataset guard and always emits sum(sample_weight), so a missing column becomes a Snuba error and the gate in organization_events_stats is bypassable. It also sets default_result_type to number while count() is an integer, so series metadata changes type. If private functions are rejected by the same column parser the stats rewrite uses, marking it private will 400 the rewrite; the weight sum should be applied inside the query builder under the allowlist check rather than exposed as a public function.

Accidental gitlink committed without .gitmodules

This pull request adds a gitlink at sentry-repo pointing at commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a, which is the PR base, and does not add a .gitmodules entry or URL. A submodule pointer without a URL cannot be checked out. git submodule update, CI jobs that clone recursively, and tools that reject unexpected gitlinks will fail, and the link is unrelated to error upsampling. Upsampling tests assert a 10x count the fixtures never produce

test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects stores events with client_sample_rate 0.1 and asserts each bucket count is 10. The factory only sets sample_rate to 0.1 and never sets sample_weight to 10, and no test inspects the SnQL or the stored column, so the assertion does not prove upsampling and fails unless an out-of-diff processor inverts the rate. A denial-cache hit in Check returns Allowed:false immediately and never reaches the new path that reloads permissions when the cached scope set does not allow the resource. false_positives.candidate:
installation_id is saved before OAuth state is validated

OAuthLoginView writes installation_id into the pipeline with bind_state before it checks that state matches pipeline.signature and before the authorization code is exchanged. bind_state persists the session immediately, and PipelineAdvancerView leaves csrf_protect = False, so a cross-site GET to /extensions/github/setup/?installation_id=<attacker> overwrites an in-progress install even when state is missing or wrong and the view then returns the error page. The later legitimate OAuth callback usually has no installation_id, and GitHubInstallation falls back to that poisoned value (request.GET.get("installation_id", pipeline.fetch_state("installation_id"))). The victim's org is then attached to the attacker's GitHub App installation whenever the sender check is skipped, or their own install is broken if the check runs. User-match check skipped when Integration does not exist

The new control is supposed to reject a mismatch between the OAuth GitHub login and the user who installed the app, but that comparison runs only after an Integration row is already loaded. On Integration.DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation returns pipeline.next_step() with no check. build_integration never reads github_authenticated_user; it fetches /app/installations/{id} with the GitHub App JWT, which can see every installation of this app, not only ones the OAuth user owns. Webhook creation of the Integration races the browser redirect, and any installation whose Sentry row is missing or was deleted takes this path. Combined with installation_id coming from the query string, an attacker can link a chosen GitHub App installation to the current Sentry organization and inherit the app's access to that account's repositories. Fail closed unless the OAuth user is verified against the installing user, or against installations visible to that user's token, before the org link is created.

Token request drops redirect_uri sent on authorize

The authorize redirect includes redirect_uri, but the access-token POST only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. GitHub's token endpoint, following RFC 6749 section 4.1.3, requires the same redirect_uri on the token request when it was included in authorization; otherwise it returns an error instead of access_token. This handler then always shows the invalid-installation page, so every install fails after the user authorizes, and that page is the same one used for real verification failures, so a manual check of the error UI does not prove the happy path. The comment says this mirrors OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params, which includes redirect_uri. Tests stub the token URL and ignore the POST body, so they stay green. Send the same redirect_uri used in the authorize request, build that URL with urlencode (the current f-string leaves redirect_uri unencoded), and accept both form and JSON token bodies the way the shared callback view does.

After the token exchange, get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) is called with no try/except. HTTP errors, network failures, and a non-mapping response propagate as an uncaught exception and a 500, unlike a missing access_token or a bad state, which return the installation-failed page. A GitHub /user failure during install therefore aborts opaquely, and the exception can capture the request that carries the new user access token into error reporting. Catch API failures and treat a missing login the same as the other verification failures.

That string is also returned for a state mismatch, a bad code, and a missing token, so the test can pass without comparing octocat to sender "attacker" or showing that no OrganizationIntegration was created. The token stub returns access_token regardless of redirect_uri. Recompute the webhook signature, drive a callback whose state actually matches that pipeline, and assert the specific denial for user mismatch, missing sender, and Integration.DoesNotExist.

The same skip happens when the organization feature is off if the caller mutates the instance returned by getByAlias/getById and passes it to update(): createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel then returns the cached model without copying, so the before/after comparison sees only the new state. Load the pre-image from the JPA delegate (raw flags, not the wrapper) or always invalidate the login keys, and drop resolved models that no longer match the requested mode. testCacheIDPForLogin never updates an org-linked login IdP while the org is disabled, so this is untested.

Cached getForLogin results have unstable order

getForLogin stores delegate ids with Collectors.toSet() and, on a hit, copies them into another HashSet before returning identityProviders.stream(). Set iteration order is undefined and can change between requests even when membership is unchanged. The previous implementation was the interface default, which returned the delegate getAllStream order. OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean sorts that stream with IDP_COMPARATOR_INSTANCE; List.sort is stable, so providers that compare equal (the usual case when guiOrder is unset or tied, if the comparator has no unique tiebreaker) keep this random order and can swap on the login page on every load. Callers that do not sort lose the previous query order entirely. Cache and return the ids in encounter order (List or LinkedHashSet), not a HashSet.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:

It sets enabled to the negation of FlagSqlExpressions and then returns false from both branches, so the flag cannot turn the feature back on. That matches the security intent, but it hides the kill switch, and the error returned to callers (line 131) is "sqlExpressions is not implemented", which is false — the feature existed and is being disabled because of the RCE/LFI vulnerability. The flag read also panics if ExpressionQueryReader.features is nil. This case did not touch features before, so a reader built without toggles now crashes on SQL queries instead of returning a controlled error. Return false without reading the flag, and use an error that says SQL expressions are disabled.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

UnmarshalSQLCommand always calls NewSQLCommand, and NewSQLCommand still calls sql.TablesList for every non-empty expression. reader.go itself notes that ExpressionQueryReader has not replaced the existing parser, so this is the path dashboard and alert evaluation use. TablesList now always fails because the stub RunCommands returns an error, and that failure is mapped to a BadRequest whose public message is "error reading SQL command" (lines 33-35). That text is wrong: the statement was not parsed or rejected as invalid SQL; the DuckDB engine was removed to close the RCE/LFI issue. Before returning, TablesList logs the raw expression and the assembled SELECT json_serialize_sql(...) command at Error (pkg/expr/sql/parser.go:28), and NewSQLCommand logs the raw SQL again at Warn (line 32). Instances that had enabled SQL expressions will therefore show a misleading invalid-query error and emit error-level logs containing the expression text on every panel refresh and every alert evaluation. Reject the feature in NewSQLCommand/UnmarshalSQLCommand before calling TablesList, with a stable disabled-feature error, and do not log the statement at Error.

The candidate issue describes the downstream consequence of this exact stubbing (specifically `RunCommands` returning a stub error causing `TablesList` to fail and log misleading errors in `NewSQLCommand`), which relates to the same underlying code change and concern regarding how the removed dependency was stubbed.

No regression test that SQL expressions stay disabled

This change set is the in-tree fix for the SQL-expression RCE/LFI issue, but it adds or updates no tests. Nothing asserts that ReadQuery rejects SQL queries even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, that UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand fail closed without executing a statement, or that DB.RunCommands and DB.QueryFramesInto do not run SQL or touch the filesystem. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock does not re-check cache, so waiters reload and can clear it

GetWebAssets copies entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, drops that lock, and only then takes the write lock. It never looks at the cache again after Lock. Every caller that observed a nil cache—the concurrent first requests this change is meant to protect—runs the manifest load while holding the exclusive lock and then unconditionally assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result. A later waiter whose load fails stores nil and wipes an entry an earlier waiter already published, so following non-dev calls miss the cache and reload. Even when every load succeeds, the missing re-check serializes a full disk read per waiter instead of returning the value the first loader stored. After acquiring the write lock, return the existing cache when Env is not Dev and it is already set, and do not replace a populated cache with a failed nil result.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: an incomplete double-checked locking pattern in `GetWebAssets` where the cache is checked under a read lock, the read lock is released, a write lock is acquired, and the code fails to re-check if the cache was already populated by another goroutine before reloading.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
