true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook throws on bad input and stores decrypted keys with no shape check

The handler has no method check and no try/catch around zod parse, symmetricDecrypt, or JSON.parse. A non-POST, a missing body, a string userId (the schema is z.number(), not coerce), or a ciphertext that does not decrypt to JSON becomes an unhandled 500, and the crypto or parser message can be returned to the caller. The decrypted value is written straight into credential.key. An array, string, or unexpected object is accepted, so a buggy parent can persist a shape the app later casts and crashes on, with a 200 only if Prisma happens to accept it.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the same problem as the golden comment: that the zod `.parse()` call (on `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema`) has no try/catch around it, causing invalid payloads (such as missing body or invalid userId) to result in an unhandled 500 error instead of a proper client error.

false_positives.candidate:
Salesforce refresh calls prisma without importing it

The new getClient path calls prisma.credential.update, but this file never imports prisma. Every other adapter in the PR imports @calcom/prisma explicitly, so this is not a global. SalesforceCalendarService constructs this.conn by calling getClient, so the first Salesforce calendar operation throws ReferenceError before a jsforce connection is returned. Event create, update, delete, and contact sync fail for every Salesforce user as soon as this code runs, including deployments that never enable credential sync.

Token sync request sends user id with no authentication

The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only calcomUserId and appSlug. It does not send CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, an HMAC, or any other credential, and it does not require the URL to be https. That endpoint is expected to return OAuth access tokens. The parent app therefore cannot tell Cal.com from any other caller who can reach the URL, and a client that can reach it can request tokens for arbitrary user ids. An http:// endpoint value would also put bearer tokens on the wire in cleartext. Nothing in .env.example says the caller is unauthenticated. The response is trusted with no status check, so an error body can be stored as a credential.

Lark deletes the credential before the sync refresh can run

refreshAccessToken still deletes the credential and throws when the stored refresh token is missing or refresh_expires_date is expired. That check runs before the new refreshOAuthTokens call. With credential sync the parent is the source of truth, and the sync helper documents a response that only contains an access token and expiry, so the local refresh token may be absent or already expired. In that case Cal.com deletes the Lark row instead of asking CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT for a new access token. The connection is gone and later calendar calls fail until the user reconnects; a webhook replay cannot help if the row was removed and a later findFirst misses the replacement.

Zoom sync asks for app slug zoomvideo but credentials are stored as zoom

Zoom's refresh calls refreshOAuthTokens with appSlug "zoomvideo", but the OAuth callback in this PR stores the credential with appId "zoom" and the install path uses slug "zoom". When credential sync is enabled, the parent is queried for zoomvideo and will not find the Zoom tokens it stored or received under zoom. Refresh fails and Zoom meetings cannot be created for synced users even when the webhook wrote a valid credential.

Credential sync upsert is racy and can leave a stale duplicate

The webhook does findFirst({userId, appId}) and then either updates that id or creates a row. Those steps are not in a transaction, and Credential has no unique constraint on (userId, appId). The Lark callback in this PR already notes that userId and type are not unique, which is why that flow updates by credential id. Two concurrent deliveries, including a parent retry, can both see no row and both insert, or findFirst can update an arbitrary duplicate because there is no orderBy. Calendar code also uses findFirst, so it can keep using a stale credential while the webhook returns 200. A retried sync therefore does not reliably make the parent the source of truth.

Synced credentials are not unmarked invalid

When a credential already exists, the webhook updates only key. It does not set invalid to false. Google, Webex, and Zoom in this PR set invalid true so a failed refresh stops being used. A parent that pushes a replacement token for a credential Cal.com already marked invalid still gets 200, but loaders that skip invalid rows will ignore the new keys and the integration stays disconnected.

Privileged credential webhook uses a raw reusable secret

This route can replace any user's integration credential, including calendar, video, CRM, and Stripe payment keys, for any app slug. The only check is inequality against a static header value. The compare is not constant-time, the secret is the raw header rather than an HMAC over the body, and there is no timestamp or nonce. A captured request stays valid forever and also discloses the secret itself, so the holder can forge new writes for every userId, not only replay one body. Rolling a rotated token back is enough to keep using a stolen OAuth refresh token after the parent thought it had replaced it.

No tests for credential sync or the OAuth refresh persistence change

The diff adds a privileged webhook and changes token refresh for every major OAuth app, but there are no new tests, and the PR checklist says tests were not added. The manual plan only hits the webhook and a simulated sync refresh. A unit test that refreshes Google and Office 365 with sharing disabled and asserts the stored key is still the token object, with the previous refresh_token kept when the provider omits one, would have caught the universal credential corruption. The webhook also has no coverage for a wrong secret, a non-object decrypted payload, an invalid credential being cleared, or two concurrent creates.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cancel no longer awaits reminder cancellation

handleCancelBooking used to collect workflowReminder.deleteMany promises and await them with the other Prisma work. It now calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder inside forEach and never awaits or collects those promises. The email helper only sets cancelled=true, which is the only signal the cron uses to stop SendGrid; the SMS helper cancels Twilio and deletes the row, and there is no SMS cron to finish that job. On serverless the runtime can freeze as soon as the handler returns, so those writes often never commit, the cron never sees the email as cancelled, and both email and SMS for the cancelled booking are still sent. Even when the write does commit, email cancellation is deferred to a 15-minute cron that only acts in the last hour, so a reminder due before the next tick is not stopped. Errors inside the managers are swallowed, and the handler still returns success.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same core problem: `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are called without being awaited inside `forEach` loops (specifically mentioning booking cancellation), which results in scheduled reminders not being reliably cancelled.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete refills the 100-slot SendGrid cancel cap and fails open

When immediateDelete is true and a referenceId exists, deleteScheduledEmailReminder only POSTs /v3/user/scheduled_sends with status cancel and then returns. It does not delete the WorkflowReminder and does not set cancelled=true. SendGrid keeps that cancellation in scheduled_sends until the original sendAt (up to 72 hours), and this PR exists because that queue is capped at 100 pending cancellations account-wide; once it is full, further cancels fail and emails still go out. The hot callers pass true for every already-scheduled reminder regardless of how far away the send is: reschedule in handleNewBooking.ts (line 968), workflow deletion in workflows.tsx (line 214), and step deletion in workflows.tsx (line 521). A single workflow delete can therefore enqueue one long-lived cancel per upcoming reminder and trip the cap for the whole platform. If the POST fails, the catch only logs, cancelled is never set, and the cron will not retry, so the email is still delivered. On success the row is left looking active, so nothing records that the batch was already cancelled.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same flaws described in the golden comment: when immediateDelete is true in deleteScheduledEmailReminder, it only sends the POST request to cancel the SendGrid email, failing to delete the WorkflowReminder record from the database or mark it as cancelled, and omitting the SendGrid DELETE API call (which keeps the cancellation in the scheduled_sends queue).

false_positives.candidate:
Cron cancel can miss, drop, or poison reminder cancellations

The new cancel pass does not reliably stop SendGrid sends for cancelled bookings. Before it runs, the handler deleteMany's every EMAIL WorkflowReminder with scheduledDate <= now, including cancelled=true rows whose SendGrid send has not been cancelled yet. A cron invocation that starts at or after sendAt therefore destroys the only record that could still cancel the batch, and the email goes out. The new query only selects cancelled rows due within the next hour, and this job runs every 15 minutes, while SendGrid will not honor a cancel inside roughly the last 10 minutes before sendAt. A booking cancelled after the last successful tick (for example 10 minutes before the reminder) is not stopped, and the following run deletes the row instead of cancelling it. The loop at line 56 has no per-item try/catch and only awaits the Prisma deletes in Promise.all after every SendGrid call succeeds. Prisma deletes are lazy until awaited, so one failure (null referenceId, non-email referenceId, already-cancelled batch, or a reminder inside the 10-minute cutoff) skips those deletes. Batches that were already cancelled stay cancelled=true; the next run retries them, SendGrid returns 400 on a second cancel, and that throw aborts the rest of the batch until the poisoned row ages out and the leading deleteMany removes it. findMany has no orderBy, so one too-late reminder can be first and block reminders that are still cancellable. The unscheduled-send query below still does not exclude cancelled=true or CANCELLED/REJECTED bookings, so any reminder row that cancellation failed to delete is scheduled and sent anyway.

Paid cancellation returns before reminders are cancelled

If the booking is paid, handleCancelBooking refunds it, sets status to REJECTED, and returns at line 464. Workflow reminder cancellation is only reached at line 485, after that return. Paid cancellations therefore never set cancelled=true and never call Twilio or SendGrid. Already scheduled workflow emails and SMS for refunded bookings are still sent. The new cron cannot recover them, because it only cancels rows with cancelled=true, and this path never writes that flag. The booking is also REJECTED rather than CANCELLED, so a later status check for CANCELLED would miss it too.

Reschedule cancel is not awaited and immediately consumes SendGrid cancel slots

On reschedule, handleNewBooking walks the original booking's workflowReminders with forEach and calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(id, referenceId, true) without awaiting. forEach does not return those promises, so the try/catch around it never sees async failures, and the handler can finish the response while the SendGrid calls are still in flight. Passing true takes immediateDelete, which POSTs a cancel for every reminder that already has a referenceId, including sends up to 72 hours away, and puts those entries back into SendGrid's 100-slot scheduled_sends queue — the cap this PR is trying to stay under. If that POST fails, the helper swallows the error and does not set cancelled, so the cron will not retry and the old booking's workflow email is still sent after the reschedule. Direct attendee reschedules only cancel reminders on this path.

Request-reschedule dropped the awaited reminder delete

requestReschedule marks the booking CANCELLED and then calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder from forEach without awaiting them. The previous code awaited prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany after starting the provider cancels. The email helper only persists cancelled=true inside that unawaited call, which is what the cron needs in order to stop SendGrid; the SMS helper cancels Twilio and deletes the row in the same unawaited call, and SMS has no cron fallback. If the mutation returns before those promises settle, reminders for the booking the user just asked to reschedule are still delivered, and the API has already reported success.

Workflow and step saves can lose the cancellation record

Workflow deletion calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true) and deleteScheduledSMSReminder inside forEach, then immediately awaits workflow.deleteMany. Step removal does the same at line 521 and then deletes the WorkflowStep. Both deletes cascade to WorkflowReminder. The provider calls are not awaited, so the rows can disappear before SendGrid or Twilio cancel finishes. immediateDelete also does not set cancelled=true, and a failed or frozen provider call then has no row left for the cron to retry, so those messages are still sent. Because every scheduled reminder for the workflow is cancelled immediately, one delete can also fill SendGrid's 100 pending-cancellation slots until the original send times. The same mutation dropped awaited reminder deletes when an event type is removed (line 376) and when a step is edited (line 574): those used to await workflowReminder.deleteMany and now only start unawaited manager calls. If those calls do not finish, the old reminders stay scheduled while the mutation also creates new ones, so both the old and the new messages go out.

No tests for the new reminder-cancellation behavior

This change replaces the SendGrid cancel-then-DELETE sequence and the awaited reminder deletes with a cancelled flag, a deferred cron cancel, and an immediateDelete mode, but adds no tests. Nothing covers the cron selecting cancelled rows and POSTing scheduled_sends, skipping DELETE /v3/user/scheduled_sends/{id} (which clears the cancel and lets the email send), a cancel inside the 15-minute cron gap or SendGrid's 10-minute cutoff, the 100-slot immediateDelete path, or cancel, reschedule, workflow delete, and paid-booking cancel actually stopping both email and SMS. Those are the production paths this PR is supposed to fix.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.

Blacklist and duplicate checks are case-sensitive and racy

BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS is lowercased, but the filter uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) without lowercasing or trimming guest, and split(',') does not trim entries. Blocked@example.com bypasses blocked@example.com, and a space after a comma in the env var bypasses that entry. The same === comparison against existing attendees is case-sensitive, the input array is not deduped, and the organizer address is not excluded, so one request can createMany both a@x.com and A@x.com, the same address twice, or the host as their own guest. true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner check requires both roles

isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed with && between isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner. A membership has a single role, so this is either always false (if the helpers check ADMIN and OWNER exclusively) or true only for owners (if isTeamAdmin already treats OWNER as admin). Team admins who are not the booking host and not an attendee are rejected with FORBIDDEN, even though the flag is named and used as an admin-or-owner grant and the bookings UI treats team admins/owners as managers. They cannot add guests to team bookings they otherwise manage. This should be ||, and it should not query team id 0 when eventType.teamId is null.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the team admin/owner permission check mistakenly uses the logical AND (&&) operator instead of OR (||) between `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Add-guest emails ignore event-type email opt-out

Every other sender in this file checks eventTypeDisableHostEmail and eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail before sending. sendAddGuestsEmails does not take event-type metadata and always emails the organizer, every existing attendee, and each new guest, including full calendar invites. Event types with standard emails disabled still emit these messages when a guest is added. The handler has booking.eventType loaded and should pass its metadata so the same opt-out applies.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: the `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the event type metadata for email opt-out flags (disableStandardEmails / eventTypeDisableHostEmail / eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail), causing emails to be sent to hosts and attendees even when standard emails are disabled for that event type.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancelled, past, and no-guest events still accept new guests

After the permission check the handler never reads booking status, endTime, or eventType.disableGuests before inserting attendees and emailing invites. Any logged-in attendee (not only the host) may call this with a numeric booking id. disableGuests is on the included event type and is ignored, so a host who turned guests off can still have arbitrary addresses emailed a CONFIRMED invite that includes the video URL and meeting password from the booking references. The same path runs for CANCELLED, REJECTED, and PENDING bookings, and for meetings that already ended. The new ICS builders hardcode status CONFIRMED. The bookings menu also offers this action for past confirmed rows (BookingListItem bookedActions, rendered around line 554), so this is not only a raw-API issue. Reject anything that is not an upcoming accepted booking, and honor disableGuests.

Seated events are not capacity-checked and get no seat rows

createMany inserts plain Attendee rows and later copies seatsPerTimeSlot onto the calendar payload, but never compares current attendees plus new guests to seatsPerTimeSlot and never creates the per-attendee seat rows (reference UIDs) seated bookings use. Occupancy, the seats UI, and seat-scoped cancel/reschedule links will not include these people. Depending on whether availability counts attendees or seats, the slot is either overfilled with people who still have the meeting link, or marked full without usable seat records. Paid-per-seat events also skip payment for these extra people. Block this mutation when seatsPerTimeSlot is set, or add real seats through the seat booking path and enforce the cap.

Attendee insert is not rolled back if calendar sync fails

prisma.booking.update createMany commits the new attendees before eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees, with no transaction and no compensating delete. If the calendar call throws (revoked credential, provider error, or the wrong user's credentials), the mutation fails but the rows remain. A retry then filters those emails out as already attending and throws BAD_REQUEST emails_must_be_unique_valid, so the caller cannot finish calendar sync or notifications. The host sees an error while the booking already lists the guests, and the guests were never emailed because sendAddGuestsEmails runs only after the calendar call. Persist guests only after sync succeeds, or roll the insert back on failure.

Calendar update uses the caller's credentials, not the host's

EventManager is constructed from ctx.user and getUsersCredentials(ctx.user), not from the booking host. The query already loads booking.user.credentials and never uses them. Calendar references on the booking are stored against the host credential. Attendees are explicitly allowed to call this mutation, and the team-owner branch is meant to allow non-hosts; those callers do not have the host credential, so updateCalendarAttendees cannot update the host event. It will throw (leaving the rows committed with no rollback) or skip. Either way the host calendar, and Meet/Zoom guest lists derived from it, do not gain the new guests. Build EventManager from the booking owner (and that user's calendar credentials), including co-host credentials for collective events.

One occurrence is updated but the event is marked recurring

The handler updates only the given bookingId, but evt.recurringEvent is set from booking.eventType.recurringEvent for every instance of a recurring type. That field is what scheduled emails and calendar updates use to treat a CalendarEvent as a series (RRULE / series update). The recurring tab hides this action, so it is used on a single upcoming occurrence, yet the invite and calendar payload still describe the whole series. A guest is then on every occurrence in Google/Outlook (or holds an RRULE invite) while only one Booking row lists them, so later instances disagree between Cal.com and the external calendar. Either omit recurringEvent and target that occurrence's calendar reference, or add the guest to every future booking in the recurringEventId group and update the series once.

New guests are stored with an empty name

guestsFullDetails sets name to an empty string for every new guest. New guests are emailed via AttendeeScheduledEmail, which addresses them as `${name} <${email}>`, so the To header is ' <guest@example.com>'. Some mailers reject or blank that address, and calendar attendees are created with an empty display name. OrganizerAddGuestsEmail also interpolates attendees[0].name into the subject with no fallback (organizer-add-guests-email.ts line 28), so a blank first attendee yields 'with ' and no name. Store the email (or its local part) as the name when the guest did not provide one.

Guest list has no upper bound

guests is an unbounded z.array of emails, and MultiEmail can append fields without a cap. Any authenticated host or attendee can submit thousands of addresses in one call. The handler insert them and fans out a calendar invite per address containing the meeting URL. OrganizerAddGuestsEmail also puts every attendee email in replyTo, so a large list can exceed header limits and fail the send after the rows are already committed. Cap and dedupe the array in the schema before any writes or sends.

No tests for add-guests authorization or side effects

The new mutation ships with no handler or UI tests. Permission (admin vs owner vs attendee vs stranger), blacklist and case-variant duplicates, cancelled and seated bookings, the single-occurrence recurring case, and calendar or email failure after the insert are all untested, so the authorization, seat, and rollback bugs above would not be caught in CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Valid backup codes are rejected unless they match lowercase hex exactly

Stored codes are lowercase hex from `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`. Login compares with `indexOf` after removing only "-" characters. The same check is in `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts` at the `replaceAll("-", "")` / `indexOf` call. There is no `toLowerCase()` or trim. The entry field (`apps/web/components/auth/BackupCode.tsx`) uses placeholder "XXXXX-XXXXX", which reads as uppercase, and does not set `autoCapitalize="none"` or `autoCorrect="off"`, so mobile keyboards will capitalize the first character. Pasting a line from the downloaded file often includes a trailing newline or space; a code entered as uppercase or with whitespace will not match and the user gets "incorrect backup code" for a real code. Normalize by stripping whitespace and dashes and lowercasing before compare, on both login and disable.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: backup code validation using `indexOf` is case-sensitive, causing validation to fail when users enter uppercase hex characters instead of lowercase.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
One-time backup codes can be replayed or restored under concurrent logins

After a backup code matches, the handler nulls that array slot and writes the re-encrypted list with a plain `prisma.user.update` on user id. The read, check, and write are not in a transaction and the update is not conditional on the previous ciphertext. Two parallel logins with the same code can both see it as unused and both receive sessions. Two parallel logins with different codes can also lose an update: the later write is based on a stale array and can put a just-consumed code back. Backup codes are documented as single-use, but that is not enforced. Consume the code with a row lock or compare-and-swap on the stored ciphertext so only one request can spend a given code.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the exact same race condition where backup codes are read, modified in memory, and written back without synchronization, allowing concurrent login requests to bypass the single-use restriction.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code alone can log in if any TOTP field is sent

Password verification in credentials authorize runs only when `user.password` is set and `credentials.totpCode` is empty. The new branch then treats any non-empty `backupCode` as a full login: it decrypts the stored codes, and on a match it burns that code and returns a session. It never checks the password itself. A caller who knows only a backup code (the plaintext file this feature downloads as cal-backup-codes.txt, a clipboard copy, or the setup response) can POST email, `totpCode` set to any non-empty value such as "1", and that backup code, and get a session without the password. The normal UI often avoids this only because it clears `totpCode` before submit; the credentials endpoint does not. The code is also consumed on that request, so the attacker takes the account and destroys a recovery code. The grant shortcut is characters at indexes 4 and 5 of the six-character prefix (onrtac is ac), but the matcher uses substring(3, 5), which is ta for that id. The condition is also backwards: it returns false when that slice equals the expected shortcut. For every built-in shortcut these helpers pass, the wrong slice is not equal to the expected value, so the inverted check does not fire and any id with a colon and a UUID suffix passes, including the na fallback used when GRANT_TYPE was never set. The new assertions therefore do not fail if grant encoding is missing or wrong, and they never check session type or token type. A prefix shorter than 5 characters throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException from the matcher instead of a mismatch.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies both issues in the golden comment: the grant shortcut should use substring(4,6), not substring(3,5), and a matching shortcut should return true when combined with the UUID check rather than false.

false_positives.candidate:
First offline access token is encoded as an online session

createTokenResponse calls createClientAccessToken, which stamps the jti session-type from userSession.isOffline(), before generateRefreshToken() and before the online session may be deleted. On the first offline_access response the login session is still online at that point, so the prefix is online (on…). Lines 116-120 then issue an offline refresh token and, when the FIRST_OFFLINE_ACCESS note is set, remove that online user session. Offline sessions live in a separate store but keep the same session id, so today's validation only finds the session by falling back from online to offline. The prefix names the store that no longer holds the session. Callers that use it to pick a single store, which is the stated reason for encoding session type, will miss the session and reject the access token returned with that first offline refresh token. ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType has the same order and is stricter: generateAccessToken() at line 139 runs first, then any offline refresh token causes removeUserSession at lines 142-146, not only the first-offline-access case. Later refreshes are fine because the loaded session is already offline. No test issues an offline_access token and checks the session-type characters.

getShortcut() has no default and breaks existing grant factories at startup

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an existing extension SPI, and getShortcut() was added as a new abstract method with no default implementation. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit loads every OAuth2GrantTypeFactory and calls getShortcut(). A custom grant factory built against the previous interface throws AbstractMethodError there, and Keycloak fails to start. A default method that returns a stable two-character fallback would keep existing providers loading.

Grant shortcuts are not constrained to the two-character encoding

Decoding assumes every grant shortcut is exactly two characters and contains no colon, so the prefix is always six characters and the first colon separates the raw id. getShortcut() is documented as usually like a 3-letter shortcut, and postInit only checks that the two maps end up the same size. A unique shortcut of any other length is stored, encodeTokenId writes it into the jti, and getTokenContextFromTokenId then throws IllegalArgumentException because the prefix length is not 6. That exception text says the token id is expected to have length 6, but the check is only on the prefix; a valid id is six characters, a colon, and a UUID, so the message is wrong. The lazy reload in getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut, meant for grants deployed after startup, inserts the new shortcut with no length check and no collision check, so a duplicate shortcut overwrites another grant and later tokens decode as the wrong grant type.

setFormParams leaves the cached grant type stale

Context snapshots grant_type from the constructor form parameters, and getGrantType() returns that field. setFormParams replaces formParams but does not update grantType. A caller that uses this public setter to change the request parameters after construction will encode the original grant type, or na if the original map had no grant_type, rather than the grant type actually being processed. The getter should read the current form parameters, or the setter should refresh the cached value.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recovery-code login form crashes unless storage returns Keycloak's internal model

The bean loads a credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential and immediately calls Optional.get() and RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel. That parser requires credentialData and secretData in the hashed recovery-code schema and throws NoSuchElementException or RuntimeException otherwise. When user storage's updateCredential returns true, createRecoveryCodesCredential does not persist that model; it only sends a JSON array of raw codes on a UserCredentialModel. isConfiguredFor can still be true, so the authenticator renders this bean. A provider that stores the updateCredential payload and returns it, or that implements supportsCredentialType, updateCredential, isConfiguredFor, and isValid but not getCredentials, makes recovery-code login fail with a server error before a code can be submitted. There is no fallback to a local credential or a default index. Only the test storage papers over this by rebuilding a model in getCredentials.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the unchecked Optional.get() call on RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential and the resulting NoSuchElementException when storage does not return a credential. This matches the golden comment's underlying bug, despite the candidate adding storage-schema and persistence concerns.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getCredentials drops the stored id and renumbers codes

updateCredential sets an id with KeycloakModelUtils.generateId, but getCredentials ignores that CredentialModel and returns a new one from RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues. That factory does not copy the stored id and assigns fresh indexes starting at 0 to whatever list it is given. The same method now sets an id on OTP credentials because listing and deletion need it; recovery codes are returned with a null id, so account-console delete and removeStoredCredentialById cannot target them. If used codes are removed from the stored list, the remainder is renumbered and the login page asks for code 0 instead of the next original number. The rebuilt view also cannot be written back: its credentialData is metadata JSON, not the raw list isValid reads.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that rebuilding the recovery-code credential omits the stored credential ID, leaving getId() null and preventing removal by ID. This matches the golden issue, despite additional concerns about renumbering and serialization.

false_positives.candidate:
User-storage recovery codes are reusable and not ordered

isValid deserializes the stored raw code list and returns true if any entry equals the submitted value, then leaves the list unchanged. Recovery codes are one-time and must be used in order: the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider hashes the input, matches only the next remaining code, and deletes it. credentialManager().isValid stops at the user-storage validator when that provider supports and is configured for the type, so the local provider never runs for credentials accepted by CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator does not consume the code after a successful check; it only re-reads the credential. The same backup code can be replayed forever, and a code other than the one the login form requested is accepted. The new test logs in only once, so it does not catch this.

Plaintext recovery codes are sent to user storage

createRecoveryCodesCredential JSON-encodes the raw generatedCodes list and puts that string in the UserCredentialModel passed to updateCredential. The RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel argument already contains only hashes. Local storage persists those hashes; this path gives the federation provider every unused code in cleartext and drops userLabel and generatedAt, so they cannot be stored either. BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage writes that string unchanged into credentialData and keeps it for later equality checks. A storage dump or credential-update log discloses all backup codes, which authenticate as the user. Verification only needs the existing hashRawCode/verifyRecoveryCodeInput helpers, so the hashed secret data should be what is handed off, and the reference provider should not keep reversible codes.

Recovery codes cannot be disabled in the new storage support

disableCredentialType clears OTP and otherwise only logs that the type is unsupported. getDisableableCredentialTypesStream only reports OTP, so recovery-authn-codes is not advertised as disableable. Admin REST disableCredentialType and account-console removal therefore leave myUser.recoveryCodes set. isConfiguredFor stays true and isValid still accepts the codes, so an administrator cannot revoke recovery codes after this provider has stored them.

New test never checks replay, next-code index, revocation, or local fallback

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only checks that setup writes no Keycloak DB credential, that the storage flag is set, and that the first displayed code logs in once. It never submits that code again, never asserts a later login asks for the next index, never disables or deletes the credential, and never covers a user storage that returns false from updateCredential so the helper must keep the local hashed credential. Those are the paths this change adds and the ones the new storage implementation gets wrong, so the suite stays green while replay and revocation are broken.

Caution falsely says the Operator fails without rolling-updates

The new caution says that during preview the `rolling-updates` feature must be enabled or the Keycloak Operator will fail. That contradicts both the note later in this same section and the operator test added in this PR. UpgradeTest.createInitialDeployment returns immediately when the update strategy is null and does not set spec.features.enabled to rolling-updates. Those cases still call deployKeycloak with wait-for-ready, and a cache max-count change is expected to roll rather than fail. So a normal Keycloak CR reconciles, becomes ready, and applies the documented 26.1-compatible default (recreate only on image change, roll on other config) with the preview feature off. The feature is only enabled in that test when spec.update.strategy is set explicitly. As written, the caution tells every Operator user that an upgrade breaks unless they turn on a preview feature, which will cause unnecessary preview opt-in or blocked upgrades. Narrow the warning to explicit spec.update usage, or change the test if fail-closed is actually required.

Exit code 4 is documented as an upgrade decision

The new exit-code row says code 4 means "Rolling Upgrade is not possible" because `rolling-updates` is disabled. That is the same decision wording as exit code 3, and the paragraph above the table says these codes are how automation determines the upgrade type. The implementation does not decide compatibility: both update-compatibility check and update-compatibility metadata print "Unable to use this command. The preview feature 'rolling-updates' is not enabled." and exit 4 before reading metadata or comparing versions. The only other upgrade type this guide defines is recreate (shut the deployment down before applying config). A pipeline that treats "rolling is not possible" as that outcome will take an unnecessary outage when the flag was merely omitted. Describe code 4 as a precondition failure, state that the upgrade type was not determined, and note that the metadata subcommand returns 4 as well; the table currently sits only under the check command.

Changed exit codes 3 and 4 are never asserted

This PR changes CompatibilityResult.RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 and adds FEATURE_DISABLED = 4, and the guide tells users to branch automation on those codes. testFeatureNotEnabled only checks that stderr contains the disabled-feature sentence and never asserts the process exit code is 4; it also covers only the metadata subcommand, not check. testWrongVersions only checks the incompatibility log line and never asserts exit code 3. CLIResult.assertError succeeds for any non-zero status, so leaving recreate at 4, or picocli.exit collapsing the custom code to 1, would still pass. That docs-vs-code mismatch (docs already said 3, the constant was 4) is exactly what this PR is fixing, and nothing locks the new contract.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Null Clients type resource NPEs permission checks

When no per-client authorization resource exists, hasPermission sets resource from AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource and immediately calls PolicyStore.findByResource(server, resource) with no null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null if the Clients type resource was never created (init skips existing admin-permissions clients) or was deleted. findByResource then dereferences null and the admin call fails with 500 instead of denying the permission. Treat a null type resource as no all-clients permission.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same null-handling bug in ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission: getResourceTypeResource may return null, which is passed to findByResource and causes a NullPointerException. The candidate also recommends treating the null resource as no permission.

false_positives.candidate:
All-clients view bypasses an explicit per-client view deny

ClientPermissionsV2.canView(ClientModel) returns true as soon as canView() is true. canView() is true not only for the view-clients/manage-clients admin roles, but also when a fine-grained permission grants the view scope on the Clients resource type (all clients). The per-client check is then skipped, so a Logic.NEGATIVE view permission for that same caller on one client is never evaluated. requireView(client) and every admin operation gated on canView(client) (client representation, protocol mappers, client scopes) still succeed for the client that was explicitly denied. Negative permissions are already part of this model (user FGAP tests use Logic.NEGATIVE on the same permission API). Short-circuit only on the admin-role helper (canViewClientDefault), then evaluate the per-client decision so an explicit deny overrides all-clients view. The new client tests never create a negative permission, so this bypass is untested.

A per-client resource suppresses all-clients permissions

hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) loads the authorization resource named with the client id and, if that row exists, evaluates only that resource. The Clients type resource (all clients) is consulted only when no per-client resource exists. A per-client resource is created for any permission that targets that client, including a permission for a different user or a different scope. An administrator granted manage, configure, view, or map-roles on all clients then loses that grant on the client, because their all-clients policy is attached to the type resource and is never evaluated; a per-client grant of scope A also hides an all-clients grant of scope B. Evaluate both resources, and let a per-client policy override all-clients only for the scopes that policy actually covers. PermissionClientTest only covers a lone per-client grant or a lone all-clients grant, never both.

Existing admin-permissions clients never receive the Clients schema

AdminPermissionsSchema.init returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and that is the only place schema scopes and the per-type all-resource records are created. This change adds the Clients resource type and the configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes, but realms that already enabled admin permissions V2 already have that client (created earlier with only Users). After upgrade those scopes and the Clients resource are never inserted, so creating a Clients permission fails with a missing-scope validation error and all-clients evaluation cannot find the type resource. init must add any schema scopes and resource types that are not already present instead of treating a non-null admin-permissions client as fully initialized.

Client deletion throws when v1 and v2 admin-permission features are both enabled

The removal listener runs when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (v1) is enabled and then calls management().clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException. The two flags are independent, so enabling v2 does not turn v1 off. Deleting a client then throws from the provider event listener and can roll back the removal. Guard the v1 cleanup with the same condition management() uses (v1 evaluator actually selected), or make the v2 removal path a no-op instead of throwing. Role and group removal in this listener call management() as well; clients() is the override that now throws.

Client permission resources are returned with a null display name

getResourceName resolves Users policies to "All users" or the username, but has no Clients branch and falls through to resource.getDisplayName(). Per-client resources are stored with the client UUID as the name and no display name, and the all-clients resource is stored as name "Clients" without a display name, so the admin permissions API returns null. The console cannot show which client a permission applies to, unlike users in the same API. Resolve the stored id to the clientId, return a label such as "All clients" for the type resource, and fail clearly if the client no longer exists, matching the user path.

canExchangeTo throws instead of returning an authorization decision

ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException. AdminPermissions.evaluator installs this class whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and token exchange calls clients().canExchangeTo to decide whether the caller may exchange into another client's audience. That call now fails the token request with an unhandled server error instead of allow or deny. The same class throws from isPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, and setPermissionsEnabled; this PR only guards the removal listener, and only behind the v1 feature flag. A boolean permission check must not throw — return false until exchange is actually implemented (getEvaluationContext in this class is unused). Otherwise enabling v2 breaks token exchange and any client management-permissions endpoint that still reaches these methods.

Client tests rotate myclient's secret and leave realm mutations behind

testConfigureOnlyOneClient calls generateNewSecret and invalidateRotatedSecret on myclient and never restores the original secret. realmAdminClient is injected as client myclient using the secret from the realm config, and AbstractPermissionTest's @InjectRealm does not request a per-method lifecycle, so the realm is shared by every method in the class. The next test that must obtain a token authenticates with a secret that no longer exists and fails. The same class also leaves other shared state: testManageOnlyOneClient renames myclient and moves a default client scope to optional, and testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient creates myclient-role and myclient-subRole with no cleanup. AfterEach only deletes scope permissions. Restore the secret, name, and scopes, and delete the roles, or results depend on test order.

requireView javadoc claims a boolean result for void methods

requireView and requireViewClientScopes are void and throw ForbiddenException when the matching can* check is false, but the new javadoc says each "Returns true if canView()/canViewClientScopes() returns true". That describes the boolean methods, not these require* methods. Neighboring require* docs correctly say they throw ForbiddenException. Callers reading the interface will think these methods return a decision instead of aborting the request.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-groups VIEW is treated as permission to manage groups

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns true if hasPermission finds either the VIEW or MANAGE scope on the all-groups resource. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup authorizes group creation with requireManage(), which calls this method, and any other caller of canManage()/requireManage() treats it as a write check. A fine-grained admin granted only view access to groups can therefore create top-level groups. That contradicts canManage(GroupModel) in the same class, which correctly requires only MANAGE, and contradicts V1, which only checks the manage-users role. The new javadoc on GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage repeats the same mistake by documenting VIEW as sufficient. canManage() must require the MANAGE scope only.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(): accepting VIEW as well as MANAGE lets view-only users pass a write authorization check. Both require restricting canManage() to MANAGE scope only.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Group-scoped user search and counts use authorization resource ids, not group ids

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission is what UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource pass to the user store (session attribute UserModel.GROUPS, and getUsersCount) so that an admin who cannot view all users only sees members of groups they may view. The callback passes groupResource.getId() into hasPermission and stores that same value. hasPermission treats the argument as a group id and looks it up with resourceStore.findByName, but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource stores the group id as the resource name and the authorization store assigns a different resource id. The lookup therefore misses. findByType(GROUPS) also cannot see per-group resources, because getOrCreateResource never calls setType, so only the type resource named "Groups" (if present) is visited. The set ends up empty or filled with authorization UUIDs. User search pagination then either is not restricted to the permitted groups or is restricted to ids that match no membership, and the count API returns 0 or a count for a non-existent group. Return the group id (resource name), skip the type resource, and persist instance resources with type Groups.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core mismatch: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes and returns authorization resource IDs, while hasPermission resolves by resource name and downstream user filtering/counts require underlying group IDs. Its additional claims about resource types and suggested fixes do not change that underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
Group deletion throws when FGAP V2 is enabled

GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException (as do the other GroupPermissionManagement methods). AdminPermissions.registerListener still handles GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent by calling management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled. management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, and therefore GroupPermissionsV2, whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. With both features on, which is the normal combination if V1 is a default feature and V2 is enabled for this work, realm.removeGroup and the admin delete-group API fail with that exception and the group is not removed. If only V2 is enabled, the listener is not registered at all, so the V2 authorization resource named by the group id is never deleted and remains orphaned on the admin-permissions client. Group removal needs a V2 cleanup path; the V1 listener must not call the throwing methods while V2 is active.

A per-group permission resource hides all-groups grants

hasPermission looks up the per-group resource by name and, if it exists, evaluates only that resource. The all-groups resource is used only when no per-group resource exists. Creating any permission on a group (including one for a different administrator) creates that resource, after which an admin who holds VIEW or MANAGE on all groups is denied for that group because their all-groups policy is never evaluated. canView, canManage, canViewMembers, canManageMembers, and canManageMembership all go through this helper. GroupsResource.getGroups and GroupResource.getSubGroups no longer short-circuit on global canView() and now depend entirely on canView(group), so listing is affected as well. The new tests never combine an all-groups grant with a specific grant for another user. Evaluation has to combine the instance resource and the resource-type resource under the schema decision strategy; preferring the instance resource drops legitimate grants and also drops all-groups denies when only the instance is evaluated.

Existing admin-permissions clients never gain the Groups schema

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and no other path creates the Groups resource type, the "Groups" all-resource, or the new scopes manage-membership, manage-members, and view-members. Realms that already enabled fine-grained admin permissions (the client was created when only Users and Clients existed) do not pick up this change, and turning admin permissions off and on does not help if the client row remains. Creating a group permission then fails in getScope with "Scope [view-members] does not exist". GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission also calls getResourceTypeResource, gets null, and invokes policyStore.findByResource and resource.getScopes() with no null check, so group admin calls from users without manage-users/view-users become 500s instead of a deny. Upgrade must add the missing scopes and the Groups type resource to existing admin-permissions clients, or init/getResourceTypeResource must create them lazily.

Group permission resources have no human-readable name

getResourceName resolves only the Users resource type ("All users" or the username) and otherwise returns resource.getDisplayName(). Group resources created by getOrCreateResource use the group id as the name and never set a display name, and the new Groups type is not handled here. Permission listings for group policies therefore show a null name or a raw id instead of the group name or path, and there is no "All groups" label for the type resource. A missing user already throws ModelIllegalStateException; a missing group is silently unlabeled. Resolve group resources the same way users are resolved.

requireManageMembers javadoc cites the wrong check

The javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws ForbiddenException when canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. The implementation enforces canManageMembers, which is the manage-members scope, not manage-membership. Those are different permissions (managing the users in a group versus changing a user's group membership). An implementor or caller following the javadoc will check or document the wrong scope.

Public group permission methods were removed and renamed

GroupPermissionEvaluator is public. This change deletes getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel) and renames getGroupsWithViewPermission() to getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() with no bridge method. In-repo callers were updated, but any extension that implements the interface or calls the old methods will fail to compile or throw NoSuchMethodError at runtime. If this interface is part of the supported admin-permissions contract, keep the old methods as deprecated delegates; otherwise call the break out in the release notes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider

CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() is specified to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS Provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the platform keystore provider (SUN for the Java 8 default JKS keystore, and typically SUN for the Java 9+ default PKCS12 keystore). That provider is not BC and does not implement ECDSA (SHA256withECDSA and the other SHA*withECDSA algorithms are on SunEC). Callers that pass this object to Signature.getInstance or Cipher.getInstance, or that treat a non-null result as "BC is available" / compare the name to BC or BCFIPS, will throw NoSuchAlgorithmException or take a non-BC path. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null for the same method to mean there is no BC; a non-null wrong provider bypasses those null checks. Return null or throw; do not hand back the keystore provider.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default JDK keystore provider rather than the expected BouncyCastle provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() is a new abstract method and breaks existing implementations

order() was added to the public CryptoProvider interface with no default body. In-tree Default, Elytron, and FIPS implementations were updated, but any already-compiled implementor (a downstream or older crypto provider jar, or a test double) has no order() method. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider loads every provider via ServiceLoader and then calls CryptoProvider::order. That invocation throws AbstractMethodError and aborts detection entirely, so init fails even if a valid newer provider is also on the classpath. Source compatibility for external implementors is broken as well. Give the method a default that is higher than AuthzClientCryptoProvider's 100 (for example default int order() { return 200; }) so existing providers still outrank the authz-client stub and do not crash provider detection.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding an abstract order() method to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations that do not implement it. The candidate adds runtime and source-compatibility details without changing the underlying concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Tied crypto providers are chosen silently instead of failing startup

detectProvider used to abort startup with IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It now sorts by order() descending and keeps the first, logging the rest only at debug. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so they tie, and ServiceLoader/classpath enumeration order picks the winner. A deployment that contains both the FIPS provider and a non-FIPS provider, which previously refused to boot, now starts and can run non-FIPS algorithms with no warn or error. Constructors of every discovered provider still run before the choice, so the non-selected provider has already mutated JVM security state (provider insertion, securerandom.strongAlgorithms, KeyManagerFactory/TrustManagerFactory properties) while the process continues. Nothing in this PR tests two providers that share the top order. Fail when more than one provider shares the highest order (AuthzClientCryptoProvider at 100 can still coexist with a single order-200 provider), and if a priority is intended give FIPS a strictly higher order than Default and Elytron.

ECDSAAlgorithmTest cannot compile with this module's dependencies

ECDSAAlgorithmTest imports org.keycloak.crypto.ECDSAAlgorithm and org.keycloak.crypto.JavaAlgorithm and calls ECDSAAlgorithm.getSignatureLength() and JavaAlgorithm.getJavaAlgorithm(). Those types live in keycloak-server-spi, not in keycloak-core. authz/client/pom.xml only depends on keycloak-core (plus logging, httpclient, and jackson); this PR adds junit and hamcrest but not keycloak-server-spi. Maven test-compile of keycloak-authz-client-tests will fail with cannot find symbol, so the only test of the new ECDSA ASN.1 conversion never runs. The suite builds one KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and no ECGenParameterSpec, so the JDK default curve (secp256r1) is used for testES256, testES384, and testES512. ES384 and ES512 therefore never produce 48-byte or 66-byte R and S values; those components stay about 32 bytes and are only zero-padded to 96 or 132. Every real ES512 DER signature uses a long-form SEQUENCE length (content longer than 127 bytes), so ASN1Encoder.writeLength and ASN1Decoder.readLength's long-form path is never executed. The only assertion is that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip to each other. The DER from concatenatedRSToASN1DER is not passed to Signature.verify and is not compared to the original JCA signature, so an encoder that this decoder accepts but JCA or another JOSE stack rejects still passes, including for ES256. Initialize P-256, P-384, and P-521 for the matching algorithms and verify the converted DER with Signature.verify.

AuthzClient.create permanently latches the process-wide crypto provider

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) before building the client. init only runs detection while the static cryptoProvider field is null; later calls, including the server's own init, are ignored. Detection uses ServiceLoader on that classloader only, which does not see providers visible solely on a child or thread-context classloader. If this runs first in a JVM whose view of the classpath is the authz-client jar (AuthzClientCryptoProvider, order 100) without Default, Elytron, or FIPS (order 200), the stub is installed for the whole process and cannot be replaced. The stub throws UnsupportedOperationException for getSignature, getPemUtils, ciphers, certificate utilities, and truststore wrapping, so a later embedded server or in-process testsuite that expected its own CryptoProvider fails on ordinary crypto calls. Do not latch a lower-priority provider forever: also search the context classloader, and allow a later init to replace the current provider when a higher-order one is found.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can return without stopping every flusher process

SpanFlusher.join sets stopped, then calls next_step.join(timeout) before waiting on flusher workers. The deadline is that same timeout, and the new loop breaks as soon as it has passed, skipping process.terminate() for every worker not yet visited. If next_step.join consumes the timeout, or the first stuck worker uses up the rest, the remaining shard flushers are never signaled. close() intentionally does not stop them, so join() is the only shutdown path. Those workers are daemons, but the consumer process stays up across rebalances, so a leaked flusher keeps calling flush_segments and producing to the buffered-segments topic for shards that may already have been revoked and assigned to another consumer. That races Redis flush state and emits duplicate segments. This is a regression from the previous single-process join, which always called terminate() after the wait even if the deadline had already passed. Workers that do get terminate() are never join()ed, so join() can return while they are still alive, and there is no try/finally, so an exception from next_step.join skips cleanup entirely. Always stop every worker (kill if needed) and join() it, including on the timeout and exception paths.

The thread backend used whenever produce_to_pipe is set is not interrupted at all (kill/terminate are skipped for non-Process workers). A hung thread therefore keeps flushing the same shards after a new thread is started; each hang restart adds another live flusher until MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS trips, and those threads all call flush_segments and produce, duplicating segments and racing done_flush_segments. On the process backend the replacement is spawned while the killed worker may still be inside Redis flush or Kafka produce. Join (or join-after-kill) the old worker, and do not start a second thread while the first is alive, before creating the replacement.

A seconds value is always less than a millisecond timestamp, so every error is emitted before every breadcrumb; if the stored timestamp is a string, `str < float` raises TypeError and the summarize request 500s. The feedback list page is wrapped in page filters, so the list and search respect the environment selector while the summary does not. Search index misses writes committed during startup indexing

init lists every namespace and only afterward calls WatchWriteEvents. That snapshot records the latest resource version and the SQL poller only returns history newer than that snapshot. The RV returned by build is discarded. Any create, update, or delete committed after a namespace was listed and before the watch snapshot, including writes from other HA replicas, is neither in the bulk index nor replayed. The watch starts only after the slowest namespace finishes, so namespaces that finished early have a gap as long as the rest of the index build, which is the long operation this change is about. Search will keep serving missing, stale, or already-deleted objects until that document is written again. Each errgroup worker assigns s.build's result to the outer err variable and then returns err. When WorkerThreads is greater than 1 those goroutines race on that variable. A failed build can return nil if another worker stores nil into err before the return, so group.Wait succeeds and NewResourceServer starts with some namespaces never indexed. A successful worker can also return another worker's error and fail startup. This is a real data race, not just a logic race. totalBatchesIndexed is incremented from the same goroutines with no synchronization, so the trace attribute is racy as well. After indexing, init starts a goroutine that loops on v := <-events and calls handleEvent, using context.Background rather than the server context. The SQL backend poller closes that channel when the backend stops (it selects on backend done and defers close). A receive on a closed channel yields a nil event, and handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type, which panics. An unrecovered goroutine panic crashes the process during graceful shutdown, skipping the rest of cleanup. server.Stop cannot stop the loop because it only cancels s.ctx. The loop must exit when the channel is closed or the context is cancelled, and the watch must be tied to the server lifetime.

The comment that was removed even said the last RV should be checked so an unchanged index can be skipped. NewResourceServer calls Init and, on error, logs and returns nil without calling cancel or Stop. lifecycle.Init may already have opened the database. If search.init succeeded and initWatcher then failed, search.init has already started a WatchWriteEvents poller and an event goroutine on context.Background. The caller never receives the server, so it cannot Stop those resources, and the connection pool and pollers live until the process exits. On the error path, stop the lifecycle/backend and cancel the server context, while still returning the original init error.

The context now used for the full index build is created from context.Background inside NewResourceServer, which does not accept a caller context. The only cancel is Stop, and Stop cannot run until NewResourceServer returns, which is blocked on GetResourceStats and every ListIterator in the index build. A stuck database call therefore hangs process startup with no deadline, and a shutdown signal cannot abort the build. The old request context cancelled too early; this replacement needs a long but bounded startup context that process shutdown can cancel.

TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration coverage for the storage-server target, and this PR makes that target initialize unified storage and build the search index during construction. Fix the Postgres failure instead of skipping it.
