WipeMyCal reschedule marks the booking CANCELLED, then starts cleanup with bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) / deleteMeeting(...) }). Array.forEach does not await async callbacks, and the surrounding try/catch cannot see their rejections. The handler continues to sendRequestRescheduleEmail and returns true while Google/Outlook deletion and video deletion are still in flight (or not started, if the runtime suspends first). Failures are unhandled rejections rather than logged errors. A cancelled booking can leave the external event and meeting in place, blocking the time slot. Replace forEach with an awaited Promise.all(map(async ...)) or a for...of loop.

Recurring cancel never joins per-calendar deletes to apiDeletes

When cancelling all remaining occurrences, calendar deletion is bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... const deletedEvent = await calendar?.deleteEvent(...); apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); }). forEach does not return those promises. The push happens only after deleteEvent has already settled, and it pushes the resolved value rather than the in-flight promise. The later await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) therefore does not wait for this work and cannot observe its failures. The handler still returns "Booking successfully cancelled." The non-recurring branch in the same function was converted to a for...of that pushes calendar.deleteEvent's promise before awaiting; this recurring branch was only given an inner await and still races the request lifetime. That keeps the cold-start and memory cost of the old static barrel and adds a burst of parallel module loads. Each import() promise is also stored with no .catch(). If any app module rejects and that key is not awaited, the rejection is unhandled; Node's default unhandledRejection behavior throws and can exit the process, including for an app the current request never uses. A failed optional app should not be able to crash the server. Lazy-load on first access and attach rejection handling so an unused or broken app degrades instead of rejecting in the background.

Those are the paths this change adds and the ones the new storage implementation gets wrong, so the suite stays green while replay and revocation are broken.

Caution falsely says the Operator fails without rolling-updates

The new caution says that during preview the `rolling-updates` feature must be enabled or the Keycloak Operator will fail. That contradicts both the note later in this same section and the operator test added in this PR. UpgradeTest.createInitialDeployment returns immediately when the update strategy is null and does not set spec.features.enabled to rolling-updates. Those cases still call deployKeycloak with wait-for-ready, and a cache max-count change is expected to roll rather than fail. So a normal Keycloak CR reconciles, becomes ready, and applies the documented 26.1-compatible default (recreate only on image change, roll on other config) with the preview feature off. The feature is only enabled in that test when spec.update.strategy is set explicitly. As written, the caution tells every Operator user that an upgrade breaks unless they turn on a preview feature, which will cause unnecessary preview opt-in or blocked upgrades. Narrow the warning to explicit spec.update usage, or change the test if fail-closed is actually required.

Exit code 4 is documented as an upgrade decision

The new exit-code row says code 4 means "Rolling Upgrade is not possible" because `rolling-updates` is disabled. That is the same decision wording as exit code 3, and the paragraph above the table says these codes are how automation determines the upgrade type. The implementation does not decide compatibility: both update-compatibility check and update-compatibility metadata print "Unable to use this command. The preview feature 'rolling-updates' is not enabled." and exit 4 before reading metadata or comparing versions. The only other upgrade type this guide defines is recreate (shut the deployment down before applying config). A pipeline that treats "rolling is not possible" as that outcome will take an unnecessary outage when the flag was merely omitted. Describe code 4 as a precondition failure, state that the upgrade type was not determined, and note that the metadata subcommand returns 4 as well; the table currently sits only under the check command.

Changed exit codes 3 and 4 are never asserted

This PR changes CompatibilityResult.RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 and adds FEATURE_DISABLED = 4, and the guide tells users to branch automation on those codes. testFeatureNotEnabled only checks that stderr contains the disabled-feature sentence and never asserts the process exit code is 4; it also covers only the metadata subcommand, not check. testWrongVersions only checks the incompatibility log line and never asserts exit code 3. CLIResult.assertError succeeds for any non-zero status, so leaving recreate at 4, or picocli.exit collapsing the custom code to 1, would still pass. That docs-vs-code mismatch (docs already said 3, the constant was 4) is exactly what this PR is fixing, and nothing locks the new contract.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Null Clients type resource NPEs permission checks

When no per-client authorization resource exists, hasPermission sets resource from AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource and immediately calls PolicyStore.findByResource(server, resource) with no null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null if the Clients type resource was never created (init skips existing admin-permissions clients) or was deleted. findByResource then dereferences null and the admin call fails with 500 instead of denying the permission. Treat a null type resource as no all-clients permission.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: getResourceTypeResource can return null in hasPermission, and findByResource then throws an NPE. Both also call for a null check.

false_positives.candidate:
All-clients view bypasses an explicit per-client view deny

ClientPermissionsV2.canView(ClientModel) returns true as soon as canView() is true. canView() is true not only for the view-clients/manage-clients admin roles, but also when a fine-grained permission grants the view scope on the Clients resource type (all clients). The per-client check is then skipped, so a Logic.NEGATIVE view permission for that same caller on one client is never evaluated. requireView(client) and every admin operation gated on canView(client) (client representation, protocol mappers, client scopes) still succeed for the client that was explicitly denied. Negative permissions are already part of this model (user FGAP tests use Logic.NEGATIVE on the same permission API). Short-circuit only on the admin-role helper (canViewClientDefault), then evaluate the per-client decision so an explicit deny overrides all-clients view. The new client tests never create a negative permission, so this bypass is untested.

A per-client resource suppresses all-clients permissions

hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) loads the authorization resource named with the client id and, if that row exists, evaluates only that resource. The Clients type resource (all clients) is consulted only when no per-client resource exists. A per-client resource is created for any permission that targets that client, including a permission for a different user or a different scope. An administrator granted manage, configure, view, or map-roles on all clients then loses that grant on the client, because their all-clients policy is attached to the type resource and is never evaluated; a per-client grant of scope A also hides an all-clients grant of scope B. Evaluate both resources, and let a per-client policy override all-clients only for the scopes that policy actually covers. PermissionClientTest only covers a lone per-client grant or a lone all-clients grant, never both.

Existing admin-permissions clients never receive the Clients schema

AdminPermissionsSchema.init returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and that is the only place schema scopes and the per-type all-resource records are created. This change adds the Clients resource type and the configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes, but realms that already enabled admin permissions V2 already have that client (created earlier with only Users). After upgrade those scopes and the Clients resource are never inserted, so creating a Clients permission fails with a missing-scope validation error and all-clients evaluation cannot find the type resource. init must add any schema scopes and resource types that are not already present instead of treating a non-null admin-permissions client as fully initialized.

Client deletion throws when v1 and v2 admin-permission features are both enabled

The removal listener runs when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (v1) is enabled and then calls management().clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException. The two flags are independent, so enabling v2 does not turn v1 off. Deleting a client then throws from the provider event listener and can roll back the removal. Guard the v1 cleanup with the same condition management() uses (v1 evaluator actually selected), or make the v2 removal path a no-op instead of throwing. Role and group removal in this listener call management() as well; clients() is the override that now throws.

Client permission resources are returned with a null display name

getResourceName resolves Users policies to "All users" or the username, but has no Clients branch and falls through to resource.getDisplayName(). Per-client resources are stored with the client UUID as the name and no display name, and the all-clients resource is stored as name "Clients" without a display name, so the admin permissions API returns null. The console cannot show which client a permission applies to, unlike users in the same API. Resolve the stored id to the clientId, return a label such as "All clients" for the type resource, and fail clearly if the client no longer exists, matching the user path.

canExchangeTo throws instead of returning an authorization decision

ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException. AdminPermissions.evaluator installs this class whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and token exchange calls clients().canExchangeTo to decide whether the caller may exchange into another client's audience. That call now fails the token request with an unhandled server error instead of allow or deny. The same class throws from isPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, and setPermissionsEnabled; this PR only guards the removal listener, and only behind the v1 feature flag. A boolean permission check must not throw — return false until exchange is actually implemented (getEvaluationContext in this class is unused). Otherwise enabling v2 breaks token exchange and any client management-permissions endpoint that still reaches these methods.

Client tests rotate myclient's secret and leave realm mutations behind

testConfigureOnlyOneClient calls generateNewSecret and invalidateRotatedSecret on myclient and never restores the original secret. realmAdminClient is injected as client myclient using the secret from the realm config, and AbstractPermissionTest's @InjectRealm does not request a per-method lifecycle, so the realm is shared by every method in the class. The next test that must obtain a token authenticates with a secret that no longer exists and fails. The same class also leaves other shared state: testManageOnlyOneClient renames myclient and moves a default client scope to optional, and testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient creates myclient-role and myclient-subRole with no cleanup. AfterEach only deletes scope permissions. Restore the secret, name, and scopes, and delete the roles, or results depend on test order.

requireView javadoc claims a boolean result for void methods

requireView and requireViewClientScopes are void and throw ForbiddenException when the matching can* check is false, but the new javadoc says each "Returns true if canView()/canViewClientScopes() returns true". That describes the boolean methods, not these require* methods. Neighboring require* docs correctly say they throw ForbiddenException. Callers reading the interface will think these methods return a decision instead of aborting the request.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

All-groups VIEW is treated as permission to manage groups

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns true if hasPermission finds either the VIEW or MANAGE scope on the all-groups resource. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup authorizes group creation with requireManage(), which calls this method, and any other caller of canManage()/requireManage() treats it as a write check. A fine-grained admin granted only view access to groups can therefore create top-level groups. That contradicts canManage(GroupModel) in the same class, which correctly requires only MANAGE, and contradicts V1, which only checks the manage-users role. The new javadoc on GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage repeats the same mistake by documenting VIEW as sufficient. canManage() must require the MANAGE scope only.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() accepts the VIEW scope when it should require MANAGE only, which lets view-only users perform write operations.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Group-scoped user search and counts use authorization resource ids, not group ids

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission is what UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource pass to the user store (session attribute UserModel.GROUPS, and getUsersCount) so that an admin who cannot view all users only sees members of groups they may view. The callback passes groupResource.getId() into hasPermission and stores that same value. hasPermission treats the argument as a group id and looks it up with resourceStore.findByName, but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource stores the group id as the resource name and the authorization store assigns a different resource id. The lookup therefore misses. findByType(GROUPS) also cannot see per-group resources, because getOrCreateResource never calls setType, so only the type resource named "Groups" (if present) is visited. The set ends up empty or filled with authorization UUIDs. User search pagination then either is not restricted to the permitted groups or is restricted to ids that match no membership, and the count API returns 0 or a count for a non-existent group. Return the group id (resource name), skip the type resource, and persist instance resources with type Groups.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes and stores groupResource.getId(), while hasPermission looks resources up by name, which holds the group id. Both also note that only the type-level resource is effectively evaluated, and that the wrong ids break UserModel.GROUPS filtering and the counts. Both suggest using resource names (group ids) instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Group deletion throws when FGAP V2 is enabled

GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException (as do the other GroupPermissionManagement methods). AdminPermissions.registerListener still handles GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent by calling management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled. management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, and therefore GroupPermissionsV2, whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. With both features on, which is the normal combination if V1 is a default feature and V2 is enabled for this work, realm.removeGroup and the admin delete-group API fail with that exception and the group is not removed. If only V2 is enabled, the listener is not registered at all, so the V2 authorization resource named by the group id is never deleted and remains orphaned on the admin-permissions client. Group removal needs a V2 cleanup path; the V1 listener must not call the throwing methods while V2 is active.

A per-group permission resource hides all-groups grants

hasPermission looks up the per-group resource by name and, if it exists, evaluates only that resource. The all-groups resource is used only when no per-group resource exists. Creating any permission on a group (including one for a different administrator) creates that resource, after which an admin who holds VIEW or MANAGE on all groups is denied for that group because their all-groups policy is never evaluated. canView, canManage, canViewMembers, canManageMembers, and canManageMembership all go through this helper. GroupsResource.getGroups and GroupResource.getSubGroups no longer short-circuit on global canView() and now depend entirely on canView(group), so listing is affected as well. The new tests never combine an all-groups grant with a specific grant for another user. Evaluation has to combine the instance resource and the resource-type resource under the schema decision strategy; preferring the instance resource drops legitimate grants and also drops all-groups denies when only the instance is evaluated.

Existing admin-permissions clients never gain the Groups schema

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and no other path creates the Groups resource type, the "Groups" all-resource, or the new scopes manage-membership, manage-members, and view-members. Realms that already enabled fine-grained admin permissions (the client was created when only Users and Clients existed) do not pick up this change, and turning admin permissions off and on does not help if the client row remains. Creating a group permission then fails in getScope with "Scope [view-members] does not exist". GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission also calls getResourceTypeResource, gets null, and invokes policyStore.findByResource and resource.getScopes() with no null check, so group admin calls from users without manage-users/view-users become 500s instead of a deny. Upgrade must add the missing scopes and the Groups type resource to existing admin-permissions clients, or init/getResourceTypeResource must create them lazily.

Group permission resources have no human-readable name

getResourceName resolves only the Users resource type ("All users" or the username) and otherwise returns resource.getDisplayName(). Group resources created by getOrCreateResource use the group id as the name and never set a display name, and the new Groups type is not handled here. Permission listings for group policies therefore show a null name or a raw id instead of the group name or path, and there is no "All groups" label for the type resource. A missing user already throws ModelIllegalStateException; a missing group is silently unlabeled. Resolve group resources the same way users are resolved.

requireManageMembers javadoc cites the wrong check

The javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws ForbiddenException when canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. The implementation enforces canManageMembers, which is the manage-members scope, not manage-membership. Those are different permissions (managing the users in a group versus changing a user's group membership). An implementor or caller following the javadoc will check or document the wrong scope.

Public group permission methods were removed and renamed

GroupPermissionEvaluator is public. This change deletes getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel) and renames getGroupsWithViewPermission() to getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() with no bridge method. In-repo callers were updated, but any extension that implements the interface or calls the old methods will fail to compile or throw NoSuchMethodError at runtime. If this interface is part of the supported admin-permissions contract, keep the old methods as deprecated delegates; otherwise call the break out in the release notes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider

CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() is specified to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS Provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the platform keystore provider (SUN for the Java 8 default JKS keystore, and typically SUN for the Java 9+ default PKCS12 keystore). That provider is not BC and does not implement ECDSA (SHA256withECDSA and the other SHA*withECDSA algorithms are on SunEC). Callers that pass this object to Signature.getInstance or Cipher.getInstance, or that treat a non-null result as "BC is available" / compare the name to BC or BCFIPS, will throw NoSuchAlgorithmException or take a non-BC path. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null for the same method to mean there is no BC; a non-null wrong provider bypasses those null checks. Return null or throw; do not hand back the keystore provider.
true_positives.reasoning: Both say getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider instead of BouncyCastle. This is the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() is a new abstract method and breaks existing implementations

order() was added to the public CryptoProvider interface with no default body. In-tree Default, Elytron, and FIPS implementations were updated, but any already-compiled implementor (a downstream or older crypto provider jar, or a test double) has no order() method. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider loads every provider via ServiceLoader and then calls CryptoProvider::order. That invocation throws AbstractMethodError and aborts detection entirely, so init fails even if a valid newer provider is also on the classpath. Source compatibility for external implementors is broken as well. Give the method a default that is higher than AuthzClientCryptoProvider's 100 (for example default int order() { return 200; }) so existing providers still outrank the authz-client stub and do not crash provider detection.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same problem: order() was added to CryptoProvider as an abstract method, which breaks backward compatibility for existing implementations.

false_positives.candidate:
Tied crypto providers are chosen silently instead of failing startup

detectProvider used to abort startup with IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It now sorts by order() descending and keeps the first, logging the rest only at debug. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so they tie, and ServiceLoader/classpath enumeration order picks the winner. A deployment that contains both the FIPS provider and a non-FIPS provider, which previously refused to boot, now starts and can run non-FIPS algorithms with no warn or error. Constructors of every discovered provider still run before the choice, so the non-selected provider has already mutated JVM security state (provider insertion, securerandom.strongAlgorithms, KeyManagerFactory/TrustManagerFactory properties) while the process continues. Nothing in this PR tests two providers that share the top order. Fail when more than one provider shares the highest order (AuthzClientCryptoProvider at 100 can still coexist with a single order-200 provider), and if a priority is intended give FIPS a strictly higher order than Default and Elytron.

ECDSAAlgorithmTest cannot compile with this module's dependencies

ECDSAAlgorithmTest imports org.keycloak.crypto.ECDSAAlgorithm and org.keycloak.crypto.JavaAlgorithm and calls ECDSAAlgorithm.getSignatureLength() and JavaAlgorithm.getJavaAlgorithm(). Those types live in keycloak-server-spi, not in keycloak-core. authz/client/pom.xml only depends on keycloak-core (plus logging, httpclient, and jackson); this PR adds junit and hamcrest but not keycloak-server-spi. Maven test-compile of keycloak-authz-client-tests will fail with cannot find symbol, so the only test of the new ECDSA ASN.1 conversion never runs. Add a test-scoped dependency on the module that contains org.keycloak.crypto, or stop referencing those types and hardcode the JCA algorithm names and signature lengths.

ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key and never check DER with JCA

The suite builds one KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and no ECGenParameterSpec, so the JDK default curve (secp256r1) is used for testES256, testES384, and testES512. ES384 and ES512 therefore never produce 48-byte or 66-byte R and S values; those components stay about 32 bytes and are only zero-padded to 96 or 132. Every real ES512 DER signature uses a long-form SEQUENCE length (content longer than 127 bytes), so ASN1Encoder.writeLength and ASN1Decoder.readLength's long-form path is never executed. The only assertion is that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip to each other. The DER from concatenatedRSToASN1DER is not passed to Signature.verify and is not compared to the original JCA signature, so an encoder that this decoder accepts but JCA or another JOSE stack rejects still passes, including for ES256. Initialize P-256, P-384, and P-521 for the matching algorithms and verify the converted DER with Signature.verify.

AuthzClient.create permanently latches the process-wide crypto provider

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) before building the client. init only runs detection while the static cryptoProvider field is null; later calls, including the server's own init, are ignored. Detection uses ServiceLoader on that classloader only, which does not see providers visible solely on a child or thread-context classloader. If this runs first in a JVM whose view of the classpath is the authz-client jar (AuthzClientCryptoProvider, order 100) without Default, Elytron, or FIPS (order 200), the stub is installed for the whole process and cannot be replaced. The stub throws UnsupportedOperationException for getSignature, getPemUtils, ciphers, certificate utilities, and truststore wrapping, so a later embedded server or in-process testsuite that expected its own CryptoProvider fails on ordinary crypto calls. Do not latch a lower-priority provider forever: also search the context classloader, and allow a later init to replace the current provider when a higher-order one is found.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

When the cached group has already been deleted, getSubGroupsCount returns null instead of a count. Other GroupModel implementations do not do this: a subgroup count query returns 0 when the parent row is gone, and null is also how the admin API signals that the count was not requested. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: getSubGroupsCount returns null when it should not, which can cause NPEs in callers. The candidate adds context about the deleted-group delegate case and suggests returning 0L instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrency test never joins the reader and can miss the race

createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti starts a non-daemon reader that calls groups() in a loop, but never waits for that thread to enter the loop or to finish. deletedAll is set true immediately after the deletes and caughtExceptions is asserted on the next line, so the assertion can run before any list call has started or before an in-flight list has recorded its exception. The test never joins the reader thread, and deletedAll is set true right before the assertion, so exceptions recorded afterward can be missed and the test can pass when it shouldn't. Its extra points about the daemon thread and the latch don't change that it identifies the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Conditional passkeys UI is no longer set up on the initial login page

isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) is true only when its user argument is non-null, and both setup sites now use that helper: authenticate() around line 115 and the error challenge() override around line 137. Previously fillContextForm ran when passkeys were enabled and the user was not yet selected (context.getUser() == null). true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

SpanFlusher.join sets stopped, then calls next_step.join(timeout) before waiting on flusher workers. The deadline is that same timeout, and the new loop breaks as soon as it has passed, skipping process.terminate() for every worker not yet visited. If next_step.join consumes the timeout, or the first stuck worker uses up the rest, the remaining shard flushers are never signaled. close() intentionally does not stop them, so join() is the only shutdown path. Those workers are daemons, but the consumer process stays up across rebalances, so a leaked flusher keeps calling flush_segments and producing to the buffered-segments topic for shards that may already have been revoked and assigned to another consumer. That races Redis flush state and emits duplicate segments. This is a regression from the previous single-process join, which always called terminate() after the wait even if the deadline had already passed. Workers that do get terminate() are never join()ed, so join() can return while they are still alive, and there is no try/finally, so an exception from next_step.join skips cleanup entirely. The thread backend used whenever produce_to_pipe is set is not interrupted at all (kill/terminate are skipped for non-Process workers). A hung thread therefore keeps flushing the same shards after a new thread is started; each hang restart adds another live flusher until MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS trips, and those threads all call flush_segments and produce, duplicating segments and racing done_flush_segments. On the process backend the replacement is spawned while the killed worker may still be inside Redis flush or Kafka produce. Join (or join-after-kill) the old worker, and do not start a second thread while the first is alive, before creating the replacement.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the whole build, so a second GetIndex blocked until the finished index was published. The mutex is now taken only around the cache insert. getOrCreateIndex still does check-then-act (GetIndex, and on a miss build) and even has a TODO that same-key builds must not run together. After startup, two Search calls, or a Search and a watch event, for a namespace that was not built during init (count at or below InitMinCount) both see a cache miss and both call BuildIndex. Memory indexes both succeed and the later cache write overwrites the earlier one without closing it, so documents already written to the discarded index disappear from search and the Bleve index is leaked. File indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory; the loser fails with a path-exists error, so the caller gets a search error even if the other build published a usable index. Parallel builds of different keys are fine, but same-key builds need a per-key lock or singleflight held from the existence check through cache publish.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same race as the golden comment. The cacheMu lock was narrowed from covering the whole BuildIndex call to only the cache insert. As a result, concurrent same-key builds can run. The candidate adds consequences such as a leaked index and a path-exists error, but the core issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

TotalDocs ranges the index cache without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no RLock, while BuildIndex writes that map under cacheMu. Narrowing the lock means builds now publish into the map concurrently, during startup and for later cold namespaces. In Go, a concurrent map read and write is a fatal runtime error, not a missed update. init also calls TotalDocs immediately after starting the watch goroutine that can BuildIndex on a cache miss, and TotalDocs is part of the SearchBackend interface so any other caller can hit the same crash. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization while BuildIndex can write to it concurrently, including from the watcher goroutine started in init, which risks a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Search index misses writes committed during startup indexing

init lists every namespace and only afterward calls WatchWriteEvents. That snapshot records the latest resource version and the SQL poller only returns history newer than that snapshot. The RV returned by build is discarded. Any create, update, or delete committed after a namespace was listed and before the watch snapshot, including writes from other HA replicas, is neither in the bulk index nor replayed. The watch starts only after the slowest namespace finishes, so namespaces that finished early have a gap as long as the rest of the index build, which is the long operation this change is about. Search will keep serving missing, stale, or already-deleted objects until that document is written again. Record the RV before listing, or buffer watch events first, and replay history from that RV after the bulk load.

Parallel index builders share err and can hide failures

Each errgroup worker assigns s.build's result to the outer err variable and then returns err. When WorkerThreads is greater than 1 those goroutines race on that variable. A failed build can return nil if another worker stores nil into err before the return, so group.Wait succeeds and NewResourceServer starts with some namespaces never indexed. A successful worker can also return another worker's error and fail startup. This is a real data race, not just a logic race. totalBatchesIndexed is incremented from the same goroutines with no synchronization, so the trace attribute is racy as well. Use a local error inside the closure and an atomic counter.

Search watch loop panics when the event channel closes

After indexing, init starts a goroutine that loops on v := <-events and calls handleEvent, using context.Background rather than the server context. The SQL backend poller closes that channel when the backend stops (it selects on backend done and defers close). A receive on a closed channel yields a nil event, and handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type, which panics. An unrecovered goroutine panic crashes the process during graceful shutdown, skipping the rest of cleanup. server.Stop cannot stop the loop because it only cancels s.ctx. The loop must exit when the channel is closed or the context is cancelled, and the watch must be tied to the server lifetime.

File-backed indexes cannot be reopened, so restart fails startup

When size is above FileThreshold (the zero value is 0, so any positive count takes this branch unless the option is overridden), BuildIndex calls bleve.New on a directory under Root and never bleve.Open. bleve.New fails if that path already exists, and a failed builder returns without closing the index or removing a partial directory. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer and any error aborts construction, so a restart after a successful file index, or a retry after a build that left the directory behind, cannot start the storage server. The comment that was removed even said the last RV should be checked so an unchanged index can be skipped. Open an existing index when the directory is present, and delete or uniquely name the directory if a build fails, or every file-backed namespace wedges process startup.

Init failure in the constructor leaks the backend and watchers

NewResourceServer calls Init and, on error, logs and returns nil without calling cancel or Stop. lifecycle.Init may already have opened the database. If search.init succeeded and initWatcher then failed, search.init has already started a WatchWriteEvents poller and an event goroutine on context.Background. The caller never receives the server, so it cannot Stop those resources, and the connection pool and pollers live until the process exits. On the error path, stop the lifecycle/backend and cancel the server context, while still returning the original init error.

Startup index build cannot be cancelled or given a deadline

The context now used for the full index build is created from context.Background inside NewResourceServer, which does not accept a caller context. The only cancel is Stop, and Stop cannot run until NewResourceServer returns, which is blocked on GetResourceStats and every ListIterator in the index build. A stuck database call therefore hangs process startup with no deadline, and a shutdown signal cannot abort the build. The old request context cancelled too early; this replacement needs a long but bounded startup context that process shutdown can cancel.

TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration coverage for the storage-server target, and this PR makes that target initialize unified storage and build the search index during construction. The change skips the test whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB is postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone but works locally. Postgres is a primary deployment database, so CI no longer runs storage-server startup there, and a startup regression from eager init will not be caught. Fix the Postgres failure instead of skipping it.

Pass build_fingerprint(group_key) into the hook or overwrite the returned occurrence's fingerprint before publishing.

Occurrences are published before dedupe and detector state are committed

process_detectors sends each result to Kafka via create_issue_occurrence_from_result and only then calls handler.commit_state_updates(), which is what persists the dedupe value and active/priority transition queued during evaluate. This PR is what starts attaching an IssueOccurrence to threshold breaches on that path. If publish raises on a later group key, or the process stops before the commit, the dedupe key and stored status are unchanged. The same packet is evaluated again as a new transition and another occurrence is emitted. Occurrence ids are chosen by the subclass and are not derived from detector id, group key, and dedupe value, so the retry is not idempotent and users can get duplicate issues.

The returned dict ignores that copy and sends monitor_environment.monitor.config instead. The display conversion never reaches Kafka, so contexts.monitor.config.schedule_type stays the raw stored value (typically an integer) on every monitor incident occurrence. The payload also aliases the live config dict, so any later in-place mutation of the event context mutates the in-memory monitor. Return the adjusted copy.

false_positives.candidate:
Incident opens before failure_issue_threshold consecutive failures

In try_incident_threshold, when failure_issue_threshold is greater than 1, the code loads at most that many recent check-ins (ordered by date_added, then reversed) and returns early only if one of them is CheckInStatus.OK. It never requires the window to contain failure_issue_threshold rows. A shorter history has no OK row, so execution still sets MonitorEnvironment.status to ERROR, get_or_creates a MonitorIncident, emits issue occurrences, and sends monitor_environment_failed. A new or ACTIVE monitor with failure_issue_threshold of 3 therefore opens an incident on its first failed check-in, and stays in ERROR so later failures keep attaching occurrences, until a success resolves it. The configured consecutive-failure tolerance is ignored whenever fewer than N check-ins exist. An empty slice also falls through this check and then raises IndexError on previous_checkins[0], aborting failure processing instead of returning False. Non-failure check-ins count toward the failure threshold

The threshold gate only tests whether any row equals CheckInStatus.OK. Every other status, including in-progress check-ins that are stored as MonitorCheckIn rows, is treated as part of the failure streak and also occupies a slot in the limited window. With failure_issue_threshold 2, a recent window of one in-progress check-in plus one error contains no OK row, so the environment is marked ERROR and an incident is opened after a single real failure. An in-progress row can also push an older OK check-in out of the N-row window so that success is ignored. Only error, missed, and timeout rows should count toward the consecutive-failure threshold.

Mixed failure-reason text does not match the documented message

get_failure_reason is shown as the Failure reason evidence on monitor issues. Its docstring specifies strings such as "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected" and "A failed check-in was detected". For more than one failure it formats each status as "%(count)d %(status)s" using the bare words missed/timeout/error, joins them, and appends a single "check-ins detected". Mixed failures therefore render as "2 missed, 1 timeout and 1 error check-ins detected" (no per-status "check-in(s)", and a plural noun for the whole list). The singular path returns "An error check-in was detected" (or missed/timeout), not the documented sentence. The docstring also misspells the summary as "humam readible". The evidence copy users see for multi-status incidents is wrong relative to the function's own contract.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued is frozen at import time

queued is declared as queued: datetime = timezone.now() on the dataclass. That expression is evaluated once when the class body runs, not when an instance is created. true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
to_dict() embeds a datetime in Celery task kwargs

to_dict() returns asdict(self), so queued is a raw datetime. sync_group_assignee_outbound passes that dict straight to sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async as assignment_source_dict. A JSON task transport (Celery JSON serializer, or Sentry taskworker) cannot encode datetime and raises TypeError while enqueueing. That apply_async call is synchronous inside GroupAssignee.assign and deassign, so an inbound webhook can persist the assignee and then fail, and the change is never pushed to any other integration. from_dict only does cls(**input_dict) inside a ValueError/TypeError handler and does not parse ISO-8601 strings. If a serializer stringifies the timestamp, queued is left as a string; if construction raises, from_dict returns None. The outbound task treats a None source as "not an echo" and performs the sync anyway, which brings the assignee loop back. self.tasks() runs eagerly and does not round-trip the serializer, and no test calls from_dict(source.to_dict()), so CI will not catch this.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem. to_dict() returns a raw datetime for queued, that dict is passed to apply_async task kwargs, and JSON serialization then fails at enqueue time.

false_positives.candidate:
Echo guard drops every linked issue on the source integration

should_sync returns False for the entire integration whenever sync_source.integration_id matches org_integration.integration_id. AssignmentSource does not record the external issue key, and sync_group_assignee_outbound attaches that same source to every GroupLink on the Sentry issue. A group may be linked to multiple external issues on one integration; GroupLink uniqueness is on the external-issue id, not the integration. An assignee webhook from Jira ticket A therefore skips outbound sync for ticket A and also for ticket B on the same Jira integration, so ticket B's assignee stays stale even with outbound assignee sync enabled. sync_group_assignee_inbound already has external_issue_key, and the outbound task already loads the target ExternalIssue, so the guard should skip only the originating issue. Skipping that one key still stops the echo; GroupAssignee.assign does not enqueue outbound sync when the assignee is unchanged, so a follow-up webhook that maps to the same Sentry user will not bounce.

Inbound wiring and cross-integration sync are untested

The new test calls GroupAssignee.objects.assign directly with an AssignmentSource and only covers the matching-integration assign case. test_assignee_sync_inbound_assign and test_assignee_sync_inbound_deassign call sync_group_assignee_inbound, which is the production webhook entry point that must pass assignment_source into assign and deassign, but they never assert that outbound sync to the source integration is skipped. Removing those assignment_source= arguments in sync.py would leave both inbound tests green and restore the loop. There is also no test that a second integration still receives the outbound update, and no test that deassign with a matching source skips outbound (test_assignee_sync_outbound_unassign still expects assignment_source=None). A guard that dropped every sourced sync, or a deassign path that forgot the source, would pass CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and races the commit loop

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says a processing error must not block commits for other messages, but the assertion requires that the partition was not committed (len(committed_offsets) == 0 or the partition is absent). The worker completes the offset in a finally block even when result_processor raises, so after both messages (offsets 100 and 101) the factory's commit callback should record 102 once the commit loop runs. That loop waits 1 second before its first commit, and the test breaks out as soon as both calls have run (usually a few hundred milliseconds), so it passes without ever observing a commit and will fail on a slower run once the commit arrives. Wait long enough for the commit thread and assert the offset required by the chosen retry policy.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says the test's assertion contradicts its docstring, which is the issue the golden comment describes. It also adds a point about a race with the commit loop.

false_positives.candidate:
Rebalance kills the shared pool and later results are committed unprocessed

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategies, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/join and ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown both call queue_pool.shutdown(). Arroyo calls close() then join(), then create_with_partitions() again on every assignment, including ordinary rebalances during deploys. shutdown() stops the workers and Queue.shutdown()s the queues, so later Queue.put raises queue.ShutDown. The new strategy still submits into that dead pool; submit()'s except block marks the offset complete without calling the result processor, and the new strategy's commit thread commits those offsets through the new commit callback. In the steady state the queues are empty, so nothing is outstanding and the commit cursor advances: those uptime results are skipped permanently. If a backlog left outstanding offsets, commits freeze and processing never resumes until the process is restarted. The OffsetTracker is also shared and never reset, so revoked partitions and the new assignment share one cursor. Recreate the pool per create_with_partitions (and tear it down only with that strategy), or do not shut the pool down on strategy close.

Offset commits run on a background thread against the Kafka consumer

_commit_loop is a daemon thread started from SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls commit_function, which invokes Arroyo's commit callback (result_consumer commit_offsets). That callback stages or commits offsets on the Kafka consumer. The confluent_kafka Consumer is not thread-safe, and Arroyo runs submit/poll and its own ONCE_PER_SECOND commit on the processor thread that owns the consumer. Committing from this side thread races with poll() and can raise inside librdkafka, commit a torn offset map, or deadlock when close() joins the commit thread while it is inside the callback and the callback needs the processor thread. Perform commits from poll() and from join/close on the processor thread, and force a final commit there after in-flight work has finished.

Unbounded queues never apply backpressure and can OOM the consumer

Each work queue is queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and submit() always put()s without blocking or raising MessageRejected. The class docstring says queues provide natural backpressure, but they never fill. If handling is slower than the topic, or one item is slow, the consumer keeps polling and retains every later message in the queues, in WorkItem (full payload), and in OffsetTracker.all_offsets, because a commit cannot move past the oldest outstanding offset on that partition. get_committable_offsets then walks range(start, max_offset+1) while holding the partition lock every second, so a large backlog also stalls workers completing offsets. poll() only emits a gauge, so the healthcheck keeps succeeding until the process OOMs. This is worse than batched-parallel, which caps memory at max_batch_size, under the exact slow-item failure this mode is meant to solve. Bound the queues and signal backpressure from submit so read-ahead stays finite and the processor can still poll. A worker that exits is also never restarted, so one dead thread permanently stalls its queue and that partition's commit cursor.

Shutdown abandons queued work and never commits the in-flight tail

close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown(). The commit loop then exits after at most one more pass, so offsets completed while workers finish are never committed and will be redelivered. FixedQueuePool.shutdown also sets worker.shutdown = True before Queue.shutdown(immediate=False). The worker loop checks that flag before Queue.get(), so it will not drain: it finishes at most the item already dequeued and leaves the rest outstanding. Combined with unbounded queues, a restart replays the whole buffered backlog, which can duplicate uptime incidents or notifications if handling is not idempotent. join() ignores the timeout Arroyo passes and calls close() again; Arroyo already calls close() before join(), so Queue.shutdown() runs twice and the second call raises queue.ShutDown, logged as an error for every queue on every shutdown. Drain first (do not set the worker flag until the queue is empty; let shutdown(immediate=False) unblock get), then force one final commit on the processor thread, make close() idempotent, and honor join's timeout.

Any submit exception is acked and the message is never retried

submit()'s bare except marks the BrokerValue offset complete after logging. That path runs for build_payload_grouping_key failures, Queue.put failures (including queue.ShutDown after the pool is shut down), and the decoder's AssertionError on FilteredPayload. The commit loop will then commit that offset, so the result is never retried and never sent to a DLQ. Returning None from the decoder is an intentional skip and matches serial mode; unexpected exceptions are not. Serial processing lets those exceptions fail the strategy so Arroyo can retry. A transient grouping error or a put failure therefore permanently drops an uptime result. Only complete offsets that were actually handled or deliberately filtered, and let unexpected submit failures propagate so the partition is not acked past them.

Graceful shutdown depends on Python 3.13-only queue APIs

Queue.shutdown and queue.ShutDown were added in Python 3.13. FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown() and the worker catches queue.ShutDown, with no fallback. On 3.11/3.12, shutdown raises AttributeError, which the bare except logs and swallows, so workers blocked in Queue.get() never wake. Each worker.join then waits out its 5 second timeout (default 20 queues is up to about 100 seconds) and in-flight DB work is abandoned when the daemon threads die at process exit. If this runtime is not guaranteed to be 3.13+, shutdown needs a compatible unblock path, such as a sentinel or get(timeout) that observes the shutdown flag.

Queue-depth assertion races the worker threads

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts get_stats()["total_items"] > 0. The pool's workers are already running and the test handler only appends to a list, so they can dequeue every item before get_stats() runs. The assertion fails intermittently on a fast machine. Block the handler until after the depth check, or pause the workers before submitting.

--mode help misstates parallelism and omits the new mode

uptime_options still says "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." Mode parallel builds a MultiprocessingPool; batched-parallel is the thread-pool mode; thread-queue-parallel, added in this change, is not described at all, nor is the fact that --max-workers becomes the queue count in that mode. Operators selecting the new mode from --help will misunderstand the concurrency model.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Optimized audit-log pagination crashes on datetime ordering

When optimized_pagination=true and the caller is a superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access, the audit log endpoint paginates AuditLogEntry with OptimizedCursorPaginator and order_by=-datetime. That paginator's get_item_key runs math.floor/math.ceil on the raw field, which is a datetime, so build_cursor raises TypeError as soon as a page contains any rows. value_from_cursor also returns the raw cursor number instead of converting it back to a datetime the way DateTimePaginator does, so a following page would compare the datetime column to an integer. The new path therefore 500s for every organization that has audit log rows. enable_advanced_features is passed into Endpoint.paginate, which this PR does not change; if that method does not forward unknown kwargs, the request fails even earlier with TypeError. false_positives.candidate:
SET-to-ZSET change breaks in-flight segment keys on deploy

Segment buffers are now written with ZADD and read with ZCARD, ZUNIONSTORE, and ZSCAN (add-buffer.lua and _load_segment_data). The previous release stored the same span-buf:s:* keys as Redis SETs (SADD/SUNIONSTORE/SSCAN). There is no new key prefix, dual-read, or WRONGTYPE handling. On a rolling deploy, keys still held as SETs (redis_ttl defaults to 3600s) make ZADD and ZSCAN raise WRONGTYPE; one such error fails the whole non-transactional pipeline, so both insert and flush abort for any batch that touches an old key. Old processes still running set commands fail the same way on keys the new code has already converted to sorted sets. Segments that cannot be flushed remain until TTL and are then dropped, so in-flight spans are lost and the consumer retries until those keys expire.

Insert-time eviction ignores max_segment_spans and drops spans silently

When a segment has more than 1000 members the Lua script ZPOPMINs it down to 1000. That limit is hardcoded and is not SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001, and a constructor argument callers can change). The flush-time backstop that skipped segments with more than max_segment_spans, logged an error, and incremented spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded was removed from _load_segment_data. A segment of 1001 spans, which the default config previously flushed intact, now loses a span with no metric, log, or truncation flag on the flushed payload. Changing max_segment_spans has no effect. The cap also only runs inside the script, which is a separate pipeline from the earlier ZADD; if the script errors after that ZADD, nothing else enforces a span count before the flusher loads and produces the segment. ZPOPMIN keeps the highest end_timestamp_precise scores, so a root span that does not have the latest end time can be deleted while the has-root-span flag stays set and the segment is still flushed on the shorter root timeout, missing its root payload.

ZUNIONSTORE sums timestamp scores and evicts the wrong spans

Both ZUNIONSTORE calls (the span-key merge and the parent-key merge) omit AGGREGATE, so Redis uses SUM. Member scores are end_timestamp_precise values, and ZPOPMIN later drops the lowest scores to enforce the cap. If the same payload is in both inputs — a retry after a partial write, or the same span stored under its own id and under the parent id — the scores are added, roughly doubling the timestamp. Those members then sort as newer than spans with a real later end time, so once the segment is over the cap the script keeps the corrupted members and drops newly ingested spans. The union needs AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN) so each member keeps an actual timestamp.

Redirect walk cap cut from 10000 to 1000 without a failure signal

The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects to find the segment key was reduced from 10000 iterations to 1000, and the comment that this cap can fail to join a deep chain was removed. If the chain is longer than 1000, the script stops on an intermediate span id, records the new span's redirect to that intermediate node, and merges into the wrong buffer. Flush then emits a split or mis-joined trace and nothing increments a metric when the cap is hit. Typical traces are shallower than this, but the old limit was intentional and the new one fails closed only by silently attaching spans to the wrong segment.

No test covers eviction, score order, or the ZSET migration

The buffer tests only add end_timestamp_precise to existing fixtures of four or five spans that all use the timestamp 1700000000.0. Nothing builds a segment larger than 1000 spans, asserts that the lowest scores are the ones removed, checks that max_segment_spans is the cap that is actually applied, or merges two sorted sets that share a member and checks the resulting score. Insert-time eviction, wrong-span drops from summed scores, and ZSCAN of sorted-set segment keys can all regress without a failing test. The new audit-log paginator path is also untested.

Glossary still calls segment keys sets that hold every span

The SpansBuffer glossary still describes span-buf:s:* as set keys that contain all span payloads for a segment, and the insert steps above still say the payload is added to a set. Those keys are now sorted sets scored by end_timestamp_precise, and members over the cap are deleted during insert, so a flushed segment may already be missing spans. Operators following this text will run SCARD or SSCAN, which fail with WRONGTYPE on the new keys, and will not know truncation is expected.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision ignores the dataset and query actually executed

_get_event_stats decides whether to upsample by passing the closed-over request dataset and request.GET query into is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects, not scoped_dataset and the query argument this call actually runs. The dashboard widget split path in the same method invokes _get_event_stats with the discover dataset and a rewritten query such as (query) AND !event.type:transaction or AND event.type:transaction, while the closed-over dataset is metrics_performance or metrics_enhanced_performance (that branch only runs when metrics_enhanced is true). _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns false for metrics datasets, so those error-event widget queries never upsample even when every project is allowlisted. The request query is also not the executed query: a request containing event.type:error would mark the transaction-only probe eligible, and a request without that substring would skip an errors-only split. Dashboard error charts for allowlisted projects keep showing sampled counts, and the eligibility bit can disagree with the query sent to Snuba.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug. The upsampling check uses the outer dataset (metrics) instead of scoped_dataset (discover) in the dashboard split path, so upsampling is skipped even when all projects are allowlisted. It also raises a related point about the query, but the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Upsampled count sums sample_weight but nothing stores that weight

upsampled_count is defined as toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) and is substituted for count() on allowlisted error queries. This change never writes sample_weight and never computes an inverse sample rate. The only data-path edit, _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling in the test factory, copies contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate (for example 0.1) onto the existing event field sample_rate, which is the server-side sampling rate, not a weight. ClickHouse sum skips nulls, and the aggregate does not use ifNull(sample_weight, 1), so events with a missing weight contribute nothing; toInt64 then truncates a fractional sum toward zero, so a stored rate of 0.1 becomes 0 rather than 10. OrganizationEventsStatsEndpoint only catches ValidationError, so if sample_weight is absent on the queried entity the chart request 500s instead of falling back to count(). The new stats test expects each 0.1-sampled event to contribute 10, which this code cannot produce. Once the allowlist is non-empty, error count charts for those projects will be zeroed, truncated, or failed.

Error detection is a substring match and treats negations as errors

_is_error_focused_query treats a discover query as error-only if the raw query string contains the substring event.type:error after lowercasing. That is true for negations and mixed filters: !event.type:error contains event.type:error, and so does event.type:error OR event.type:transaction. The helper says sample_weight must not be applied to transactions and that the check should err on the side of caution, but this match does the opposite of a parsed filter. For allowlisted projects, count() is then rewritten to sum(sample_weight) on a query that still includes transactions. That either fails in Snuba because the column is not on the transactions entity, or returns a meaningless sum. The stats endpoint does not catch SnubaError, so the chart 500s. The unit test only covers the exact strings event.type:error, event.type:transaction, and an empty query, so the false positive is untested.

Only an exact y-axis count() is rewritten; sort, equations, and filters stay raw

transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling replaces a column only when its text is exactly count() (case-insensitive, stripped). In the top-events branch that rewritten list is passed as timeseries_columns / y_axes, but orderby=self.get_orderby(request) is left unchanged, so a normal sort=-count() still ranks groups by the raw count() aggregate while the plotted series is upsampled_count() as count. Top-N groups are chosen by sampled volume, so a low sample rate and high true volume group can be omitted; if the builder treats ORDER BY count() as a different aggregate from the alias, the top-events query errors instead. Equations (equation|count() * 2 and get_equation_list) and aggregate conditions in the query string (count():>N) are not rewritten either, so filters and equation series do not match the upsampled count series. Other count-derived y-axes such as epm() and eps() stay sampled, so one response can show an upsampled count beside a sampled rate. Columns that are already aliased, such as count() as errors, also fail the exact match and silently skip upsampling.

Shared cache around an in-memory option read slows and can fail stats

is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects calls cache.get and cache.set on Sentry's shared cache (Redis in production) on every events-stats query, including each dashboard split subquery, to avoid options.get of issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist. That option read is already a process-local dict lookup, so the cache adds a network round trip on a hot endpoint instead of removing work. Cache errors are not caught here, and OrganizationEventsStatsEndpoint does not catch them either, so a Redis timeout fails the chart. Keys are one per organization plus hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))), which is high-cardinality, and Python hash() is not a collision-resistant digest, so a collision would reuse another project set's allowlist boolean and could enable sum(sample_weight) for a set that is not fully allowlisted. invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called and can delete only one exact key, so it does not flush eligibility after an allowlist change. The docstring on _are_all_projects_error_upsampled, which says each call reads the latest configuration, is false once this 60-second cache is in front of it.

upsampled_count is registered on Discover's function converter without private=True, unlike the neighboring function in the same list (private defaults to false). It therefore becomes a user-facing function on every discover endpoint that shares this converter, not only the allowlisted stats path. Clients can request yAxis=upsampled_count(), or use it in other discover and alert queries, for projects that are not allowlisted and for queries that include transactions. The aggregate itself has no allowlist or dataset guard and always emits sum(sample_weight), so a missing column becomes a Snuba error and the gate in organization_events_stats is bypassable. It also sets default_result_type to number while count() is an integer, so series metadata changes type. If private functions are rejected by the same column parser the stats rewrite uses, marking it private will 400 the rewrite; the weight sum should be applied inside the query builder under the allowlist check rather than exposed as a public function.

This pull request adds a gitlink at sentry-repo pointing at commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a, which is the PR base, and does not add a .gitmodules entry or URL. A submodule pointer without a URL cannot be checked out. git submodule update, CI jobs that clone recursively, and tools that reject unexpected gitlinks will fail, and the link is unrelated to error upsampling. The factory only sets sample_rate to 0.1 and never sets sample_weight to 10, and no test inspects the SnQL or the stored column, so the assertion does not prove upsampling and fails unless an out-of-diff processor inverts the rate. The unit tests never call is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects, never seed or clear the new cache, and never cover !event.type:error, mixed event.type:error OR event.type:transaction, dataset=errors (which the helper always rewrites), events missing sample_weight, or topEvents sorted by count(). Those are the paths that currently mis-apply or skip the rewrite.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

Denial cache key joins name and parent with underscore, so distinct resources collide

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name and parent with "_", but both values are resource UIDs and Grafana UIDs may contain underscores. A deny for dashboard "report" in folder "q1_2024" and a check for dashboard "report_q1" in folder "2024" produce the same key (namespace.perm_<user>_<action>_report_q1_2024). Check treats any hit as definitive deny and does not consult permissions, so one resource's deny is applied to the other for 30 seconds. That is a wrong authorization decision, not just a missed cache optimization.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: userPermDenialCacheKey builds keys by joining components with underscores, which makes keys ambiguous when a component contains an underscore. That can produce collisions and wrong denial cache hits. The candidate gives a concrete example of such a collision.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key drops identity type and collides anonymous with renderer

Check builds the denial-cache key from only the subject id (checkReq.UserUID), not the identity type. This package's own Check tests use subjects "anonymous:0" and "render:0", so both parse to UserUID "0" and share one key for the same namespace, action, name, and folder. The denial lookup at the start of Check returns Allowed:false on any hit, before getRendererPermissions or anonymous permission logic runs. Renderer is supposed to be allowed dashboards:read, folders:read, and datasources:read unconditionally, but an anonymous deny for that dashboard (or the reverse, a renderer deny for an action anonymous is allowed) sticks for shortCacheTTL (30s) and 403s the other identity. Image rendering, alert screenshots, and anonymous access can deny each other.

Sticky denial cache skips the DB refresh and outlives a stale folder tree

A denial-cache hit in Check returns Allowed:false immediately and never reaches the new path that reloads permissions when the cached scope set does not allow the resource. Denials are also stored whenever the post-refresh checkPermission call is false, including when the negative answer came from the cached folder tree rather than from fresh permission rows. checkInheritedPermissions returns false if ParentFolder is missing from that tree, which is exactly the case for a dashboard just created in a new child folder whose access is inherited from an ancestor. Folder cache and denial cache are both 30s, but they are written at different times, and nothing deletes a denial when permissions are later reloaded or the folder tree is rebuilt. So a check that races permission insert, or that runs while the folder tree is stale, keeps 403ing for up to 30s even after a later reload has already cached the grant. That reintroduces the creator lockout this PR is fixing, and a refreshed perm cache cannot override the denial because the denial entry is consulted first.

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

Integrations created before sender was stored, or created by build_integration when pipeline state has no sender, have no sender object. That raises KeyError, or TypeError if sender is null, and the install 500s instead of rendering the installation-failed page. This is exactly the re-link branch (Integration exists, no OrganizationIntegration), so those records cannot be reinstalled. false_positives.candidate:
installation_id is saved before OAuth state is validated

OAuthLoginView writes installation_id into the pipeline with bind_state before it checks that state matches pipeline.signature and before the authorization code is exchanged. bind_state persists the session immediately, and PipelineAdvancerView leaves csrf_protect = False, so a cross-site GET to /extensions/github/setup/?installation_id=<attacker> overwrites an in-progress install even when state is missing or wrong and the view then returns the error page. The later legitimate OAuth callback usually has no installation_id, and GitHubInstallation falls back to that poisoned value (request.GET.get("installation_id", pipeline.fetch_state("installation_id"))). The victim's org is then attached to the attacker's GitHub App installation whenever the sender check is skipped, or their own install is broken if the check runs. Persist installation_id only after state validation succeeds, and do not update pipeline state on the failure path.

User-match check skipped when Integration does not exist

The new control is supposed to reject a mismatch between the OAuth GitHub login and the user who installed the app, but that comparison runs only after an Integration row is already loaded. On Integration.DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation returns pipeline.next_step() with no check. build_integration never reads github_authenticated_user; it fetches /app/installations/{id} with the GitHub App JWT, which can see every installation of this app, not only ones the OAuth user owns. Webhook creation of the Integration races the browser redirect, and any installation whose Sentry row is missing or was deleted takes this path. Combined with installation_id coming from the query string, an attacker can link a chosen GitHub App installation to the current Sentry organization and inherit the app's access to that account's repositories.
