The authorize redirect includes redirect_uri, but the access-token POST only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. GitHub's token endpoint, following RFC 6749 section 4.1.3, requires the same redirect_uri on the token request when it was included in authorization; otherwise it returns an error instead of access_token. This handler then always shows the invalid-installation page, so every install fails after the user authorizes, and that page is the same one used for real verification failures, so a manual check of the error UI does not prove the happy path. The comment says this mirrors OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params, which includes redirect_uri. Tests stub the token URL and ignore the POST body, so they stay green. After the token exchange, get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) is called with no try/except. HTTP errors, network failures, and a non-mapping response propagate as an uncaught exception and a 500, unlike a missing access_token or a bad state, which return the installation-failed page. A GitHub /user failure during install therefore aborts opaquely, and the exception can capture the request that carries the new user access token into error reporting. Catch API failures and treat a missing login the same as the other verification failures.

test_installation_not_found used to assert "The GitHub installation could not be found." when the installation API returned 404. It now calls the callback with state ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which is not the pipeline signature 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3, so it fails the state check and never reaches build_integration. test_github_user_mismatch mutates the installation webhook body (installation id and sender login) but keeps HTTP_X_HUB_SIGNATURE sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486 from the original fixture, so signature verification rejects it when enabled, and then it reuses that same hardcoded state for a second user while asserting only the generic "Invalid installation request." string. That string is also returned for a state mismatch, a bad code, and a missing token, so the test can pass without comparing octocat to sender "attacker" or showing that no OrganizationIntegration was created. The token stub returns access_token regardless of redirect_uri. true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.

With the organization feature on, getById() returns the organization-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() is false unless the IdP is enabled and its organization exists, the organization provider is enabled, and the organization itself is enabled. The previous implementation was the interface default, which returned the delegate getAllStream order. OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean sorts that stream with IDP_COMPARATOR_INSTANCE; List.sort is stable, so providers that compare equal (the usual case when guiOrder is unset or tied, if the comparator has no unique tiebreaker) keep this random order and can swap on the login page on every load. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

Every caller that observed a nil cache—the concurrent first requests this change is meant to protect—runs the manifest load while holding the exclusive lock and then unconditionally assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result. A later waiter whose load fails stores nil and wipes an entry an earlier waiter already published, so following non-dev calls miss the cache and reload. Even when every load succeeds, the missing re-check serializes a full disk read per waiter instead of returning the value the first loader stored. After acquiring the write lock, return the existing cache when Env is not Dev and it is already set, and do not replace a populated cache with a failed nil result.

Cleanup interval accidentally reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

Run() now ticks the background cleanup loop every 1 minute instead of every 10 minutes. Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine and derive its context with context.WithTimeoutCause on the incoming request context (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163). A child context is cancelled as soon as its parent is cancelled, and the apiserver cancels the request context when the handler returns — which is immediately after these methods return success. The 10s timeout therefore never keeps the legacy call alive; Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection run with an already-cancelled context and fail. The new playlist mode 3 integration tests that expect the legacy HTTP API to show k8s writes will fail or flake for the same reason.

The goroutine therefore races with the storage layer and the client. Legacy create can also reject the object because resourceVersion/UID were already set by unified storage, or it can persist a different name than the one returned to the client. The previous Update loaded the unified object, ran objInfo.UpdatedObject once, and passed an updateWrapper so Legacy.Update received the exact object just written to unified storage. That wrapper is gone. Legacy.Update is now invoked with the original objInfo, so it loads the legacy row and re-runs UpdatedObject plus the client's preconditions against that row. Mode 3 serves reads from unified storage, so the resourceVersion on the update is the unified one and will not match legacy; a normal precondition check fails the legacy update with a conflict and the backup copy is never updated. Even if legacy ignores resourceVersion, a patch is applied to drifted legacy state instead of replacing it with the unified result, so the stores diverge. Delete has the same precondition problem: line 112 forwards the caller's DeleteOptions, including a unified-storage resourceVersion precondition, into Legacy.Delete.

Delete returns immediately on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound, and never starts the legacy delete. The previous implementation still deleted from legacy when unified storage returned NotFound, and only treated other errors as fatal. After a failed or cancelled legacy delete, a retry sees NotFound in unified storage (the source of truth for reads) and now leaves the legacy object in place permanently. Orphans also remain for objects that exist only in legacy. NotFound should still be returned to the client, but the async legacy delete should run so the backup store is cleaned up.

Legacy write failures are not logged

The goroutines in Create (line 56), Delete (line 113), Update (line 140), and DeleteCollection (line 166) only feed the legacy error into a duration metric and otherwise discard it. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy create/update/delete/delete-collection failures. With writes now best-effort and easy to cancel, a broken legacy path produces no log line, so operators cannot tell which object diverged or why (conflict, timeout, cancelled context, validation). List (line 87) and Delete (line 102) do the same, and the apierrors.IsNotFound guard that the old Delete used was removed. NotFound on get/delete is a normal client result (the playlist tests even delete twice and expect it). Those calls will flood error logs and hide real storage failures. Log NotFound at a higher verbosity, or not at all, and keep Error for unexpected failures.

Destroy closes Storage and then Legacy immediately and does not track the goroutines started by Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Those goroutines can still be inside Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection after Legacy.Destroy returns, which races with teardown and can panic or hit a closed database. Shutdown also drops the backup writes the goroutines were supposed to finish. A WaitGroup (or similar) should be added around the legacy goroutines and waited on in Destroy before calling Legacy.Destroy.

Unit tests never check that the legacy write happens

Mode 3 success tests register legacy mock expectations but return as soon as the unified call finishes (Create at line 65, and the same pattern in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection) and never call AssertExpectations or wait for the goroutine. The defining behavior — an asynchronous legacy write — is therefore untested, and a cancelled or skipped legacy call still passes. Legacy and unified also share one testify mock, so method names like Create cannot be attributed to a store; the "unified store fails" create case only stubs the legacy Create expectation, which the synchronous storage call consumes by accident. testify mocks are not thread-safe, so the background call can also race or panic after the test function returns.

Mode 3 playlist tests assume legacy is updated before the handler returns

The new mode 3 cases (file at line 132, unified storage at line 191, etcd at line 287) reuse doPlaylistTests. That helper creates, updates, and deletes through the k8s client and then immediately requires the legacy /api/playlists API to match (search at line 529 and getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 returns after the unified write and only then writes legacy on another goroutine whose context is tied to the request. The legacy HTTP read therefore races the backup write and, because that context is cancelled when the request ends, will often never see the object. These new integration cases will fail or flake until the test waits for the legacy write or the dual writer detaches that work from request cancellation.

runSplitQuery now passes every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before querySupportsSplitting. applyTemplateVariables interpolates with TemplateSrv.replace, and during dashboard or Explore queries that replaces $__range, $__range_s, and $__range_ms from the active time range. querySupportsSplitting then calls isQueryWithRangeVariable on that already-substituted expr, so the macro is gone and the query is treated as splittable. The comment on querySupportsSplitting says these queries must not be split: the backend fills $__range from the time range of the request it actually receives, and a split chunk is not the range the user selected. After this change, rate({job="app"}[$__range]) over several days is rewritten to a fixed full-window duration (for example [7d]) and then executed as one-day chunks, each looking back the whole window. Merged results do not match an unsplit query. The new tests cannot catch this: they stub replace to rewrite only $__auto and $step, so $__range stays in the expression under test and the guard still looks like it works. Ad hoc filters are applied on both passes (the old interpolateVariablesInQueries call did not receive request.filters; both new call sites do), so matchers are inserted once before the shard selector is injected and again after. runShardSplitQuery used to interpolate with interpolateVariablesInQueries and then drop targets with an empty expr. It now filters on the raw expr and only then calls applyTemplateVariables. true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

When device_limit is positive, CreateOrUpdateDevice counts rows in one WithDbSession and, if the count is under the limit, inserts in a second WithDbSession. Nothing wraps the two statements in a transaction or takes a lock, and the unique key is only on device_id, so it does not cap the number of rows. Concurrent anonymous requests that all observe count < limit will all insert. With 50 simultaneous new device ids and a limit of 10, all 50 can commit and the table stays at 50; nothing rolls the extras back. That is the multi-instance, multi-user load this cap is meant to control, so AnonymousDeviceLimit is not a hard limit.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race: the count check and the insert are not atomic, so concurrent requests can exceed the device limit. The candidate also mentions the lack of a transaction or lock, which is the golden comment's suggested fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault before CreateOrUpdateDevice, and a cache hit returns nil without touching the database. The cache TTL is 29 minutes and the entry is not removed when tagging fails. Authenticate now treats a nil TagDevice result as success and only denies access for ErrDeviceLimitReached. So the first request from a new device over the limit is rejected, but that rejection is stored as a successful cache entry. Every later request for that device id skips the limit check and is issued an anonymous identity, and the device is never inserted, so it never consumes a slot. A concurrent request can also observe the cache entry and be authenticated before the first request's limit check finishes. After one denial, the cap does not apply to that client for the rest of the TTL, on every instance that has seen it.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug as the golden comment. The cache is set before CreateOrUpdateDevice and is not cleared when ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned. As a result, later requests bypass the device limit for the 29-minute TTL.

false_positives.candidate:
Device limit does not actually gate anonymous access

The new access check only denies authentication when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate then still returns an anonymous identity, when X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent or when web.RemoteAddr cannot be parsed as an IP. Existing tests show client IP is taken from X-Forwarded-For, so a non-IP forwarded-for value forces the parse-failure path even if a device id is sent. Any other tagging error is only logged in client.go and authentication continues, so a request that makes the insert fail is granted access and is not counted. The device id is also chosen by the client, so many users can send one already-accepted id and all pass the update path while occupying a single slot. Omitting the header is enough to use anonymous access with no limit check at all. As written, device_limit does not bound anonymous access.

Provider signature change breaks Wire startup

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService no longer takes an anonstore.AnonStore and now requires db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a bare int64 device-limit argument. Grafana builds the server with Google Wire and commits pkg/server/wire_gen.go; this PR does not update wire.go or wire_gen.go, and the only updated call sites are tests. The generated injector still calls the old signatures, so the server package will not compile. Regenerating Wire also cannot satisfy a raw int64, so ProvideAnonDBStore has to be dropped from the provider set (it is now called internally) or the limit must be injected via *setting.Cfg. Until that is done the binary does not build.

Anonymous auth now waits on the database even when the limit is off

Device tagging used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout and did not block login. Authenticate now calls TagDevice on the request path for every anonymous authentication, including when device_limit is 0, which disables enforcement. A local-cache miss waits for a database write before an identity is returned; a non-zero limit adds a COUNT(*) first, and that count is not cached. The cache is per process, so each instance repeats the work. A slow database delays every new anonymous session, and because the call is synchronous an unauthenticated client can force a count-and-write per request by rotating X-Grafana-Device-Id. Previously that work could not stall the request.

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only inserts one device and asserts that a second new device id returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. It never checks the behavior the new branch claims: an already-registered device must still be updated and accepted once the count is at the limit. A broken updateDevice WHERE clause that rejects every device, including known ones, would still pass. Nothing at the AnonDeviceService or Anonymous.Authenticate level covers the limit either, so the 29-minute cache treating a failed tag as success, and a missing device-id header still receiving an anonymous identity, are both untested. The new test runs on SQLite only, so MySQL/Postgres placeholder or rows-affected differences in the new UPDATE are not exercised.

auth.anonymous.device_limit is read with MustInt64(0) but conf/defaults.ini and the configure-grafana docs are not updated. Operators discover settings from defaults.ini, and generated config docs come from that file, so the new cap is invisible. The code treats 0 as 'do not enforce' rather than 'allow zero devices', and that is not stated anywhere a user will see it. Setting device_limit = 0 to try to disallow anonymous devices silently leaves the limit disabled.

The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

The old allowlist accepted lines like http://eviltrout.com and https://example.com/1234 (the removed SiteSetting.allows_embeddable_host? stripped the scheme before comparing to URI#host; the new model strips scheme and path in before_validation). record_for_host compares only URI#host (example.com) to the stored string, so those migrated rows never match and existing embeds stop working. The same statement interpolates the host in single quotes (VALUES ('#{h}', ...)). A quote in the value is a syntax error that aborts the migration, or arbitrary SQL if the value is crafted. The candidate explicitly calls out the same interpolation in VALUES ('#{h}', ...) as allowing arbitrary SQL and recommends a bound/quoted insert. The file differs (migration vs controller), but the underlying issue is the same interpolated host value.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.

Migration crashes unless embed_category exactly matches a category name

The migration sets category_id from execute("SELECT c.id ... WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'] with no empty-result check. site_settings only stores overridden values, and the default embed_category is a blank string, so a normal install returns zero rows. PG::Result#[] then yields nil and nil['id'] raises NoMethodError, aborting db:migrate before the fallback. The same unguarded [0] is repeated on line 15 for uncategorized_category_id, so that fallback crashes too if the row is missing. false_positives.candidate:
Host allowlist is never copied, then the site settings are deleted

The import is gated on embeddable_hosts.cmd_tuples > 0 after a SELECT. PQcmdTuples returns an empty string for SELECT (use ntuples); the pg gem's to_i makes that 0, so the block that copies hosts never runs. Line 31 still deletes the embeddable_hosts and embed_category site_settings rows. On any database that gets past the category lookup (embed_category equal to a category name), a successful migration therefore drops the existing allowlist and leaves embeddable_hosts empty. Embedding then fails closed for every previously allowed host, and the old values are gone.

Host regex rejects real hostnames the old setting allowed

validates_format_of requires a dotted name whose final label is [a-z]{2,5}. That rejects legitimate embed hosts: TLDs longer than 5 characters (forum.museum, site.photography, and other gTLDs), IPv4 addresses, and localhost. The previous embeddable_hosts setting was a host list compared as hostnames, not this pattern, so those values can no longer be saved from the admin UI and cannot be allow-listed. The same regex's port and path alternatives are misleading: before_validation strips the path but not the port, and a stored port never matches URI#host (see record_for_host).

No uniqueness on host, so category assignment is nondeterministic

embeddable_hosts.host is not unique, and EmbeddableHost has no uniqueness validation (the format regex is case-insensitive, so Example.com and example.com are both valid). The admin UI can save the same host twice with different categories. record_for_host uses where(...).first with no ORDER BY, so topic import and the embed allow-check attach an arbitrary category. Add a unique index on lower(host) and a validation that returns a JSON error instead of a duplicate row.

Save paints category from the client id, ignoring the server default

After host.save resolves, the component sets host.category to Discourse.Category.findById(this.get('categoryId')) and does not use the payload. New rows start with categoryId null, and cantSave only checks the host string, so saving without touching the category chooser is allowed. The server replaces a blank category_id with SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id and returns that id. findById(null) does not return the uncategorized category, so the row leaves edit mode with an empty category badge even though a category was stored. The same overwrite drops the badge whenever categoryId does not resolve, which is the default path for the host/category editor this PR adds.

Plural id hydration throws when the ids value is null

A null embeddable_host_ids (or any other null *_ids key) raises TypeError and rejects store.find / findAll for the parent record. The singular _id branch already no-ops when lookup fails; the plural branch should treat null or a non-array as an empty list instead of throwing.

New controller and migration behavior are not tested

Admin::EmbeddableHostsController and Admin::EmbeddingController specs only assert the class is a subclass of AdminController. They never POST/PUT/DELETE, so a missing record 500, a nil host 500, invalid hosts, and duplicate hosts are untested. There is no migration spec, so the unguarded embed_category lookup, the cmd_tuples check that skips the copy, and the raw INSERT of scheme-prefixed hosts are not caught. EmbeddableHost specs cover scheme/path trimming on the model but not record_for_host with a port, mixed-case referer, or nil host. The topic expandable_first_post? example titled as failing when no embeddable host exists no longer sets that condition; the method only checks embed_truncate and has_topic_embed?, so the example passes for the wrong reason.

Those model methods only call findMembers on success and have no failure path. save and destroy in this same controller show a bootbox alert. A 400, 422 from an automatic group, or 500 therefore leaves the list unchanged with no message, so the admin cannot tell a failure from a no-op. next and previous also write offset before findMembers resolves, so a failed page load leaves the pager on a page whose members were never fetched. true_positives.golden_comment: The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Members action requires group_id but the route sets id

The rewritten members action still calls find_group(:group_id), and find_group does params.require on that key. The route is get "members" inside resources :groups, i.e. GET /groups/:id/members, so the group name arrives in params[:id]. show in this same controller correctly uses find_group(:id); posts and counts have the same mismatch. Group#findMembers requests /groups/:name/members.json and only sends limit and offset, not group_id. The action 400s before it can return the new members/meta payload, so both the admin member list and the public members page stay empty. Use find_group(:id).
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: the members action reads params[:group_id] while the route supplies params[:id], so group memberships cannot be loaded.

false_positives.candidate:
remove_member passes an integer to association delete

remove_member calls group.users.delete(user_id) with a raw integer. On Rails 4, CollectionAssociation#delete type-checks its arguments and raises ActiveRecord::AssociationTypeMismatch (User expected, got Fixnum) instead of deleting the group_users join row. Once the group_id param bug is fixed, removing a member still 500s and the user stays in the group. The new spec expects 200 and a user count of 0, so it fails if run. Load the user and call group.remove(user), which is what the previous membership update path used, or pass a User record to delete.

Public members page cannot show past the first 50 users

The public members route only calls model.findMembers() once, and Group#findMembers always sends limit 50 (the model default). groups/members.hbs has no pager and does not show the new meta.total. GroupsController#members now applies that limit to every group. Previously non-automatic groups returned every member and automatic groups defaulted to 200. Anyone opening a group with more than 50 members sees a silently truncated list and has no way to load the rest. The admin screen has next/previous; this page does not. Either paginate here or request a limit large enough to preserve the old full list.

Create ignores alias_level the form submits

create sets name and visible but never alias_level. The new-group form shows the alias-level combo outside the id check, and Group#asJSON posts alias_level on create. The column stays at the default 0 (nobody can mention the group). The client only copies resp.basic_group.id back onto the model, so the UI keeps the level the admin chose and then transitions to the group page. They have no reason to hit Save again; after a reload the mention permission has reverted. update does persist alias_level. The create spec only checks that the name is stripped.

Member reloads use the unsaved group name

findMembers requests /groups/ plus this.get('name') plus /members.json. In the admin form the name text field is two-way bound to that same property, and pagination, add, and remove all call findMembers before Save. An edited but unsaved name is sent to the server. If it matches no group the reload 404s and the member list fails with no error UI (next/previous have already moved offset). If it matches a different group, that group's members are shown on this group's screen while add/remove still target this group's numeric id, so the admin can change the wrong memberships. Fetch with the persisted name, not the in-progress field.

Enter in the group form activates Add instead of Save

The admin group editor is now wrapped in a form, but Add, Save, and Delete are button elements with no type attribute, so they default to submit. On an existing non-automatic group the first submit button is Add. Pressing Enter in the name field (or the user selector) activates Add rather than Save: members are added, or addMembers returns immediately because the username box is empty, and the name, visibility, and alias level are not saved. Delete is also a submit button. Set type="button" on these action buttons. If the action helper does not preventDefault, the browser will also GET-submit the form to the current URL and reload the page, dropping unsaved edits.

Spaced usernames are skipped and add still succeeds

add_members splits the usernames string on commas and calls User.find_by_username on each token without stripping. A space after a comma, which is normal when typing into the selector ("alice, bob"), does not match username_lower, so that user is not added. Unknown names are skipped the same way. If group.save then succeeds, the action still renders success_json even when nobody was added. The admin UI reloads the current page and does not clear the input (the controller has a TODO for that), so the add looks successful. The endpoint is available to anyone who can see the group. limit=1000000 loads and serializes every member of a large automatic group such as trust_level_0 in one response, which is a straightforward DoS. offset=-1 or limit=-1 makes PostgreSQL reject the statement (OFFSET/LIMIT must not be negative) and the action returns 500. GET /groups/:name/members.json used to return a top-level JSON array of users (the previous client called result.map on it). It now returns an object with members and meta. When limit is omitted the action also returns at most 50 rows instead of the full roster for custom groups or the previous default of 200 for automatic groups. In-repo callers in this PR were updated, but external API clients, scripts, and plugins that still expect an array will throw or stop listing members, and callers that omitted limit silently lose everyone past 50. There is no version flag or fallback to the old shape.
